cbi-pre-1.title: Identifying Barriers
summary: Agreeing that treatment costs something lowers resistance faster than arguing that it does not.
Inside barriers are thoughts and feelings; outside barriers are circumstances and logistics.
Outside barriers get problem solving; inside barriers get spotting and replacing thinking later in the program.
Responsivity factors (age, culture, history with the system) can make someone look less motivated than they are.
Rules the members write themselves are rules they are more likely to keep.

items.stem: First group. Dante says, "This program is a waste. I lose my canteen job hours to sit here." The facilitator answers, "You find time for everything else." What is Dante most likely to do for the rest of the hour?
options: Ask for extra worksheets to prove the point wrong
Open up, since the facilitator was direct with him
Shut down or push back
Thank the facilitator for the honest feedback
items.explain: A put-down reply confirms the suspicion that the program is against him. Validating the real cost would have kept the door open.

items.stem: During the roadblock list, Lorenzo says, "Honestly, I don't need this. I've been clean six months inside." What is the best facilitator move?
options: Reflect it and add it to the inside-barrier list
Point out that being locked up is not the same as staying clean outside
Skip him and come back when he is ready
Ask the group whether they agree with Lorenzo
items.explain: In this session a claim of not needing help is data about readiness, not defiance to correct. Reflecting it and writing it down keeps him in the exercise.

items.stem: Nia says, "The bus from the halfway house takes ninety minutes and my shift ends at four." Which kind of barrier is this?
options: An outside barrier
A thinking error to challenge right away
An inside barrier, because it shows low motivation
A responsivity factor that the facilitator should ignore
items.explain: Transport and schedules are situations, not attitudes. They are handled by listing options and choosing one, the way the practice work does.

items.stem: Carl says, "Every time I sit in a group I feel like they are judging me." Which kind of barrier is this?
options: An outside barrier about the room setup
A rule violation to address now
Not a barrier, just small talk
An inside barrier rooted in a feeling and a belief
items.explain: It lives in his thoughts and feelings. Inside barriers are later worked on by noticing and replacing the thinking behind them.

items.stem: A rookie quarterback has a coach who runs a confusing playbook and also believes he chokes in big games. Which split matches the lesson?
options: Both are inside barriers because he controls his reactions
Both are outside barriers because the coach caused them
Playbook outside, "I choke" inside
Neither counts, since sports are not treatment
items.explain: The distinction is about where the obstacle lives, not the setting. A circumstance calls for problem solving; a belief calls for working on the thinking.

items.stem: Elijah, 58, has done three prior programs that ended in violations. He sits arms crossed and answers in one word. What is the most useful read?
options: He is testing whether rules will be enforced
He probably cannot read the worksheet
Past experience may be driving distrust
He has no motivation and should be referred out
items.explain: Age, background and past experience with the system shape how people engage. Treating guardedness as zero motivation can be a misread.

items.stem: A younger member jokes constantly while two older members roll their eyes. The facilitator wants everyone to engage. What fits the lesson best?
options: Ask the younger member to leave until he is serious
Pair older members as mentors and tell them to fix his attitude
Invite each to name what makes this hard, in his own terms
Ignore it, since group dynamics are not part of pre-treatment
items.explain: Responsivity means adjusting delivery to who is in the room. Inviting each person to name barriers their own way respects those differences.

items.stem: Ramona's group wrote "no side talk" on their own rules list. Halfway through, two members start whispering. What is likely to work best?
options: A warning that the program rules forbid it
Moving the whispering members apart without comment
A reminder that this was a rule the group itself chose
Ending the session early
items.explain: Rules the members wrote belong to them, so pointing back to their own agreement carries more weight than an outside rule.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session have members write the group rules instead of handing them a list?
items.explain: Rules the group writes become its own, which builds buy-in and lowers the sense that the program is imposing control. The facilitator still makes sure essentials like confidentiality and punctuality land on the list.
key_points: Lowers resistance from people forced into treatment
Facilitator steers until key rules appear

items.stem: In your own words, why does this session treat outside barriers with problem solving rather than motivation talk?
items.explain: An outside barrier is a real circumstance, so pep talks do not move it. Listing options and choosing the best one gives a concrete path and a first taste of the problem-solving skill used later.
key_points: Practice work rehearses brainstorm and choose

items.stem: A nurse keeps missing her night-school class because her daycare closes at six. A friend tells her she just needs to want it more. Using the lesson, what is the flaw?
options: The friend should confront her excuses more firmly
The nurse should drop the class to avoid stress
The friend is right; motivation solves logistics
It treats a logistics problem as a willpower problem
items.explain: Outside barriers are fixed by changing the situation. Telling someone to want it more misreads where the obstacle lives.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says, "I can't afford the fees, but I always have money for weed." Another member points out the contradiction before you can respond. Should you let the peer challenge stand?
items.explain: No single verdict. Peer honesty can land harder than a facilitator's, but in a first session it can feel like an ambush and harden resistance.
key_points: Letting it stand: peers carry credibility and it is true
Redirecting: this session's job is validation, and confrontation now usually backfires
Middle path: acknowledge both the cost and the observation, then turn it into a problem to solve later

cbi-pre-2.title: Personal Reasons to Engage
summary: Readiness needs two things: the change matters to me (importance) and I can do it (confidence).
Low importance calls for awareness and rethinking; low confidence calls for practice and small wins.
Rating how use helped and hurt each life area produces a normal, useful mixed picture.
Starring the three areas that matter most points the conversation where motivation lives.
Nobody is pushed to admit a reason to change; forcing it builds defensiveness.

items.stem: Tasha says, "Getting my daughter back is everything to me, but I have failed every program they put me in." What is her readiness profile?
options: High on both
Low importance, high confidence
High importance, low confidence
Low on both
items.explain: She clearly values the goal but doubts her ability. That gap calls for skill practice and early wins, not more reasons why it matters.

items.stem: Brandon says, "I could quit tomorrow if I felt like it. I just don't see why I should." What is his readiness profile?
options: High confidence, low importance
Ready for action
High importance, low confidence
Ambivalent on both, so no read is possible
items.explain: He believes he can but does not see the point yet. The work is raising awareness and reconsidering priorities, as the life-area ratings do.

items.stem: A member rates importance 9 and confidence 2. What should the facilitator emphasize with him?
options: More information about the harms of use
Small steps he can succeed at
A referral to a higher level of care
A stronger push to commit in front of the group
items.explain: Low confidence is built by doing and succeeding. More reasons to change would not close the gap he has.

items.stem: A historian notes that a 19th-century reformer believed in abolition deeply but felt powerless until she joined a local society that gave her one small, doable task. Which readiness gap did the society address?
options: Importance and confidence equally
Confidence, by giving her a manageable action that worked
Neither; she was simply ambivalent
Importance, by reminding her why abolition mattered
items.explain: She already valued the cause. A small, achievable task builds self-efficacy, which is the confidence side of readiness.

items.stem: Javier rates drinking +2 for "relaxing" and "fitting in" and -3 for work and his marriage. When the facilitator asks about it, what is he most likely to feel?
options: Torn, and the costs feel more real
Embarrassed that he rated anything positive
Sure that drinking was all bad
Annoyed that the sheet allows positive ratings
items.explain: Admitting the real benefits makes the exercise honest. A mixed picture is normal and gives the costs more credibility than a lecture would.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the worksheet let members score substance use as helping some life areas?
items.explain: Use did serve real functions for many people, and pretending otherwise makes the exercise feel like propaganda. Admitting benefits builds trust and sets up an honest comparison with the costs.
key_points: Benefits reveal the needs use was meeting

items.stem: Malik stars freedom, his kids and housing. The facilitator spends the discussion on his health ratings instead. What is likely to happen?
options: Malik engages more because health is important
Nothing changes; any area works equally
He re-stars health to please the facilitator
His interest fades
items.explain: Motivation sits where the person's priorities are. Steering toward the facilitator's priority wastes the starring step.

items.stem: A financial coach asks clients to circle the three goals they care most about before building a budget. Why does that mirror this session?
options: Because circles are easier to read than lists
It proves the coach knows best
It lets the coach skip the rest of the budget
It aims effort where motivation already is
items.explain: Starring the top areas works in any field: change talk is strongest around what the person values most.

items.stem: Cole leaves every "how change could help" line blank and says, "None of this applies to me." Best move?
options: Tell him he is in denial
Accept it and lift up what peers name
Ask the group to help him find reasons
Fill in a couple of examples for him so he gets the idea
items.explain: Pushing him to admit reasons triggers defensiveness. Accepting his answer and amplifying peers keeps him in the room and lets ideas reach him indirectly.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member who stays silent all session is due in court next week, and his attorney wants proof he engaged. Should the facilitator press him harder to name one reason to change?
items.explain: No single verdict. Pressure may produce a statement for the record, but it could be hollow and erode trust.
key_points: Press: a stated reason could help him and may plant a seed
Hold back: forced change talk tends to provoke pushback
Alternative: meet one-on-one and ask a softer, open question

items.stem: In your own words, why does each reason to change get paired with a personal goal?
items.explain: A reason by itself is a wish; tying it to a goal turns it into a direction to act on. The goal must also improve life without hurting anyone, which keeps it prosocial.

items.stem: Luis writes: "If my mother trusted me again" and then "Call her every Sunday and keep my word on small things." What has he done?
options: Made a cost-benefit analysis
Written a relapse plan
Listed a barrier and a coping skill
Linked a reason to change to a concrete personal goal
items.explain: The pairing of a reason with a matching goal that harms no one is exactly the move the session teaches.

cbi-pre-3.title: Weighing the Pros and Cons
summary: Mixed feelings about treatment are a good sign: they show the person sees some payoff.
Four boxes lay out the near and far gains and prices of keeping things as they are versus changing.
Healthy choices usually pay later; risky ones usually pay now and cost later.
Costs of staying the same and benefits of change are motivators; the other two boxes are barriers.
The facilitator stays neutral and never supplies anyone's pros or cons.

items.stem: Andre says, "I hate coming here, but my PO is easier on me now and that budgeting thing last week actually helped." What is this?
options: Ambivalence, which shows he sees some payoff
Readiness for action
A thinking error called minimizing
Resistance that needs confronting
items.explain: Mixed feelings mean part of him sees value. That tension is the raw material for change.

items.stem: A facilitator treats Andre's "I hate coming here" as a problem to fix and debates him. What is most likely?
options: The rest of the group starts debating for him
Andre drops the complaint and engages fully
Andre asks for more homework
He digs in on the negative side
items.explain: Arguing one side of ambivalence pushes the person to argue the other. Exploring both sides lets the pro-change side grow.

items.stem: "If I keep skipping group, tonight I get to sleep in." Which box does this belong in?
options: Short-term cost of changing
Short-term benefit of staying the same
Long-term cost of staying the same
Long-term benefit of changing
items.explain: Sleeping in is an immediate perk of the current behavior, which belongs in Part 1, short-term benefits.

items.stem: "If I really do this program, I'll have to give up the guys I hang with, at least for a while." Which box fits?
options: Short-term benefit of changing
Long-term cost of staying the same
Short-term cost of changing
Long-term benefit of staying the same
items.explain: Losing the old crowd is a price paid soon for the new behavior, so it sits in Part 2 as a short-term cost.

items.stem: In the fable of the ant and the grasshopper, the grasshopper sings all summer while the ant stores food. In this lesson's terms, what is the grasshopper's pattern?
options: Long-term benefit, short-term cost
Short-term cost, long-term cost
A balanced cost-benefit choice
Short-term benefit, long-term cost
items.explain: The grasshopper enjoys the now and pays later, the same shape the lesson gives to risky or illegal behavior.

items.stem: A startup founder ships a product early with known bugs to beat a rival. Which framing does the lesson give you to think about it?
options: Only long-term outcomes count
Weigh near and far consequences of both paths
Short-term gains always outweigh long-term ones in business
It is always wrong, so no analysis is needed
items.explain: The four-box tool works anywhere: it lays the near and far consequences of both options side by side instead of judging one moment.

items.stem: When the group charts results, five members check "my kids see me as stable" under benefits of changing. What should that tell the facilitator?
options: The group is saying what the facilitator wants to hear
It is a shared motivator to explore
It is a cliché and should be set aside
Those members are already in maintenance
items.explain: Benefits of change are motivators, and items many members mark show where group energy toward change sits.

items.stem: In your own words, which boxes push toward change and which hold people back?
items.explain: The costs of staying the same and the benefits of changing push toward change. The perks of the old way and the costs of change hold people back.
key_points: Motivators: costs of status quo, benefits of change
Barriers: perks of status quo, costs of change

items.stem: Hector stares at his blank "costs of staying the same" box. The facilitator knows his record well. Best move?
options: Tell him to finish it as homework
Ask what he might lose if nothing changes
Write "more prison time" in the box to get him started
Read out other members' answers for him to copy
items.explain: Supplying costs makes members passive and can sound like judgment. An open question lets him find his own.

items.stem: A member lists six reasons the old way works for him and asks, "Can you help me think of more?" What should the facilitator do?
options: Refuse and tell him the exercise is about change
Help him, since the exercise values honesty
Acknowledge it, add nothing, turn to the other boxes
Say his reasons are excuses
items.explain: The facilitator stays neutral but does not help build the case for the status quo. Turning toward the unfilled boxes keeps balance.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member lists "selling pays my mother's rent" as a long-term benefit of staying the same. Should the facilitator let it stand unchallenged?
items.explain: No single verdict. The benefit is real to him, and challenging it could end the conversation, but leaving it alone may seem like approval.
key_points: Let it stand: what counts as a benefit is personal; neutrality builds trust
Explore: ask what else could meet the same need, without arguing
Watch: the long-term cost boxes may carry the weight on their own

items.stem: In your own words, what marks a member in the preparation stage, and why is that today's target?
items.explain: They weigh the pros of changing above the cons, feel more confident, are less tempted, and are starting to plan. People there are the most likely to engage in treatment.

items.stem: Gina says, "The pluses of doing this outweigh the minuses now. I've already asked my sister to watch the baby on group nights." Which stage does this suggest?
options: Contemplation, since she is still weighing it
Precontemplation
Maintenance
Preparation
items.explain: Pros above cons plus concrete planning is the mark of preparation, the point the session aims to move members toward.

cbi-1.title: Introduction to the Curriculum
summary: Thoughts drive feelings and actions, so changing thinking changes behavior.
The group itself is a treatment ingredient: members practice skills in the room first.
Resistance is information and shifts as importance and confidence change.
Motivation needs concrete skills, which is why every session practices one.
The Success Plan works like a relapse-prevention plan built across the program.

items.stem: In chow line someone bumps Kenji's tray. If Kenji thinks "He's disrespecting me in front of everyone," what is he most likely to do next?
options: Report it to staff calmly
Feel guilty about his own clumsiness
Shrug it off
Feel anger and confront the man
items.explain: The thought sets the feeling and the action. A disrespect interpretation pushes toward anger and confrontation.

items.stem: Same bump, but Kenji thinks "Guy looks exhausted, it was an accident." What is he most likely to feel?
options: Fear for his safety
Mild irritation that passes quickly
Shame
Anger he has to work hard to hold back
items.explain: The event did not change; the interpretation did. This is the core cognitive-behavioral idea of the program.

items.stem: Two violinists hit the same wrong note in a recital. One thinks "I ruined it," the other "Keep going, nobody will remember one note." Which outcome does the lesson predict?
options: The first plays better because the stakes feel higher
The outcome depends only on talent
The second recovers faster
Both play equally well afterward
items.explain: Identical events, different thoughts, different feelings and actions. That is the model that later sessions train.

items.stem: In the first session a member says icebreakers are childish and wants to get to "the real stuff." Best response?
options: Ignore him
Briefly say trust is part of how the program works
Insist and make him go first
Agree, skip the icebreaker and go straight into the curriculum content
items.explain: Cohesion is a working ingredient, since members practice social skills in the room. A short explanation gives the reason without a lecture.

items.stem: In your own words, why is group cohesion treated as part of treatment rather than a nice extra?
items.explain: Members rehearse social skills with each other and get feedback before using them outside. Without trust and respect, that practice stalls and people hide.

items.stem: A member who did pre-treatment groans, "We already did this." The facilitator says, "You did. Where would you rate yourself now?" What is likely to happen?
options: The group demands to skip ahead
He refuses to answer
He rates himself, and the rerun becomes data
He feels called out for repeating and stops participating for the night
items.explain: Motivation changes, so a rerun is a chance to measure. Acknowledging the repetition removes the reason to resist.

items.stem: "I'll do your program, but I'm telling you, it's not going to change anything." How does this lesson frame the statement?
options: Readiness information that can shift
A sign he is not appropriate for the group and needs a different referral
A refusal to participate
A thinking error to confront now
items.explain: Resistance is read as a signal about readiness, not as defiance to beat.

items.stem: A new manager is fired up to give feedback but freezes when an employee pushes back. In this lesson's terms, what was missing?
options: A rehearsed skill for the hard moment
A clear goal
Motivation
Values
items.explain: Wanting to act is not enough without tools. The program builds and rehearses a skill every session for the same reason.

items.stem: Ray truly wants to stay away from his old crew. Friday night, one of them calls with a party invite. Ray has never practiced what to say. What is most likely?
options: He calls his PO for help
He declines smoothly because his motivation is strong
He blocks the number without thinking
He gets talked into "just stopping by"
items.explain: Under pressure, people fall back on what they have rehearsed. Without a practiced refusal, motivation often loses.

items.stem: In your own words, describe the Success Plan and why must members keep their worksheets?
items.explain: It is a roadmap for after the program that pairs specific risks with specific ways to handle them, much like a relapse-prevention plan. It is built from marked worksheets across all modules, so a lost sheet has to be redone.
key_points: Missing sheets leave holes in the plan

items.stem: A member says he tossed last week's worksheet because it was "just homework." What does the facilitator explain?
options: That sheet feeds his Success Plan, so he will need to redo it
Worksheets are only for the facilitator's records, so it does not matter much
He can borrow someone else's
Nothing; homework is optional
items.explain: Marked worksheets are building blocks of the final plan, which is why they are kept.

items.stem: Weigh it: during introductions a member says, "I only had a couple beers, the cop was out to get me." Should the facilitator address the minimizing now?
items.explain: No single verdict. Letting it pass protects early cohesion, but the group might hear it as accepted.
key_points: Hold: confronting in session one tends to breed resistance
Note it: the minimizing will be worked on in thinking sessions later
Risk: others may follow with their own minimizing stories

cbi-2.title: Creating an Emergency Plan
summary: An emergency plan only works if rehearsed until it is automatic.
Cravings are normal, common, time-limited and a sign of change.
Each person needs several distraction and calming tools that fit different settings.
Deep breathing with a longer exhale calms the body and pulls attention off risky thoughts.
Pleasant imagery and positive self-talk must stay clear of using, crime or sex.

items.stem: Omar read about deep breathing but never practiced it. At a tense family dinner his brother brings up an old debt. What is most likely?
options: He teaches his brother the technique
He leaves calmly to practice it
He uses the breathing well, because reading about it once is usually enough
He forgets the tool in the moment and reacts on autopilot
items.explain: Like stop, drop and roll, a crisis tool needs rehearsal so it shows up without thinking.

items.stem: Why do pilots drill engine-failure procedures in simulators again and again?
options: Mainly to satisfy insurance and regulatory paperwork
Because they forget easily
So the response is automatic when there is no time to think
To make flying boring
items.explain: Emergency responses must be overlearned. The same reasoning drives practicing every craving tool in session.

items.stem: "I had a craving this morning, so this program obviously isn't working." Which craving fact does this miss?
options: Strong cravings mean the person was never really ready
Cravings are normal and signal change
Cravings last for days
Cravings only happen to heavy users
items.explain: Cravings are expected, especially early. Riding one out weakens the trigger's hold.

items.stem: On payday Shawna feels a strong urge. She tells herself, "This will peak and pass," and goes for a walk. What usually happens?
options: The urge rises, peaks and fades within a limited time
The urge stays at the same strength until something else replaces it
The walk causes a stronger urge later
The urge grows until she uses
items.explain: Cravings are time-limited. Each one ridden out without using reduces the pull of that trigger next time.

items.stem: In your own words, why is it useful to call a craving "a sign of change"?
items.explain: Cravings show up because the person is not giving the brain what it expects. Seeing them that way turns a scary signal into evidence of progress, which lowers panic and shame.
key_points: Riding one out weakens the trigger

items.stem: A member's only distraction tool is push-ups. He starts a job at a warehouse next month. What does the facilitator help him do?
options: Tell him push-ups will work anywhere
Wait until Module 4
Add options that fit a job site
Drop distraction for medication
items.explain: Strategies must fit the setting. Several options give coverage when one is not possible.

items.stem: A traveling salesperson manages stress with her home gym. On the road for two weeks, her stress spikes. What principle explains the spike?
options: She needed more motivation
Gyms are not real coping
She relied on one tool that did not travel with her
Travel stress is mostly physical, so coping tools would not have helped
items.explain: One tool is fragile. A menu of options for different places is what the lesson builds.

items.stem: Which instruction matches the breathing taught here?
options: Slow in through the nose, longer slow exhale
Take a deep breath in, hold it, and push it out fast to release tension
Quick, shallow breaths through the mouth
Breathe normally and count to ten
items.explain: The longer exhale is the key detail; it calms the body signs of rising emotion.

items.stem: Waiting outside his PO's office, Dimitri feels his heart race. He does five slow breaths with long exhales. What is likely?
options: He becomes sleepy and misses the meeting
No change, since breathing only works lying down
He calms somewhat and his focus shifts
His anxiety doubles
items.explain: Slow breathing targets the physical side of rising emotion and gives a mental break from risky thoughts.

items.stem: During pleasant imagery a member describes a beach party with drinks and old friends. Best move?
options: Gently redirect to a trigger-free scene
Tell him he is not taking it seriously
Let him finish, then discuss with the group why the scene might be risky
Let him continue; any calm scene counts
items.explain: Imagery must be free of triggers, or it rehearses the urge instead of calming it.

items.stem: A member says closing his eyes in a room full of men feels unsafe. What fits the lesson?
options: Offer eyes open, gaze on the floor
Ask the group to promise not to look
Excuse him from the exercise entirely
Insist, since the exercise needs closed eyes
items.explain: For people with trauma histories or in institutional settings, an eyes-open option keeps the tool usable.

items.stem: Weigh it: Victor's self-talk line is "I'm stronger than this, I don't need anyone." It helps him in the moment. Should the facilitator nudge him to change it?
items.explain: No single verdict. The line builds confidence, but it may undercut asking for support later in the program.
key_points: Keep: it is his own words and it works now
Adjust: add a line that pairs strength with reaching out
Watch: whether it is used to avoid support people

items.stem: A marathoner at mile 20 tells herself, "I've finished three of these; I can do six more miles." Which tool from this session is she using?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation
Distraction
Positive self-talk drawing on past success
Pleasant imagery
items.explain: Reminding yourself of past wins to get through the present is the self-talk tool, the same move as "I made it 60 days, I can get through tonight."

cbi-3.title: Values Clarification
summary: Values are what a person finds important; they steer goals and the life they pursue.
Cognitive dissonance, the discomfort when actions clash with values, can fuel change.
The same value can drive prosocial or antisocial behavior.
Acting on one value can undercut another.
The facilitator reflects gaps but stays neutral, and stops peers from confronting.

items.stem: "I tell everybody I'm a good father, but I missed my son's birthday because I was high." What is he experiencing?
options: A thinking error, since he is judging himself too harshly
An outside barrier
Cognitive dissonance between a value and a behavior
Ambivalence about attending group
items.explain: The tension between who he says he is and what he did is dissonance, which this session surfaces on purpose.

items.stem: Once Rafael sees that his use clashes with his top value, honesty, what are the two most likely ways he resolves the discomfort?
options: Lower the rank of honesty so his cards match how he lives
Change the behavior or justify it
He will feel nothing
Forget the exercise
items.explain: Dissonance pushes toward consistency. People either change the action or rationalize it, which is why the facilitator highlights change-leaning statements.

items.stem: Festinger's classic study observed a group whose predicted end of the world did not come. Some core members grew more committed, not less. What does that show about dissonance?
options: Dissonance always leads to change
People may resolve it by justifying rather than changing
Groups protect members from feeling dissonance at all
Beliefs never respond to evidence
items.explain: Dissonance creates pressure, but rationalizing is one way out. A facilitator's job is to support the change path without forcing it.

items.stem: Marcus and Tyrell both rank family first. Marcus sells drugs "for the kids"; Tyrell refuses any crime because it could cost him his kids. What does this teach a facilitator?
options: Tyrell is more motivated by fear
A shared value can drive opposite actions
Values do not matter, only behavior
Marcus does not truly value family; he is using it as an excuse
items.explain: Sharing a value does not guarantee the same actions. The work is exploring how a person acts on it.

items.stem: Two generals both value loyalty. One protects his soldiers by retreating; the other refuses to retreat to honor fallen comrades, and more die. What lesson idea fits?
options: One value can drive very different actions, with very different outcomes
The second general valued loyalty more, which is why he held his ground
The first general lacked loyalty
Loyalty is a bad value
items.explain: Values guide but do not dictate behavior. Examining how each acts on loyalty is the useful step.

items.stem: Keisha loves excitement and also values staying free for her kids. She shoplifts "for the rush." What is this?
options: An external barrier
Two values in harmony
A sign that her values are unclear and need to be clarified first
Acting on one value undercutting another
items.explain: The thrill-seeking value collides with freedom and family. Seeing that collision is part of the session.

items.stem: A member says, "I value loyalty, so I'll never testify against my friends, even if it means more time." Best facilitator move?
options: Ask the group to vote on whether he is right
Reflect it, then ask how it fits his other values
Tell him loyalty to criminals is not a real value
Agree that loyalty matters most and move on so the group stays calm
items.explain: Staying neutral while inviting him to weigh his own values lets him notice any conflict for himself.

items.stem: Donnell places his "weed" card third, above his job. What is the most useful facilitator read?
options: It shows how much use matters to him now
He is mocking the exercise
The activity failed for him
He misunderstood, so the facilitator should have him redo the sort
items.explain: A high placement is information, not failure. It gives material to explore with curiosity.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the card sort include a card naming the person's substance?
items.explain: Placing it among their values shows how much room the substance takes in their life and makes conflicts visible. The person sees the clash themselves instead of being told.

items.stem: Two members start telling a third that his stack "makes no sense" because family should be first. Best move?
options: Let it run briefly, since peers often say what staff cannot
Interrupt and refocus on each person's own stack
Ask the third member to rearrange his cards
Let them; peer feedback is powerful
items.explain: Confrontation, even from peers, produces defensiveness. Each person's ranking stays theirs.

items.stem: In your own words, why spend a whole session on values before teaching thinking skills?
items.explain: Values give the reasons to use the skills. Later sessions tie consequences back to what members care about, so knowing their values makes the rest of the program personal.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member names "respect" as his top value and explains that respect means never backing down. Should the facilitator explore a different meaning of respect?
items.explain: No single verdict. Offering a different meaning might open new behavior, but it could feel like replacing his value with yours.
key_points: Explore: ask what respect has cost and earned him, letting him redefine it
Hold: neutrality means not editing his values
Use later: the anger and assertiveness sessions revisit it

items.stem: Ines ranks "education" as a top value. Six months after release, which choice is she most likely to put energy into?
options: Taking the highest-paying job regardless of hours
Whatever her friends are doing that week
Enrolling in a GED or college class, even when it is inconvenient
Avoiding any commitments until she feels ready
items.explain: Values steer goals and daily choices. Knowing someone's top values lets you predict where they will invest effort.

items.stem: A facilitator tells a member, "Family should come before partying, don't you think?" What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing; it is an open question
The facilitator's own values are steering the member
It is fine as long as the tone is warm
The facilitator should have asked the group instead
items.explain: A leading question imposes the facilitator's ranking. Neutral reflection lets the discovery belong to the member.

cbi-4.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis
summary: Leaving an antisocial lifestyle is a long string of small daily choices, not one fork in the road.
Risky and illegal choices tend to pay now and cost later; prosocial ones tend to cost now and pay later.
Members name the real perks of the risky behavior themselves; if it paid nothing they would not do it.
Warmth and empathy lower resistance and dropout more than persuasion does.
The analysis ends by tying the choice to a value and a goal with concrete steps.

items.stem: Three weeks out, Terrence has ignored his old connect's texts every day. Tonight he is tired and the text says "first one's free." What does the lesson suggest about tonight?
options: His choice depends mostly on luck
Tonight barely matters because his streak shows he has already changed for good
Tonight decides everything; one slip erases three weeks
It is one more choice in a long series, and each one shifts the balance
items.explain: The lesson frames change as many small decisions. The aim is for healthy ones to outnumber unhealthy ones, not a single heroic moment.

items.stem: A novelist finishes a book by writing 300 words a day for a year. How does that mirror this session's view of change?
options: Daily goals are less reliable than yearly ones
Only talent determines whether change sticks
Many small repeated choices add up to a new way of living
Big results usually come from one inspired burst of effort
items.explain: Change is built from a long series of ordinary choices, the same arithmetic the session applies to leaving an old lifestyle.

items.stem: "Selling gets me rent money this week, but if I get caught I lose years." What timing pattern is this?
options: Benefit now, cost later
Cost now, benefit later
Costs and benefits both arrive right away
Both arrive years later
items.explain: Illegal choices typically front-load the payoff and delay the price. Seeing that shape on paper is the point of the analysis.

items.stem: Lena starts a GED class. The first month is boring, costs her free time, and she sees no payoff yet. Without the lesson's framing, what is she most likely to conclude?
options: That the slow start is normal and the payoff is just further down the road
That boredom proves she is learning
That she should take a harder class
That it isn't worth it, since the costs are all she can feel
items.explain: Prosocial choices often cost up front and pay later. Knowing the pattern helps people hold on through the costly start.

items.stem: Historians often describe the Marshall Plan as expensive for the U.S. at first and beneficial for decades of trade and alliances. Which pattern from the lesson fits?
options: Benefit now and cost later, the same shape as most risky choices in the lesson
A pure short-term gain
A choice with no long-term consequences
Cost now, benefit later, like most prosocial choices
items.explain: The four-box logic applies to nations as well as people: some choices pay off only after an expensive start.

items.stem: Asked for the benefits of using, the group goes silent. One member jokes, "There aren't any, right?" Best move?
options: List common benefits on the board to get them started
Skip the benefits box for this group
Agree there are none and move straight on to the costs, since the group clearly gets it
Say plainly that people use because it gives them something, and ask what it gave them
items.explain: Members must name the perks themselves. Normalizing that use pays something makes it safe to be honest.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the facilitator want members to list the benefits of a risky behavior?
items.explain: If it gave them nothing, they would not do it. Naming real benefits without judgment builds trust, makes the analysis honest, and shows which needs a new behavior must meet.
key_points: Reveals what a replacement has to provide

items.stem: A facilitator frowns and sighs as members list "partying with my cousins" and "feeling numb" as benefits. What is the most likely effect?
options: Members feel guided toward better answers
Members push back and list even more honest benefits to test how he reacts
Nothing; facial expressions do not matter in groups
Members censor their answers and the analysis becomes a performance
items.explain: Judgment, even nonverbal, shuts down honesty. The research link here is that facilitator empathy reduces resistance and dropout.

items.stem: A member says, "Using is the only time I don't feel the pressure of everything." Which response fits the session best?
options: "Plenty of people find other ways to handle that kind of pressure without using."
"Let's put that under costs, since it's avoidance."
"So it gave you a real break from the pressure. That matters."
"That's the drugs talking."
items.explain: A warm reflection accepts the benefit as real, which keeps the person talking and sets up the later question of other ways to get that relief.

items.stem: In the debrief, "my daughter visits again" is marked as a benefit of changing by four members. How is it sorted?
options: As a neutral item to drop
As a short-term cost of staying the same
As a motivator shared by several members
As a barrier, since it puts pressure on members
items.explain: Benefits of change push toward change, and check marks show which motivators the group shares.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session end by asking how avoiding use fits a member's values and goals?
items.explain: The analysis shows tradeoffs, but values and goals give the reason to act on them. Writing one goal with at least three steps turns insight into a plan.
key_points: Goal with steps supplies the how

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's main listed benefit of dealing is "I can buy my son shoes." Should the facilitator explore other ways to meet that need now, or leave it for later?
items.explain: No single verdict. Exploring alternatives now could plant a seed, but moving too fast can feel like dismissing a real benefit.
key_points: Now: the need is concrete and alternatives could feel hopeful
Later: today's job is honest weighing, not problem solving
Either way: acknowledge the need as legitimate first

items.stem: Pedro's chart shows his perks of using far outnumber his costs of using, but his benefits of changing box is full too. What does the sorting tell the facilitator?
options: That he is lying in one of the boxes
That strong barriers and strong motivators are both live, so ambivalence is the work
That he is not ready and the exercise failed
That he should weight the boxes until change wins
items.explain: Perks of the old way and costs of change are barriers; costs of staying and benefits of change are motivators. Strong items on both sides mean ambivalence to explore, not a failed exercise.

items.stem: After his analysis, Abel writes: "Goal: keep my job at the shop. Steps: set two alarms, ride with my uncle, no Thursday nights out." What part of the session is this?
options: A Behavior Chain
Sorting motivators and barriers
The short-term cost box
Tying the analysis to a goal with steps
items.explain: The session closes by linking the choice to a goal with at least three concrete steps.

cbi-5.title: Setting a Goal
summary: Writing a goal and naming the reasons for it is one of the strongest motivators available.
A good goal is realistic (doable in the time planned, clearly defined) and positive (harms no one).
Compliance reasons, like finishing supervision, are acceptable reasons to be in the room for now.
Mapping barriers, the cost of missing, strengths and supports makes a goal sturdier.
One concrete next step before the next group turns the goal into action.

items.stem: Which goal is realistic in the session's sense?
options: "Be a better person to everyone"
"Stay out of trouble and be there for my family from now on"
"Get my life together this year"
"Attend two recovery meetings a week this month"
items.explain: It is doable in the time planned and clear enough to check off.

items.stem: Diego's goal is "Fix things with my family." What is the most useful edit?
options: Keep it broad but add a deadline, so it feels urgent and motivating over the whole year
Remove the family part, since it is too emotional
Leave it; vague goals let people adapt
Narrow it to something checkable, like a weekly call to his mother for a month
items.explain: A realistic goal is specific enough that you can tell when it is met.

items.stem: A city council promises to "end traffic." A rival promises "add two bus lines by June." Which promise meets the lesson's test for a goal?
options: Both equally, since both aim at the same problem and voters can judge them on intentions
The second, because it is defined and checkable in a set time
The first, because ambitious goals motivate more
Neither; public goals do not follow these rules
items.explain: The realistic-goal test works anywhere: defined, time-bound and checkable beats grand but vague.

items.stem: "Make fast money to pay off my fines." The plan is to flip stolen phones. Which test does the goal fail?
options: Positive: it would harm others or the member
Realistic
It fails only because it is short-term
Neither; paying off fines is a responsible, court-friendly aim regardless of the plan
items.explain: A goal must not hurt the member or anyone else. The aim is fine; the means makes it harmful.

items.stem: Asked why he is here, Wes says, "To get off paper. That's it." Best move?
options: Tell him that attitude will keep him stuck
Ask the group whether that is good enough
Accept it as a real reason and build a goal from it
Push for a deeper reason so his goal means something
items.explain: Finishing supervision is an acceptable reason. Goals can grow as the program goes on; pressure now breeds resistance.

items.stem: Wes's goal of completing supervision is accepted without argument. Over the next months, what is a plausible outcome the session counts on?
options: He stays exactly as motivated as he was
He will drop out eventually, since compliance-only motivation rarely survives a hard month
He will resent the program more
His reasons may broaden as skills and small wins pile up
items.explain: Motivation shifts. Accepting a modest starting reason keeps him engaged long enough for other reasons to appear.

items.stem: Nadia's goal is to stay off cocaine, but she lives with a roommate who uses. She skips the barriers section. What is most likely?
options: Her roommate will quit too
The barrier won't matter much, because a strongly held goal usually carries people through
She will move out without planning
The roommate's use catches her unprepared at a weak moment
items.explain: Naming barriers in advance lets a person plan around them. An unplanned barrier is where goals usually break.

items.stem: In your own words, why ask members to write what happens if the barriers win?
items.explain: Spelling out the cost of missing the goal, like a violation or lost visits, makes the stakes concrete and raises importance. It also clarifies why planning around barriers is worth the effort.

items.stem: A member says he has no healthy people in his life. What does the session's approach suggest?
options: Tell him to rely on willpower alone
Help him name places to find support, like peer recovery groups or staff
Pair him with the most stable member of the group and make that person his support
Skip the supports section for him
items.explain: When healthy people are scarce, the next step is knowing where support can be found.

items.stem: A first-generation college student lists her persistence as a strength and her advisor and a study group as supports. Which part of the goal map is she doing?
options: Costs of missing the goal
Short-term benefits
Barriers
Strengths and supports
items.explain: Naming personal traits and people who can help is what makes a goal more likely to survive setbacks.

items.stem: In your own words, why does each person pick one task to do before the next group?
items.explain: A goal stays abstract until something is done. One small, doable task creates momentum and an early win that builds confidence.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's only goal is "Keep my PO off my back," and he refuses to name anything about substances. Should the facilitator require a substance-related goal on this worksheet?
items.explain: No single verdict. The worksheet aims at substance goals, but forcing one may produce an empty answer.
key_points: Require: the program needs substance goals for the Success Plan
Accept: compliance is a legitimate start and pressure backfires
Bridge: ask what might get the PO on his back and see if use appears

items.stem: Which goal passes the "positive" test?
options: "Save $50 a week from my job for a deposit"
"Get back at the guy who snitched, legally"
"Make my ex regret leaving me"
"Prove to my PO I can't be controlled"
items.explain: A positive goal improves life without harming the member or anyone else.

items.stem: Which is the best "before next group" task for a goal of finding stable housing?
options: Call one listed housing program and ask about its waitlist
Think about where to live
Save enough for a year of rent
Find an apartment
items.explain: The next step must be small, concrete and doable before the next session.

cbi-6.title: Introduction to Cognitive-Behavioral Interventions
summary: Thinking controls behavior: the same situation leads to different actions depending on the thought.
The iceberg shows behavior on top, with feelings, body signs, thoughts, and beliefs underneath.
Feelings are usually one word; body signs are physical sensations like a racing heart.
Thoughts are in-the-moment self-talk; beliefs are deeper, global and steady across situations.
Structured, skill-based CBT programs tend to reduce recidivism more than less structured approaches.

items.stem: Going 70 in a 55, Rico spots a radar gun and thinks, "He can't prove it was me." What is he most likely to do?
options: Call his PO
Pull over voluntarily
Brake hard and hope the officer did not get a reading
Keep going or even speed up
items.explain: The thought drives the action. A different thought in the same moment would send him toward braking.

items.stem: A chess player loses her queen early. One thought: "It's over." Another: "Now they'll underestimate me." Which does the session predict?
options: Her thinking will shape how she plays the rest of the game
Only beginners are affected by thoughts; experienced players rely on pattern memory
The board position alone decides the rest of the game
Both thoughts lead to the same moves
items.explain: The situation is fixed; the thought shapes the next moves. That is the hopeful core of CBT.

items.stem: On the iceberg, which item sits above the waterline?
options: Believing "you can't trust anyone"
Feeling ashamed
Slamming a door
Thinking "nobody respects me"
items.explain: Behavior is the visible tip. Feelings, body signs, thoughts and beliefs are internal and below the water.

items.stem: At the very bottom of the iceberg, as the foundation, is which layer?
options: Beliefs
Thoughts
Body signs
Feelings
items.explain: Beliefs are the deepest layer, carried into every situation and shaping the thoughts above them.

items.stem: "My stomach went tight and my hands got hot." Which layer is this?
options: Body signs
Thoughts
Feelings
Beliefs
items.explain: These are physical sensations. Naming them early works like a warning light that something is building.

items.stem: "I felt like he was trying to play me." Which layer does this actually belong in?
options: Behavior
Thought, since it is an interpretation, not a one-word emotion
A feeling, because he describes it with "I felt" and it is clearly emotional
Body sign
items.explain: People often put interpretations after "I felt." A feeling is usually one word, like humiliated or angry.

items.stem: Which statement is a belief rather than a thought?
options: "This party is getting loud."
"She doesn't know I'm quitting, so she won't judge me if I have some."
"Whoever has the money has the power."
"I really want to smoke right now."
items.explain: Beliefs are global and steady. A quick test: you could put "always" in front of it and it still fits.

items.stem: "This guard is looking for a reason to write me up." Thought or belief, and why?
options: A belief, because it is about authority
A feeling, because it causes anger
A belief, because it is negative
A thought tied to this moment; the belief under it might be "staff are always out to get me"
items.explain: Thoughts belong to the situation; the deeper, general idea underneath is the belief.

items.stem: A coach thinks, "My point guard looks tired tonight." Underneath, he holds, "Rest is for the weak." Which is the belief?
options: "Rest is for the weak"
Neither; both are feelings
"My point guard looks tired tonight"
Both are beliefs
items.explain: The general rule carried into every game is the belief; the observation about tonight is the thought.

items.stem: In your own words, why is "thinking controls behavior" a hopeful message rather than a blaming one?
items.explain: If thoughts drive actions, then changing thoughts gives a person real power over outcomes. It shifts the focus from who they are to what they can learn to do differently.

items.stem: In your own words, what does research broadly say about structured CBT programs for justice-involved adults, and what is one honest limit?
items.explain: Meta-analyses generally find that structured, skill-based CBT programs reduce reoffending more than unstructured ones. Effects vary with fidelity, dosage and fit to risk level, so delivery matters.
key_points: Results depend on quality of delivery
Matching to risk and needs matters

items.stem: Members keep writing beliefs in the thoughts box. Best facilitator move?
options: Accept it, since the difference is minor
Remove beliefs from the exercise
Teach the "always" test and practice with their own examples
Correct each sheet privately after group so nobody feels embarrassed in front of peers
items.explain: This is the hardest distinction for most members, so it gets practice time with a simple test in their own words.

items.stem: A program director says, "Our groups are just open discussion; any group helps." What does the broad research say?
options: Structured, skill-based CBT tends to reduce reoffending more than unstructured groups
Structure only matters for juveniles
No group format has any measurable effect on recidivism
Open discussion groups usually outperform structured ones
items.explain: Meta-analyses of correctional programs generally favor structured cognitive-behavioral approaches, with results that depend on delivery quality.

cbi-7.title: Behavior is a Choice
summary: The Behavior Chain links situation, thoughts, feelings, behavior and consequences.
The situation is an external trigger or invitation and is often outside our control.
Thoughts drive feelings and behavior, so the situation cannot be blamed for the action.
Consequences can be positive or negative, internal or external; rewarded behavior tends to repeat.
Changing the thought is the switch that sends the chain down a different track.

items.stem: Which entry belongs in the situation box?
options: "I drank all night."
"I was stressed out from a long week and everything piling up."
"I thought nobody cared."
"My cousin handed me a bottle at the barbecue."
items.explain: The situation is the external event you could picture. Stress is a feeling; the drinking is behavior.

items.stem: A member writes "situation: I was bored." What is the problem?
options: It is a belief
Boredom is a feeling; the situation is what was happening around him
Nothing; boredom is one of the most common triggers and belongs right there
It should go under consequences
items.explain: The situation should be an external event, such as sitting alone in his room on a Saturday with nothing planned.

items.stem: Someone spills hot coffee on Ahmed at work. He thinks, "He did that on purpose." What is the likely chain?
options: Embarrassment and leaving early
Anger, a confrontation, and possibly a fight and discipline
Annoyance that he swallows, then a shrug and moving on with his shift
Gratitude for the apology
items.explain: The interpretation of intent drives anger and aggressive behavior, and the consequences follow.

items.stem: Same spill, but Ahmed thinks, "Crowded break room, it happens." What is the likely outcome?
options: He cleans up and the day goes on
He stays calm but reports the coworker to HR for carelessness
He quits his job
He still ends up in a fight
items.explain: Same situation, different thought, different chain. That comparison is the session's demonstration of choice.

items.stem: In Les Misérables, Valjean steals the bishop's silver; the bishop tells the police it was a gift. Valjean thinks, "He believes I can be good." Using the chain, why does his life change?
options: The situation forced him to change
Fear of being arrested again, the consequence he narrowly avoided, scared him into changing
A new thought about himself drives new feelings and choices
His behavior changed before his thinking did
items.explain: The chain predicts that a new thought redirects feelings and behavior. The bishop's act changed the thought, not just the circumstance.

items.stem: "I stayed at home instead of going to the party and felt proud of myself." Which kind of consequence is "felt proud"?
options: Internal and positive
External and positive
External and negative
Not a consequence
items.explain: Consequences can live inside a person. Positive ones make the behavior more likely to repeat.

items.stem: Every time Paolo drinks at family parties, people laugh at his jokes and he feels accepted. The negative costs show up months later. What does the lesson predict about the drinking?
options: It stops once he learns the costs
It depends only on how much he drinks
It fades on its own, because the long-term costs are bigger than the quick reward
It keeps repeating, since the quick reward is felt first
items.explain: Positive consequences make repeating likely, and the costs of risky behavior tend to arrive later, which is why the pattern persists.

items.stem: A member says, "He disrespected me, so I had to hit him." What is the lesson's response?
options: Agree that disrespect requires a response
Point out that the thought about the disrespect drove the action, so there were choices
Tell him he is lying about what happened
Acknowledge the disrespect and move on, since the past cannot be changed anyway
items.explain: Because thoughts drive behavior, the situation cannot be blamed. The chain shows where another choice was possible.

items.stem: In your own words, what does the train switch image teach about thoughts?
items.explain: A train heading toward a crash can change tracks with one switch. Thoughts are that switch: change them, and the feelings, behavior and consequences follow a different path.
key_points: One change redirects the whole chain

items.stem: While charting a member's chain, the facilitator rewrites "screw this, I'm out" as "I felt frustrated and decided to leave." Why is that a problem?
options: It is too long for the box
It is fine; cleaner wording helps the group see the feeling and keeps the chart readable
Feelings must never be written down
His own present-tense words are what reveal the thinking; rewording loses it
items.explain: Thoughts are written in present tense, as actually thought. Rewording removes the very thinking the chain is meant to catch.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says his chain started when a CO searched his cell roughly and called him a name. He insists the situation caused his blowup. How far should the facilitator push "behavior is a choice"?
items.explain: No single verdict. The lesson holds that thoughts drive actions, yet some situations are truly unjust and dismissing that can feel like taking sides.
key_points: Push: the point is his power over his response
Validate: the situation was hard and possibly wrong
Both: acknowledge the injustice and still map where he had choices

items.stem: In your own words, why does the chain ask for internal consequences, not just external ones?
items.explain: Internal results, like pride, shame or relief, often drive whether a behavior repeats. Including them shows hidden rewards of risky behavior and hidden rewards of good choices.

items.stem: A pilot heading into a storm can hold course or divert to another airport. In chain terms, what is the decision to divert most like?
options: The consequence
A feeling
The thought that changes the track
The situation
items.explain: The decision point is the thought. Changing it redirects everything downstream, like pulling a rail switch.

items.stem: Which entry is written the way the thoughts box asks?
options: "I had thoughts of anger"
"Just one won't hurt. Nobody will know."
"He was thinking about using"
"Thought: bad"
items.explain: Thoughts are written in present tense and in the person's own words, as they actually ran through his head.

cbi-8.title: Recognizing Risky Situations
summary: Life history factors are past events that cannot be changed and often were not chosen.
Lifestyle factors are how the person lives now, and they can be changed.
High risk situations are specific, external, time-bound moments you could picture.
One history factor can lead to several lifestyle factors, each producing many risky situations.
Trauma history belongs in individual planning and mental health services, not group processing.

items.stem: "My father was locked up most of my childhood." Which category?
options: Life history factor
Thinking error
High risk situation
Lifestyle factor
items.explain: It happened in the past, cannot be changed and was not in his control.

items.stem: "I have a lot of free time and most of my friends still use." Which category?
options: Life history factor
Lifestyle factor
Consequence
High risk situation
items.explain: This is how he lives now, which can change. It produces many specific high risk situations.

items.stem: Which is a high risk situation in the lesson's sense?
options: "Growing up in a house where everyone around me was using"
"Friday at 6, two old friends at the mall ask me back to their place"
"Hanging with bad friends"
"Having a stressful job"
items.explain: It is external, time-bound and clear enough to picture, the moment just before a decision.

items.stem: A member lists "my neighborhood" as his high risk situation. Best move?
options: Ask for a specific moment in that neighborhood, like who, where and when
Accept it; his neighborhood really is the riskiest thing in his life and naming it is honest
Move it to life history
Tell him to move
items.explain: A neighborhood is a lifestyle factor. Pinning down a concrete moment helps him recall the thoughts it set off.

items.stem: Jade grew up with parents who used, and most of her family still uses. What does the lesson predict about holidays?
options: Family invitations will keep producing specific high risk situations
She will simply avoid all family
Her history no longer matters once she is sober
Holidays will be low risk, since being with family usually supports a person in early recovery
items.explain: One history factor spawns lifestyle factors, like a using family, which keep generating risky moments such as a holiday invite.

items.stem: An economist notes that a town lost its factory decades ago (history), so many residents now work irregular gig jobs (current life), so they face monthly crises like a late rent notice (specific moments). Which lesson structure does this mirror?
options: Scoring each situation for how often it happens and how risky it is
Short-term versus long-term costs
Risk categories
History leads to lifestyle, which produces specific situations
items.explain: The same three-tier chain works in any field: a fixed past shapes changeable present conditions, which keep throwing up specific moments.

items.stem: "I got the job offer and wanted to celebrate." Which risk category is this?
options: Positive emotional state
Conflict with others
Social pressure
Negative emotional state
items.explain: Good feelings can be risky too. Celebration is a classic positive-state trigger.

items.stem: "My boss yelled at me in front of the crew." Which category fits best?
options: Conflict with others
Testing personal control
Social pressure
Positive emotional state
items.explain: An argument or clash with someone is the interpersonal conflict category.

items.stem: In your own words, why score each situation for both how often and how risky it is?
items.explain: A situation that happens rarely but is very risky needs a different plan than one that happens daily but is mild. Two scores show where each person's danger is concentrated.

items.stem: Listing life history, a member starts describing childhood abuse in detail. Best move?
options: Change the subject without comment
Invite the group to share similar experiences so he does not feel alone
Acknowledge it with care, keep it brief, and connect him with a counselor after group
Let him finish, since the group is supportive
items.explain: Trauma history belongs in one-on-one planning and mental health services. Respectful containment protects him and the group.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member wants to talk about his brother's murder because "it's the reason I started using." Should group time go to it?
items.explain: No single verdict. The link to his use is real and important, but group processing of trauma can overwhelm him and others.
key_points: For: the connection matters for his plan and he chose to share
Against: the session is not built for trauma work and safety comes first
Middle: name its importance, note the link, and follow up individually

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson separate life history from lifestyle factors?
items.explain: History cannot be changed, so focusing there can feel hopeless. Lifestyle factors can be changed, which is where planning gets traction.

items.stem: Ryan scores "payday" as frequency 3, risk 1 and "my brother's release party" as frequency 0, risk 3. Which needs a specific advance plan most?
options: The release party, since it is rare but very risky
Both equally
Payday, since it happens most often
Neither; low totals mean low risk
items.explain: A rare but very risky event can be the most dangerous if unplanned; the two scores together guide priorities.

items.stem: Tomas cannot change that he grew up in a gang neighborhood, but he can change where he spends weekends. If he focuses his plan on weekends, what is likely?
options: His history factors disappear
Nothing, because his history determines his risk
He becomes more anxious
He reduces how many high risk situations come up
items.explain: Plans gain traction on changeable lifestyle factors, which cut down the specific situations that follow.

cbi-9.title: Countering Risky Thinking
summary: Thoughts run like background recordings, many of them automatic; noticing them is step one.
Cognitive restructuring has three steps: observe without judging, identify risky thoughts, replace them.
A thought is risky if it could lead to trouble, even when it sounds innocent.
A replacement must lead away from the behavior and be believable to the person.
Values and goals make strong counters; practicing out loud strengthens the new voice.

items.stem: Jayden thinks, "I'll pick up a bottle just in case a friend stops by." Is this a risky thought?
options: Only if he has already decided to drink
No, risky thoughts always sound aggressive
Yes, because it could lead him into trouble
No, because he is thinking about being a good host
items.explain: The test is one question: could this thought lead to trouble? Innocent-sounding thoughts often set up the behavior.

items.stem: Marisol thinks, "I'll just drive past the old block to see who's around." What makes this a risky thought?
options: It contains a thinking error label
It is not risky, just curiosity
It quietly moves her toward a risky situation
It mentions a place, and places are triggers by definition
items.explain: Seemingly small decisions set up high risk moments. The question is where the thought leads, not how it sounds.

items.stem: Darnell writes down every time the thought "I deserve it" pops up, without arguing with it yet. Which step is he doing?
options: Observing his thoughts without judgment
Role-playing
Identifying which of his thoughts are thinking errors and labeling each one
Replacing the thought
items.explain: Step one is noticing and recording. Writing thoughts down makes patterns visible, such as a thought that always appears on payday.

items.stem: A mindfulness teacher tells students to notice thoughts "like clouds passing" before doing anything about them. Which step of this lesson matches?
options: Replacing risky thoughts
Rehearsing with a partner
Observing thoughts without judging them
Choosing a counter thought rooted in values, so the cloud does not take over
items.explain: Noticing without judging is the shared first move. You cannot change a recording you have not heard.

items.stem: Hugo's replacement for "One drink won't hurt" is "I will never want a drink again." What is most likely in a real moment?
options: It makes the craving disappear
He feels proud and calm
He doesn't believe it, so the risky voice wins
It works, because a firm and confident replacement drowns out the risky thought
items.explain: Replacements must be realistic enough to believe. Preachy or absolute counters collapse under pressure.

items.stem: A member's replacement for "My PO won't find out" is "Drinking is bad." Best feedback?
options: Tell him to name the thinking error instead, since a label is more precise than a counter
Have the group vote on a better line
Praise it; any anti-drinking thought helps
Ask him to answer that specific thought, like "A violation would cost me my apartment"
items.explain: A good replacement answers the specific risky thought and leads away from the behavior.

items.stem: At 2 a.m. Andrea craves. She tells herself, "My son is starting kindergarten Monday and I'm walking him in." What is the lesson's prediction?
options: The thought will make her more anxious and likely to use
Values rarely help in a craving; only distraction does
It works only if she says it out loud
A value-based counter is often among the strongest
items.explain: Thoughts tied to what a person cares about tend to carry weight when the risky voice is loud.

items.stem: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus resists the lotus-eaters' land by keeping his mind on getting home to Ithaca. Which lesson idea does that resemble?
options: Labeling a thinking error
Observing thoughts without judgment
Spotting a lifestyle factor, since the island is a risky place he can choose to avoid
Using a deeply held goal as the counter to a tempting thought
items.explain: A strong personal goal can outcompete a tempting thought. That is why the lesson builds counters from values and goals.

items.stem: Kwame has practiced his counter thoughts aloud with a partner ten times. Facing a real invitation, what is likely?
options: The new voice comes faster and stronger than before
He freezes, since rehearsed lines feel fake
The risky voice still wins, since practice in a classroom does not transfer
Nothing changes
items.explain: The stronger voice tends to win. Rehearsal out loud is what makes the replacement voice strong enough.

items.stem: In your own words, what does the shoulder-voices image teach, and why practice counters out loud?
items.explain: A risky voice and a new voice argue, and the stronger one usually decides the behavior. Saying counters out loud, with someone playing the risky side, builds that new voice before it is needed.
key_points: The stronger one tends to win

items.stem: In your own words, how does this approach differ from older "thinking errors" work?
items.explain: It cares less about naming errors like minimizing and more about catching the thought and replacing it. The goal is a usable skill in the moment, not a correct label.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's replacement is "If I use, God will punish me." He believes it fully. Should the facilitator accept it as a good counter?
items.explain: No single verdict. It meets the believability test and draws on his faith, but fear-based counters can fade or bring shame after a slip.
key_points: Accept: it is realistic to him and leads away from use
Add: pair it with a goal-based counter that holds up after a mistake
Respect: his faith is his, so build on it rather than replace it

items.stem: A member spends ten minutes debating whether his thought is "minimizing" or "justifying." Which response fits this program's approach?
options: Assign both labels to be safe
Say the label matters less; ask if the thought could lead to trouble and what could replace it
Settle the label first, since accurate names make the counter work
Move to a different member
items.explain: The program follows Cognitive Self Change, which prioritizes catching and replacing the thought over classifying it.

cbi-10.title: Putting It All Together
summary: A situation is risky because of the thinking it triggers, not on its own.
Members write a risky chain and a replacement chain for the same real situation.
Choosing the interpretation gives real control even when the situation stays the same.
The thinking-aloud role play: hand to head, old thoughts, "stop," new thoughts, new action.
Feedback follows a set pattern, and the module ends with a goal readiness check.

items.stem: Leon's daughter cancels her visit. He thinks, "She's done with me, why even try." What is the likely next step?
options: He calls his sponsor, since disappointment like this usually prompts people to reach out
He feels relieved
He feels hopeless and moves toward using
He reschedules the visit right away
items.explain: The cancellation is the same either way; the hopeless thought is what makes it risky.

items.stem: Same cancellation, but Leon thinks, "She's 15, plans change. I'll text her for Sunday." What is likely?
options: He calls her mother to complain
He still ends up drinking, since a canceled visit is a strong trigger no matter how he frames it
He stops caring about visits
Disappointment, then a calm reach-out to reschedule
items.explain: A different interpretation of the same event leads to a different feeling and action.

items.stem: Two teams get rained out of a playoff game. One coach tells players, "We're cursed." The other says, "Extra rest day." Which outcome fits the lesson?
options: Both teams react about the same, since the weather and schedule change are identical for them
Only the cursed team gets more rest
The rain itself decides each team's mood
Each team's mood and practice follow the coach's framing
items.explain: A situation's effect runs through its interpretation. Same rain, different thinking, different outcomes.

items.stem: Rasheed's replacement chain has new thoughts but the behavior box still says "went to the bar, had a few." What is wrong?
options: He should have picked a less loaded situation, since a bar is too hard to restructure this early
Nothing; the thoughts are what count
He should remove the feelings box
The new chain must end in a new behavior, not the same one
items.explain: Replacement thoughts should lead to a different action. Same behavior means the chain was not restructured.

items.stem: A member writes his risky chain about "a time things went bad." Best move before he writes the replacement chain?
options: Give him a sample situation from the manual instead, so he does not get stuck on his own history
Skip to the role play
Let him move on, since he can fill it in later
Help him pin down one specific situation he can picture
items.explain: Both chains need the same concrete situation, so each risky thought can get its own counter.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session call choosing your thoughts empowering?
items.explain: The situation stays the same, but how a person reads it is theirs to pick. That moves control away from triggers and other people and back to the member.

items.stem: Viktor Frankl wrote that even in a concentration camp, a person keeps the freedom to choose an attitude. How does that connect to this session?
options: It argues that situations do not matter at all, which is a stronger claim than CBT makes
It shows that thinking skills only work in safe places
It contradicts the CBT idea of thoughts and feelings
It stresses that interpretation remains a choice even when circumstances do not
items.explain: The session's claim is narrower and practical, but it shares the core idea that the meaning given to an event is a choice.

items.stem: Why does the actor point to his head during the role play?
options: It is a stress-relief gesture
To signal to the group that the scene is about to end and feedback should start
To show he is confused
So observers know when he is thinking, not talking
items.explain: Thinking is invisible, so the cue marks when the audience is hearing internal thoughts.

items.stem: A role player spends two minutes vividly describing how good the high will feel. Best move?
options: Ask the group to add more detail
End the session
Pause and redirect to the "stop" and the new thoughts
Let him continue, since a realistic risky part makes the replacement more convincing
items.explain: Dwelling on the risky part invites euphoric recall. Keep it short and move to the replacement.

items.stem: A role play ends. What comes first, per the protocol?
options: Facilitator critique of what went wrong
Applause from the group
The next role play starts right away
The actor scores himself
items.explain: The protocol is applause, the group says whether thoughts were restructured, the actor says how the new thoughts will help, then the facilitator reinforces.

items.stem: In your own words, what does the Goal Readiness and Progress check at the end of a module do?
items.explain: It revisits the short-term goal from Setting a Goal: members rate importance and confidence again and list steps taken. If the goal is met, they set a new one.
key_points: Resets when a goal is met

items.stem: Weigh it: a quiet member asks to skip the role play because acting in front of others "isn't me." Should the facilitator let him?
items.explain: No single verdict. Practice out loud builds the skill, but pressure can shame him and hurt engagement.
key_points: Encourage: rehearsal is the main ingredient
Adapt: let him do it one-on-one or at the start of next group
Avoid: forcing it, which can turn a skill into a humiliation

items.stem: After applause, what does the group do next in the feedback protocol?
options: Say whether the thoughts were restructured
Move on immediately
Suggest what the actor should have said instead, line by line
Rate the actor's acting
items.explain: The group checks whether the risky thoughts were actually restructured; then the actor says how the new thoughts will help.

items.stem: At the end of Module 2, Eli rerates his goal: importance went from 5 to 8, confidence from 3 to 6. What does that suggest?
options: The ratings are meaningless
He met the goal
His readiness has grown, and he may be ready for a bigger step
His motivation is falling and the goal should be dropped
items.explain: The check tracks importance and confidence over time. Rising scores suggest the skills and small wins are working.

cbi-11.title: Examining Your Success History
summary: People tend to replay the relapse and forget the clean stretch before it; this session flips the focus.
For each past clean period, members ask what and who helped them stay sober.
Current life factors like work, family and sober friends often explain why a period went well.
Relapse triggers can be happy events as well as painful ones.
Patterns repeat, so naming them makes them usable; the facilitator stays neutral.
