items.stem: Isaiah stayed sober eight months in 2023 and relapsed after. Asked about that year, what will he most likely talk about first?
options: His plans for the future
The relapse and how he messed up
The routines that kept him sober for eight months
Nothing; he will refuse to answer
items.explain: People tend to fixate on the relapse. The session deliberately turns attention to the clean stretch and what made it work.

items.stem: A member starts a long story about the night he relapsed. Best move?
options: Let him finish, since processing the relapse fully is how people learn from it
Move on to the next member
Ask the group what he did wrong
Acknowledge it, then ask what helped him in the months before
items.explain: Steering back to what helped keeps the session on success history instead of war stories.

items.stem: After a losing season, a coach studies only the losses. A consultant asks her to study the six-game winning streak too. Why does that match the session?
options: Losses reveal weaknesses more clearly, so wins are mostly worth celebrating, not studying
What worked during the streak can be rebuilt on purpose
Streaks prove the team is talented
Wins are luckier than losses
items.explain: Successes hold usable strategies. Ignoring them throws away the most practical data.

items.stem: "That year I worked early shifts, my aunt checked on me, and I kept telling myself I was done with that life." What does this answer?
options: The relapse trigger
What helped him stay sober
The costs of change
His life history factors and the lifestyle he had back then
items.explain: Daily life, self-talk and support people are the three kinds of helpers the worksheet asks about.

items.stem: Rosa notices both of her clean stretches happened while she had steady work and lived near her sister. What is she identifying?
options: Her relapse triggers
Thinking errors
Life history factors from her childhood that she cannot change now
Current life factors that supported sobriety
items.explain: Work, family and nearby supports often explain why a period went well, which makes them targets to rebuild.

items.stem: Rosa plans release to a town far from her sister with no job lined up. Based on her pattern, what does the lesson suggest?
options: Her risk is lower, since a fresh start far from old places usually helps people stay sober
Her risk is about the same, since motivation matters most
Pattern data does not apply after prison
Her risk is higher, since the factors that helped are missing
items.explain: Patterns repeat. If past success rode on certain life factors, losing them raises risk unless something replaces them.

items.stem: Which event could be a relapse trigger, according to the lesson?
options: Only a breakup
A friend's birthday party or losing a job
Only losing a job
Neither; triggers come from inside, as thoughts, not from events
items.explain: Triggers can be positive or negative. Celebrations are as real a risk as losses.

items.stem: Teo's best month in years ends with a promotion. His crew insists on a night out. What does the lesson say about the risk?
options: It may be high, because happy events can trigger use too
It depends only on whether the crew uses
It is low, since he is feeling good
Low, since good news like a promotion usually protects people against relapse
items.explain: Positive events often come with celebration norms tied to use, which is why they count as triggers.

items.stem: A member sees "my cousin's visits" in three relapse rows. Best move?
options: Reflect the pattern and ask how he could plan around those visits
Move on, since naming a family member as a trigger could upset him in front of the group
Tell him to cut off his cousin
Say patterns are coincidences
items.explain: Naming a repeating trigger turns it into something he can plan for. The decision stays his.

items.stem: Trey says, "I've never had any clean time." What fits the lesson?
options: Accept it and skip the worksheet for him
Have him list relapses instead, since those are the experiences he can actually remember
Ask about any attempt, even hours or days, including time in custody, and what it showed him
Tell him that can't be true
items.explain: Even short attempts count as data. Time in custody or a few days of trying still show what helped.

items.stem: In your own words, why look for patterns across several past clean periods instead of just one?
items.explain: One period might be luck; a helper or trigger that shows up repeatedly is a pattern a person can plan around. Repeated patterns make strategies more trustworthy.
key_points: Repetition reveals reliable helpers and triggers

items.stem: Weigh it: a member credits his clean year to "staying busy hustling," which involved illegal sales. Should the facilitator highlight "staying busy" as a strength?
items.explain: No single verdict. Structure and purpose clearly helped him, but praising it risks seeming to endorse the hustle.
key_points: Highlight: staying busy is a real, transferable helper
Separate: name the structure, not the illegal activity
Explore: ask what legal work could give the same structure

items.stem: A retired marathoner explains her best race: a training partner, a mantra she repeated, and a strict sleep routine. Which three helper types from the worksheet are these?
options: Triggers, costs and barriers
Values, goals and consequences
Life history, lifestyle and risk
Who helped, what she told herself, and her daily life
items.explain: The worksheet asks about support people, self-talk and daily routines, the same three kinds of helpers.

items.stem: Trey recalls three days he didn't use because his grandmother was visiting. Treating that as data, what can he learn?
options: Nothing, since three days is too short to count
That visits are triggers
That he has no ability to stay clean
That his grandmother's presence is a helper he might rebuild
items.explain: Even short attempts hold clues about what helps.

items.stem: Which facilitator response keeps neutrality while reinforcing change?
options: "You should have known better."
"You stayed clean four months while working nights. What made that work?"
"That was a dumb move after doing so well."
"I'd never have gone to that party."
items.explain: Neutral reflection highlights change-oriented details without judging the member's choices.

cbi-12.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis: Exploring Relationships
summary: The cost-benefit analysis now targets relationships with risky people.
Benefits and costs come from the member, never the facilitator.
Using-related choices tend to pay now and cost later; healthier ones tend to cost now and pay later.
Risky people are often family, longtime friends or partners, which makes change genuinely hard.
Others may reward old behavior and punish new behavior, so expect the pull.

items.stem: "Phoning my brother when the day goes bad, knowing he'll invite me to smoke." Where does this go?
options: As a motivator
As the target behavior at the top of Part 1
As the new behavior in Part 2
As a long-term cost of the new behavior, since it involves a family member
items.explain: The target behavior is the risky choice involving a person; the new behavior is what could replace it.

items.stem: "Calling my sponsor instead of my brother when I've had a bad day." Where does this go?
options: As a barrier
As the new behavior in Part 2
As the target behavior
As a short-term benefit of staying the same
items.explain: This is the replacement choice, weighed in Part 2 with its own short- and long-term consequences.

items.stem: Ramón weighs a night at the bar with his usual crew. Which consequence is likely to show up first?
options: A good time tonight
A probation violation
A damaged relationship with his kids
A lost job
items.explain: Using-related choices front-load the benefit; the costs arrive later.

items.stem: A teenager quits a popular but troublemaking friend group to join the debate team. What does the lesson predict about the first few weeks?
options: Instant social payoff
Immediate academic rewards
No real change in how she feels, since she is the one who chose to leave the group
Some loneliness and awkwardness before the benefits arrive
items.explain: Healthier choices tend to cost a little now and pay off over time, which is why the early stretch is the hardest.

items.stem: A member cannot think of any benefit of hanging with his old crew. Best move?
options: Tell him to fill it in at home
Accept that there are none
Ask what he gets out of spending time with them
Suggest "they're fun" to get him started, then let him add his own after
items.explain: The facilitator never supplies benefits but can prompt with an open question about what the relationship gives him.

items.stem: A facilitator fills in "they get you high" as the main benefit of Kevin's friendships. What is likely?
options: Kevin agrees and adds more benefits, since the facilitator gave him permission to be honest
Nothing changes
Kevin feels judged and stops engaging honestly
Kevin feels understood
items.explain: Supplied answers read as judgment and make members passive. What counts as a benefit belongs to the member.

items.stem: Darius stops going to his cousin's weekend parties. What should he expect from his cousin, based on the lesson?
options: Little reaction, since adults generally respect each other's choices about parties
Praise for his new choices
Pressure, teasing or cold treatment, at least at first
An offer to join him in recovery
items.explain: Others often reward the old behavior and push back on the new one. Expecting that pull helps people hold steady.

items.stem: A worker refuses to inflate her hours like the rest of her crew. In the lesson's terms, what is the likely social response?
options: Nothing; work groups don't do this
Her manager notices and rewards the whole crew for her honesty, which wins them over
Her crew starts reporting honestly too
Her crew may treat her as disloyal for breaking the norm
items.explain: Groups tend to reward behavior that fits their norms and punish what does not, which is why changing relationships is hard.

items.stem: In your own words, why is weighing relationships harder than weighing a substance?
items.explain: The risky people are often loved family, partners or longtime friends. Stepping back can feel like betrayal or loss, so ambivalence runs deep and needs patience, not pressure.
key_points: People are loved, not just used

items.stem: A member gets defensive: "You're not going to tell me my mother is a bad influence." Best move?
options: Drop the topic for the rest of the program, since family is too sensitive to bring into group
Ask the group whether his mother is risky
Keep it about specific behaviors, not her as a person, and let him decide
Explain that research shows family can be risky
items.explain: Focusing on behavior, not people, lowers defensiveness and keeps the choice his.

items.stem: "If I stop hanging with them, I'll lose friends I've had since I was ten." On the board, where does this go?
options: Long-term benefit of changing
Barrier
Not relevant
Motivator
items.explain: It holds him back. Barriers like this become things to plan around later.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's partner uses, but she is also the main reason he comes to group on time. Should the analysis push toward distance from her?
items.explain: No single verdict. Her use raises his risk, yet she provides real support, and the decision is his.
key_points: Distance: shared use is a major relapse risk
Stay: she gives structure and love that matter
Middle: explore what boundaries could keep the support and lower the risk

items.stem: "If I stop running with them, my kids won't see me getting arrested again." On the board, where does this go?
options: Short-term cost of changing
Benefit of staying the same
Barrier
Motivator
items.explain: A benefit of the new behavior pushes toward change, so it is a motivator.

cbi-13.title: Relationships & Goals
summary: Important people sort into family, friends and acquaintances; risk can come from any circle.
Each person gets a risk rating from 0 (not risky) to 3 (very risky).
Someone can be risky without using, by stirring the feelings that cue use.
Each person either moves the member toward or away from a goal; love and risk can coexist.
The point is awareness of influence, not judging or reporting anyone.

items.stem: A coworker Juan barely knows invites him to smoke in the storage room. Which circle and what lesson point?
options: Family, since anyone he works with daily becomes like family, and family carries the highest risk
Not relevant to the exercise
Friend; anyone who offers is a friend
Acquaintance; you don't need to be close for someone to be risky
items.explain: Acquaintances matter too. Risky moments often come from people a member barely knows.

items.stem: A recovering gambler's barber talks about sports bets every visit. They are not friends. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Only people he is close to can really affect his choices, so the barber is not worth rating
He should report the barber
Even a casual contact can create a risky moment worth planning for
He is too distant to matter
items.explain: Influence does not require closeness. Regular casual contacts can pull a person toward old patterns.

items.stem: Carmen's mother does not drink, but every phone call ends in a fight, and anger is Carmen's cue to drink. How should Carmen rate her?
options: 1 at most, since her mother means well and never uses, so the risk is mostly about Carmen
0, since her mother doesn't drink
It is wrong to rate a parent
Possibly 2 or 3, because the feelings she stirs are a cue
items.explain: A person can be risky because of the emotions they trigger, not only because they use.

items.stem: Ty rates his strict, sober uncle as 0. His uncle constantly calls him a failure, and shame drives Ty's use. What is likely if Ty stays with him after release?
options: The uncle's strictness will prevent use
Elevated risk Ty may not see coming, since the uncle stirs his main trigger
Lower risk than with friends, since the uncle's strictness keeps Ty in line
Low risk, because the uncle is sober
items.explain: Rating only on use misses emotional triggers. The lesson broadens the rating to include feelings the person sets off.

items.stem: Jamal's goal is to rebuild trust with his kids. His best friend wants him out every weekend. How does the worksheet classify the friend?
options: Neutral
Moving him away from that goal
Moving him toward it
Not applicable, since the friend is not family
items.explain: For each person, members decide whether they bring them closer to or further from a current goal.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the worksheet ask about goals for every person, even non-risky ones?
items.explain: A person can be safe for use but still block a goal, or be risky yet helpful in another way. Looking at goals gives a fuller picture of each relationship's influence.
key_points: Risk and goals are different questions
Safe people can still block goals

items.stem: Malia says, "My brother is my rock, and he's also who I always use with." What is the lesson's view?
options: Both can be true, and the plan can account for both
He should be rated 0 because she loves him
She must choose: he is either good or bad
She is in denial, since anyone she always uses with is a risk and not a real support
items.explain: A person can be loved and still pull someone away from a goal. Holding both truths is the honest starting point.

items.stem: In Shakespeare's Henry IV, Prince Hal loves Falstaff but finally sets him aside to become king. Which lesson idea does that illustrate?
options: Risk ratings should count only actual drug use, since affection is not a risk factor
Family is always supportive
A loved person can still stand between someone and his goal
Acquaintances are the main risk
items.explain: The play dramatizes the core tension: affection and influence are separate questions.

items.stem: A member refuses to write names: "I'm not snitching on anybody." Best move?
options: Clarify it's about influence, and initials or nicknames are fine
Tell him the list is shared with his PO
Let him skip the worksheet, since forcing it would damage trust with the whole group
Insist on full names so the exercise works
items.explain: The exercise is about awareness of influence, and names stay private. Initials remove the reporting worry.

items.stem: During discussion, a member starts detailing a past crime he did with a friend. Best move?
options: Stop the group and explain that details of past crimes may have to be reported
Keep it brief, without scolding, and refocus on the friend's influence now
Ask for more detail to understand the risk
Ask others for similar stories
items.explain: Past offenses stay brief. The focus is on current influence, not the history of what happened.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session focus on relationships as a source of risk?
items.explain: Ties to high-risk people raise the odds of use and crime and can quietly sabotage goals. Naming who acts as a barrier builds motivation to step back or set limits.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member rates his father 3 for risk but says his father is the only one offering him housing at release. What should the plan lean toward?
items.explain: No single verdict. Housing is a basic need that lowers risk, but living with a very risky person raises it.
key_points: Accept housing: stability and shelter matter a great deal
Seek alternatives: a 3 rating at home is serious exposure
Middle: take it short-term with boundaries and an exit plan

items.stem: Shaun's goal is a steady job. His roommate keeps him up gaming and partying until 4 a.m. before work days. What is the likely effect on the goal?
options: The roommate quietly sabotages the goal through lateness and fatigue
Shaun will move out automatically
No effect, since the roommate is not using around him
The goal gets stronger from the challenge
items.explain: Relationships can block goals without any drug use. Naming the barrier builds motivation to set limits.

cbi-14.title: Identifying Social Supports
summary: A support network is several people, not one, who help through hard changes and celebrate wins.
Different people are good for different needs; match the person to the need.
Good support is available, reliable, committed, honest, understands your patterns and models healthy choices.
Poor support encourages risky thinking, does what you are avoiding, or downplays your wins.
Four to six people is the target, but an honest short list beats a padded one.

items.stem: Brenda's sister puts her down; her grandmother listens and helps solve problems. Brenda is stressed about a job interview. Who fits?
options: Whoever calls first
Her sister, since family should know first
Neither; she should handle it alone
Her grandmother
items.explain: Different people are good for different needs. The one who listens and solves problems fits stress.

items.stem: A startup founder has a mentor for strategy, a lawyer for contracts, and a friend for late-night venting. Which lesson idea does that model?
options: Keeping professionals at arm's length so personal friends carry the important needs
One trusted person should handle everything
Matching each kind of need to the right person
Keeping a padded list
items.explain: A network works because different people meet different needs.

items.stem: "She always tells me straight when I'm slipping, even when I don't want to hear it." Which quality is this?
options: Honest feedback
Unreliability
Encouraging risky thinking
Downplaying wins
items.explain: Honest feedback is one of the marks of helpful support, even when uncomfortable.

items.stem: "My buddy says one beer to celebrate parole is fine; you've earned it." Which warning sign is this?
options: Being unreliable, since he isn't helping her stick to her plan
Giving honest feedback
Understanding your patterns
Encouraging the thinking that gets you in trouble
items.explain: Support that feeds risky thinking is poor support, however friendly it sounds.

items.stem: Kofi's best friend is generous, funny and loyal, and still drinks daily. Kofi lists him as top support for staying sober. What is likely?
options: He will quit drinking to support Kofi
His good qualities won't protect Kofi's recovery when they hang out
He will be useful as long as Kofi is clear with him about not drinking around him
He will be the most useful support, since loyalty matters most
items.explain: Someone with fine qualities can still be poor support for recovery, especially if they do what the member is trying to avoid.

items.stem: In your own words, how can someone be a good person and still be poor support?
items.explain: Kindness and loyalty don't cancel risky behavior. If the person uses, is unreliable, or encourages risky thinking, they can hurt recovery even while caring deeply.
key_points: Good traits differ from recovery support
Use the qualities lists to sort

items.stem: A member lists six names, including two he says he "doesn't really trust." Best move?
options: Praise him for reaching six
Keep all six, since a longer list gives him more options when someone is unavailable
Encourage him to keep only people who meet the support qualities
Accept any names to save time
items.explain: Four to six is a target, not a quota. Padding the list with poor supports weakens the plan.

items.stem: Ernesto has only two real supports and pads his list with four casual names. When a crisis hits, what is likely?
options: The padded names step up
He finds the list less useful than it looked on paper
He uses the list exactly as planned
The extra names step up once they see how serious things are
items.explain: A padded list looks strong but fails when tested. An honest short list is more usable.

items.stem: A member says, "I've got nobody." Which step from the worksheet helps most?
options: Skip the worksheet for him and revisit it once he has made new connections after release
Assign a group member as his support
Tell him to reconnect with old friends
Ask a treatment provider or officer for ideas and share local resources
items.explain: Asking an expert and knowing community resources fills gaps when personal networks are thin.

items.stem: During sharing, one member clearly has no names written. Best move?
options: Note it in his file
Ask him to share first, so the group can help him think of people while there is time
Circulate and help him quietly, without spotlighting him
Have the group suggest people for him
items.explain: Spotlighting members with few options can embarrass them. Quiet support keeps dignity intact.

items.stem: In your own words, why might a supervision officer belong on a support list, and what is the honest tension?
items.explain: An officer can help with resources, structure and accountability. The tension is that the officer also enforces rules, so trust is limited and the member decides how much to lean on that role.
key_points: Officers can provide resources and structure

items.stem: Weigh it: a member refuses to list his PO as support: "He's the one who can send me back." Should the facilitator push the idea?
items.explain: No single verdict. The PO can be a real resource, but the member's caution reflects real power dynamics.
key_points: Push gently: officers can help with jobs, housing and referrals
Respect: trust can't be forced and the concern is reasonable
Explore: what would a PO have to do to earn a spot

items.stem: "When I tell him I'm struggling, he picks up, even at midnight." Which quality is this?
options: Understanding your patterns
Honest feedback
Modeling healthy choices
Having time when you need it
items.explain: Availability when needed is one of the marks of helpful support.

items.stem: "When I got my GED, she said, 'Big deal, anyone can do that.'" Which warning sign is this?
options: Downplaying your wins
Being unreliable
Encouraging risky thinking
Doing what you are trying to avoid
items.explain: Support that shrinks achievements undermines confidence, which makes it poor support.

items.stem: Which step of the worksheet involves asking a treatment provider or supervision officer for more ideas?
options: Rating qualities
Asking an expert
Ranking from most to least helpful
The first step, listing everyone
items.explain: Asking an expert brings in resources and ideas members may not know about.

items.stem: The facilitator asks the member with no names to read his list aloud first. What is likely?
options: He feels embarrassed and disengages
He makes up names on the spot
Nothing changes
He gets helpful suggestions and feels supported
items.explain: Spotlighting members with few options can shame them. Quiet, individual help works better.

cbi-15.title: Identifying Healthy Activities
summary: How free time is spent matters: unstructured, bored time is a common lead-in to use.
Healthy activities bring balance and cut triggers like stress and boredom.
Five healthy lifestyle areas: diet, exercise, spiritual practice, mental health care, meditation.
Chosen activities must be realistic and accessible given money, transport and rules.
Each activity gets a concrete action step and a support person to join or advise.

items.stem: Andre gets off his warehouse shift at 2 p.m. and has nothing planned until bed. Two weeks in, what is the lesson's prediction?
options: His risk goes down with fewer people around
He'll rest and recover, since downtime after physical work reduces the urge to use
He'll naturally find hobbies
Empty afternoons become a lead-in to old habits
items.explain: Unstructured time, especially when bored, is a common route back to use. Structured healthy time protects.

items.stem: Retirees who lose the daily structure of work sometimes drink more. Which lesson idea explains this?
options: Losing structure leaves idle time that old habits fill
Aging lowers alcohol tolerance
Retirees have more money
Retirement removes stress, and lower stress is the main reason people drink more or less
items.explain: The same principle holds across life stages: idle, unstructured time is a lifestyle risk factor.

items.stem: Which of these is one of the five healthy lifestyle areas on the worksheet?
options: Watching sports at a bar
Meditation
Shopping
Social media use
items.explain: The areas are diet, exercise, spiritual development, mental health care and meditation.

items.stem: Joining a weekly peer support group fits best under which area?
options: Spiritual development only
Exercise, because getting out of the house counts as physical activity
Diet
Mental health care
items.explain: Self-help and counseling sit under mental health care, which helps with mood and stress.

items.stem: A member circles "join a golf club" right after release, with no car and no income. Best facilitator move?
options: Tell him golf is not a recovery activity
Cross it off his list
Check it against money and transport and help find a doable version
Praise the ambition, since big goals motivate people more than small ones do
items.explain: Activities must be realistic given money, transportation and rules. A free version, like a driving range day with a friend later, can keep the interest alive.

items.stem: Gloria picks "free yoga at the library on Saturdays," which is a bus ride from her place. What does the lesson predict compared with an expensive gym plan?
options: The gym plan is better, since paying for something makes people more committed to it
Library classes are too easy to matter
She is more likely to actually start and keep it
Neither will work without a sponsor
items.explain: A free, accessible activity removes barriers, which raises the odds of follow-through.

items.stem: Goal: join a rec basketball league. Which is an action step in the lesson's sense?
options: Call the community center Monday to ask about sign-ups
Think about whether he likes teams
Play in the league this year
Get better at basketball
items.explain: An action step answers: what would I need to do if I started today?

items.stem: A writer wants to publish a book someday. A coach asks, "What would you do today if you started?" She says, "Write one page tonight." What lesson tool is this?
options: An action step
A support person
A lifestyle factor
A long-term goal, since publishing is the outcome she is working toward this year
items.explain: The action step turns a distant aim into something doable now.

items.stem: Marcus plans to start running and asks his sober cousin to meet him at the track twice a week. What does the lesson predict?
options: He is more likely to start and stick with it
It makes running feel like an obligation
His cousin will slow him down
Little difference, since running is an individual activity that depends on personal discipline
items.explain: Prosocial supports make new activities easier to start and give encouragement and company.

items.stem: In your own words, why attach a support person to each healthy activity?
items.explain: Starting something new alone is hard, and old friends may pull toward old habits. A prosocial person gives company, advice and accountability, which makes the new activity more likely to last.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson frame healthy activities as balance rather than just "staying busy"?
items.explain: Busy time can still be risky. Balance means activities that cut stress and boredom and support health, so the person's life has fewer gaps that use used to fill.
key_points: Busy is not the same as healthy

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's main healthy activity idea is working double shifts "to stay out of trouble." Should the facilitator count it as a healthy activity?
items.explain: No single verdict. Work gives structure and income, but overwork can raise stress and leave no room for rest or relationships.
key_points: For: structure and money reduce risk
Against: chronic stress and exhaustion are triggers too
Middle: keep the work, add one restorative activity

cbi-16.title: Introduction to Emotion Regulation
summary: Use often ties to emotion: escaping, coping, boosting a good feeling, or numbness after long use.
Emotions are information, not good or bad; the goal is to handle them, not erase them.
Fight or flight is a body alarm that signals threat.
Emotion regulation has three steps: pay attention, identify, manage.
A feeling can itself be the risky situation, and risky thoughts make feelings stronger.

items.stem: "After my mom died I couldn't stand being in my own head, so I drank until I couldn't feel it." Which tie between use and emotion is this?
options: Numbness from long use
To escape a hard feeling
Social pressure
To boost a good feeling, since drinking made things feel lighter at first
items.explain: Using to get away from a painful feeling is one of the four links the lesson names.

items.stem: "I don't even know what I feel anymore. Everything's just flat." Which link fits best?
options: Coping with stress
Numbness after long use
Escaping a hard feeling
Boosting a good feeling
items.explain: Long use can blunt emotional awareness, so the person no longer knows what they feel.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson say emotions are not good or bad?
items.explain: Feelings carry information: anger can flag an injustice and sadness lets us grieve. Getting rid of them would cause problems; the aim is to respond to them without trouble.

items.stem: A car's dashboard warning light comes on. Which response matches the lesson's view of emotions?
options: Cover the light with tape so it stops being distracting while you drive
Ignore it until the car breaks down
Get angry at the light
Notice it, find out what it means, then act
items.explain: Feelings, like warning lights, are signals worth reading, not problems to silence.

items.stem: Hiking, Lucía sees a snake and jumps back before she even thinks. What just happened?
options: A craving
A thinking error that she will need to restructure later
Her body's fight-or-flight alarm reacted to threat
A planned coping strategy
items.explain: Strong fear triggers a fast body reaction preparing us to fight or run. It tells us we feel threatened.

items.stem: A member says, "When a guy steps to me, my body just goes. I can't control it." What fits the lesson?
options: Validate the alarm as real and useful, then show how noticing it early buys time
Agree that the reaction is automatic and so nothing can be done about it
Recommend he avoid all men
Tell him he's making excuses
items.explain: The alarm is natural and informative. Catching body signs early is what creates room to choose.

items.stem: "My chest is tight and my fists are clenched." Which regulation step is this?
options: Manage
Identify, since he is naming exactly what he feels
Restructure
Pay attention
items.explain: Step one is noticing what the body is doing, inside and in body language.

items.stem: "I'm not just mad. I'm humiliated." Which step is this?
options: Manage
Avoid
Identify
Pay attention
items.explain: Step two is naming the feeling precisely, beyond basic words like mad or sad.

items.stem: Kenji always calls every feeling "stressed." In a hard moment, what is the likely problem?
options: He will overreact less
He can't tell which feeling is risky or which tool fits
None, since "stressed" covers most feelings well enough to pick a coping tool
He will manage better because he keeps it simple
items.explain: Vague naming makes managing harder. Specific words point to specific responses.

items.stem: A member says his friend "was obviously angry" in a story, but the friend, also in group, says he felt embarrassed. Best move?
options: Side with the first member
Ask the group to vote on which feeling it really was, based on the story
Move on
Affirm that each person is the authority on what he feels
items.explain: No one assigns a feeling to someone else; the person who has it names it.

items.stem: Ninety days clean, Shayla feels unusually confident: "I've got this now." What does the lesson warn?
options: She is ready to stop coming to group
Confidence is protective, so this is the lowest-risk point in her recovery so far
Confidence means she has finished the program
Even a good feeling can be the risky situation
items.explain: A feeling can itself set off a chain. Overconfidence after clean time is a known example.

items.stem: In your own words, how do risky thoughts make a feeling stronger?
items.explain: Misreading a situation feeds the feeling, which then sparks more heated thoughts. Restructuring the thought turns the feeling down and makes better choices possible.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says, "If I let myself feel my grief in here, I'll break down and I can't do that on the unit." Should the facilitator encourage him to feel it?
items.explain: No single verdict. Grief is a feeling that should hurt, but a prison unit may make visible vulnerability unsafe.
key_points: Encourage: avoiding grief can fuel use later
Respect: his safety concerns are real
Middle: offer a private session and small, contained ways to feel it

cbi-17.title: Recognizing Your Feelings
summary: You cannot manage what you cannot recognize; naming feelings comes before managing them.
Step 1: tune in to body sensations and body language.
Step 2: find the situation the reaction is connected to.
Step 3: name the emotion, sometimes more than one at once.
All three steps are thinking steps, practiced in role plays with the hand-to-head cue.

items.stem: Earl doesn't notice his rising frustration during a long phone call with his ex. What is the most likely result?
options: He hangs up calmly
Nothing much, since unnoticed feelings tend to fade by themselves
The feeling builds and he snaps before he sees it coming
He feels relieved
items.explain: Without awareness, a feeling can't be managed. It grows until it shows up as behavior.

items.stem: "My face is hot, my jaw is clenched, and I'm squinting." Which step is this?
options: Tuning in to the body
Managing
Naming the emotion
Finding the connected situation
items.explain: Step one notices sensations and body language before anything else.

items.stem: A poker player notices her own hands shaking before she realizes she is nervous about a big bet. What does that show?
options: That poker players are unusually poor at reading their own feelings
That nerves always help in competition
Body signals often come before we name the feeling
That she should quit the hand
items.explain: The body often registers emotion first, which is why the skill starts there.

items.stem: "This started right when my wife brought up the paycheck I spent." Which step is this?
options: Finding the connected situation
Tuning in to the body
Naming the emotion
Making a plan
items.explain: Linking the reaction to what just happened helps the person understand the feeling.

items.stem: In a role play, a member jumps from "my chest is tight" straight to "I'm furious." What should the facilitator prompt?
options: Tell him to breathe
Ask what just happened that seems tied to the reaction
Nothing, since naming the feeling is the step that matters most here
Have him start over from the beginning
items.explain: Step two links feeling to situation. Skipping it loses the understanding that helps the naming.

items.stem: After the steps, a member says, "I'm hurt and angry." Is two feelings acceptable?
options: Only if one is positive
Only if the Feelings Chart lists both
No, the skill requires one clear word so it is easier to manage
Yes; feelings often come in pairs
items.explain: People often feel more than one thing. Naming both precisely sets up managing them.

items.stem: Researchers sometimes call fine-grained emotion naming "emotional granularity." Which practical benefit does this lesson rely on?
options: Precise labels make choosing a fitting response easier
It eliminates negative feelings
It replaces body awareness
It mainly helps people sound more educated when they describe their feelings
items.explain: Being specific about what you feel helps select the right way to manage it.

items.stem: Why does the actor point to his head during this skill's role play?
options: To signal the end of the scene
It is optional decoration
It signals to the group that he is getting a headache from the scene
All three steps happen in his head, so observers can follow
items.explain: The cue shows observers that the spoken words are internal thoughts.

items.stem: A member asks to role-play the skill alone, with no partner. Is that fine?
options: No, every role play in the program needs at least two people to be realistic
Yes; this skill needs no other person
Only after everyone else has gone
Only if the facilitator plays a part
items.explain: Because recognizing feelings is internal, solo situations work.

items.stem: The facilitator refers to "step two" without reading it aloud. What does the routine suggest instead?
options: Skip the steps once modeled
Read the full step aloud each time
Write it on the board once
That is fine, since experienced members already know the steps by heart
items.explain: Repetition is the learning. Reading the whole step each time builds recall.

items.stem: In your own words, why does recognizing feelings come before managing them?
items.explain: You can't choose a strategy for a feeling you haven't noticed or named. Knowing what you feel tells you whether it is risky and which tool fits.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member wants to role-play the skill using a real conflict with a group member present in the room. Should the facilitator allow it?
items.explain: No single verdict. A real, current situation makes practice vivid, but it may inflame the conflict in front of the group.
key_points: Allow: realistic situations make skills transfer
Decline: group safety and the other member's consent matter
Adapt: use a similar but less charged situation

cbi-18.title: Coping by Thinking—Managing Feelings Through Managing Thoughts
summary: Thoughts and feelings feed each other in a loop; breaking the loop matters more than which came first.
A strong emotion can become a runaway train, so step in early.
The Double Behavior Chain puts old thoughts, a stop sign, then new thoughts, feelings, behavior and consequences on one page.
New consequences can include an honest downside; that is not a failure.
Retraining thoughts takes repetition, because old thoughts are habits.

items.stem: Leti thinks, "My boss is setting me up to fail." She gets angrier, then thinks, "He's always had it out for me." What's happening?
options: She is restructuring
Her anger is fading
The second thought is calming her, since it explains what is going on
Thoughts and feelings are feeding each other upward
items.explain: Heated thoughts raise the feeling, which sparks more heated thoughts. The loop climbs unless broken.

items.stem: A social media pile-on grows as each angry post makes others angrier and more posts follow. Which lesson concept does this mirror?
options: A support network
The stop sign, since the platform eventually removes the posts
Urge surfing
The thought-feeling loop
items.explain: Same loop at group scale: reactions fuel the thinking that fuels more reaction.

items.stem: Bo's anger is at its peak before he tries to counter his thoughts. What does the lesson predict?
options: The counter works just as well
Countering works best at the peak, since that is when the thoughts are clearest
The anger stops instantly
Clear thinking is hardest now; earlier would have worked better
items.explain: Once a feeling peaks, reasoning gets hard. Stepping in early is the point.

items.stem: A member says his counters "never work when I'm already raging." Best guidance?
options: Tell him to use stronger counter thoughts with more force when the rage is high
Give up on thinking skills for anger
Practice catching the earliest thoughts and body signs
Wait until he's calm and then think
items.explain: The earlier the intervention, the better. Early cues buy room for counters to work.

items.stem: On the Double Behavior Chain, what does the stop sign mark?
options: The consequences of the old behavior and the end of the risky path
A warning to avoid the situation
The moment of interrupting risky thinking on purpose
The end of the exercise
items.explain: It shows the chain can be broken mid-stream to make room for new thoughts.

items.stem: Who is the Double Behavior Chain best suited for, per the lesson?
options: Members in crisis
Members who already want to change
Members who can't read
Members who are still unsure whether they even want to change their behavior
items.explain: It skips analyzing the risky path's consequences, so it fits people already committed to change. Two separate chains suit those still on the fence.

items.stem: Jade loses her job. Her new thoughts: "I can job hunt; I have experience now; one night isn't worth what I've built." What new feeling is most plausible?
options: Disappointed but steadier and more hopeful
Elation, since restructured thoughts usually make the bad news feel good
Rage
Numbness
items.explain: Restructuring doesn't erase the loss; it shifts the feeling toward something manageable.

items.stem: Jade's new consequences include "still need to find a job." Is that a flaw in her chain?
options: Only if she uses
No, an honest downside keeps the plan believable
Yes, because a good chain should end only in positive results
Yes, she should remove it
items.explain: Real life has costs on the good path too. Including them keeps the chain realistic.

items.stem: In your own words, why is it useful that the new chain can include a downside?
items.explain: Pretending the new path has no costs makes it unbelievable. Admitting real problems, like still needing work, keeps the plan honest and harder to dismiss.

items.stem: In your own words, why does retraining thoughts take repetition?
items.explain: Old thoughts are habits, practiced for years, so they come automatically. New thoughts need many reps before they show up on their own under pressure.

items.stem: A tennis player rebuilding her serve keeps reverting to the old motion under match pressure. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Pressure is the only issue
The new pattern needs more reps before it holds under pressure
The new motion is wrong, since it fails under pressure and the old one does not
She should stop practicing
items.explain: Old habits win under stress until the new pattern has been rehearsed enough.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member is ambivalent about drinking but insists on using the Double Behavior Chain like everyone else. Should the facilitator switch him to two separate chains?
items.explain: No single verdict. Two chains would explore the risky path's costs he hasn't weighed, but insisting may feel like singling him out.
key_points: Switch: ambivalence benefits from seeing risky consequences
Middle: let him do the double chain and add a short consequences review

cbi-19.title: Coping by Doing—More Strategies for Managing Feelings
summary: Managing activating emotions takes three pieces: change thoughts, calm the body, use people skills.
When emotion is high, calming the body first lets thinking come back online.
Four tools: deep breathing, counting backwards, pleasant imagery, taking a break.
A break can backfire if risky thinking continues during it.
Tools can be combined, and positive self-talk fits with any of them.

items.stem: Rey's heart is pounding after a heated argument. He tries to reason through his thoughts immediately. What does the lesson predict?
options: Thinking will be hard until his body calms down
He'll feel calmer instantly
Reasoning will work best now, while the argument is fresh in his mind
His heart rate doesn't affect thinking
items.explain: When arousal is high, calming the body first lets clearer thinking return.

items.stem: A basketball player at the free-throw line takes two slow breaths before shooting. Which lesson idea does this match?
options: Positive self-talk
Taking a break
Lowering body arousal so focus can return
Counting backwards, since breathing is a way of counting time
items.explain: Bringing the body down helps the mind focus, the same logic as the breathing tool.

items.stem: Why does counting down by threes help more than counting by ones?
options: It takes longer, so the person has more total time away from the situation
It burns more energy
Harder counting pulls more attention off the emotion
It sounds more official
items.explain: The effort shifts attention toward problem solving and away from the emotional loop.

items.stem: A member finishes counting backwards and feels calmer. What should come next, per the lesson?
options: Follow it with a replacement thought, like "I'm in control"
Return to the conversation right away while he still feels calm
Nothing
Count again for longer
items.explain: Counting buys calm; a replacement thought helps keep it.

items.stem: Which imagery scene breaks the lesson's rules?
options: A quiet river at dawn with birds and cool air
A rooftop party with music and drinks
A grandmother's kitchen smelling of bread
A mountain trail after rain
items.explain: Scenes must not involve drugs, alcohol, violence or sex.

items.stem: Someone at a bus stop is trying to start a fight with Elan. What does the lesson say to do?
options: Leave right away, since the risk is immediate
Take slow breaths and use imagery right there, since leaving looks weak
Argue calmly
Count backwards in place
items.explain: Immediate risk calls for leaving. Lower-grade stress allows stepping into something positive.

items.stem: After a rough day, Noor goes for a walk but spends the whole time replaying the insult and planning what to say. What's likely?
options: She forgets the incident
She comes back as angry or angrier
The walk calms her, since physical activity lowers stress no matter what she thinks
She feels relieved
items.explain: A physical break can backfire if risky thinking continues. Pair it with self-talk.

items.stem: In your own words, how can a break make things worse, and how is that prevented?
items.explain: If the person keeps rehearsing the risky thoughts during the break, the feeling grows. Pairing the break with positive self-talk or another tool keeps it calming.

items.stem: A member says breathing alone doesn't do enough for him. Best suggestion?
options: Drop breathing and use only counting from now on, since one tool should be mastered first
Breathe faster
Pair breathing with a replacement thought or imagery
Accept that nothing works
items.explain: Stacking tools often works better than any one alone.

items.stem: A surgeon calms herself before a hard operation by breathing slowly while telling herself, "I've done this a hundred times." Which lesson idea fits?
options: Combining a body tool with self-talk
Taking a break, since she has stepped away from the patient before starting
Counting backwards
Pleasant imagery only
items.explain: Combining a calming technique with supportive self-talk is a strategy the lesson recommends.

items.stem: In your own words, what are the three pieces of managing activating emotions?
items.explain: Replace risky thoughts, calm the body's fight-or-flight state, and use people skills. Each covers a different part of how the emotion plays out.

items.stem: Weigh it: on a unit, walking away from a man who is posturing could be seen as weakness and invite more trouble. Should a member still use "taking a break"?
items.explain: No single verdict. Leaving lowers immediate risk, but the setting's code may raise social risk later.
key_points: Adapt: exit with a face-saving line
Plan: talk with staff about safer options in advance

items.stem: A member's calm place is "my grandmother's porch in Ponce." The facilitator wants to deepen the imagery. Which prompt fits?
options: "What do you hear, smell and feel on that porch?"
"Is that a safe neighborhood now?"
"Describe what kind of person your grandmother was and why you miss her."
"How long ago was that?"
items.explain: Imagery uses every sense to make the scene vivid enough to calm the body.

items.stem: A member breathes slowly to calm down, then tells his coworker calmly what bothered him. Which two of the three pieces did he use?
options: Changing thoughts and avoiding triggers
Urge surfing and grounding
Counting and imagery
Calming the body and using people skills
items.explain: Managing activating emotions combines thought work, body calming and interpersonal skill.

cbi-20.title: Dealing With Urges
summary: A craving is an emotionally charged pull, usually set off by a reminder of past use.
Cravings are normal, common, time-limited and a sign of change.
Avoid what you can, but not every trigger can be avoided.
Urge surfing accepts and observes the urge like a wave instead of fighting it.
Grounding (mental, physical, soothing) brings a person back when they spin out or check out.

items.stem: Darren walks past his old corner store and suddenly feels a strong pull plus thoughts about how good it used to feel. What is this?
options: A craving set off by a reminder of past use
A panic attack, since it came on suddenly and strongly
A lifestyle factor
A memory with no risk
items.explain: Cravings are usually triggered by cues tied to past use and bring up positive thoughts about using.

items.stem: A former smoker smells coffee and wants a cigarette, because she always smoked with her morning coffee. What explains it?
options: A learned cue linked to past use
Coffee causes nicotine cravings chemically
She was never really quit
The smell of coffee contains nicotine-like compounds that cause the craving directly
items.explain: Repeated pairing makes everyday cues set off cravings.

items.stem: Ana rides out a strong craving without using. What does the lesson say happens to that trigger over time?
options: It stays the same
Its pull weakens with each craving ridden out
It disappears forever
It grows stronger, since resisting a craving makes the brain want it more
items.explain: Each time a craving passes without use, the trigger's hold weakens.

items.stem: A member's route to work passes his old block. What is the first line of defense?
options: Take a different route if possible
Tell no one
Quit the job
Drive through and practice urge surfing as he passes, since exposure builds strength
items.explain: Avoid risky people, places and things where possible; use other skills when avoidance is not possible.

items.stem: Hana pictures her urge as a wave and watches it build, crest and break without acting. What does the lesson predict?
options: She'll lose control
Nothing happens
The urge keeps climbing, since paying attention to a craving makes it bigger
The urge peaks and passes
items.explain: Urges are time-limited. Observing rather than fighting lets them crest and fade.

items.stem: Which description matches urge surfing rather than white-knuckling?
options: Distracting with loud music
Gripping the bunk and repeating "I won't, I won't" until it stops
Watching the urge with curiosity, like a reporter
Calling a friend
items.explain: Urge surfing accepts and observes the urge; white-knuckling fights it.

items.stem: A meditation teacher tells a student with an itchy nose to observe the itch without scratching. What does this practice share with urge surfing?
options: Observing a sensation until it fades, without acting
Both require avoiding triggers
Neither is related
Both are mainly about physical pain tolerance rather than urges or habits
items.explain: Both are acceptance practices: notice the urge, don't act, and let it pass.

items.stem: During a heated call, Leo goes blank, tunes everything out and stares at the wall. Which pattern is this?
options: Spinning out, since the call has overwhelmed him and he has lost control
Checking out
Urge surfing
Grounding
items.explain: Checking out means going blank or tuning out; spinning out means losing control.

items.stem: In your own words, why can checking out be hard to give up?
items.explain: It often started as a childhood survival tool when escape wasn't possible. It once protected the person but now gets in the way of handling feelings.

items.stem: "Name every red object you can see in this room." Which grounding type is this?
options: Urge surfing
Mental grounding
Soothing grounding
Physical grounding, since it uses the eyes and the room around him
items.explain: Mental grounding uses the mind, like categories or lists. Physical grounding uses the senses directly, like texture or temperature.

items.stem: "Tell yourself, 'You're doing the best you can right now.'" Which grounding type is this?
options: Soothing
Mental
Distraction
Physical
items.explain: Soothing grounding means being kind to yourself.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says urge surfing "feels like sitting with temptation," and he prefers to keep his mind busy every second. Should the facilitator press the acceptance approach?
items.explain: No single verdict. Acceptance builds lasting tolerance, but distraction also works and his preference matters.
key_points: Press gently: urges pass and that knowledge builds confidence
Respect: distraction is a valid tool
Combine: start with brief surfing, then distract

items.stem: "I've been out two weeks and I keep getting cravings. Something's wrong with me." Which craving fact answers him?
options: Cravings mean he should increase his treatment level right away
Cravings last until you give in
Cravings only hit people who were heavy users
Cravings are normal and especially common early on
items.explain: Cravings are normal, common, time-limited and a sign of change, especially early.

items.stem: Ty avoids every bar but works at a stadium where beer is sold everywhere. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Avoidance has failed, so he should quit the job before he uses
Avoid what he can and use surfing or grounding for what he can't
He should drink only on breaks
Avoidance alone will be enough
items.explain: Avoidance is the first line, but when triggers can't be avoided, acceptance and grounding skills fill the gap.

cbi-21.title: Practice Emotion Regulation—Using Self-Control
summary: Self-control is managing feelings and behavior well enough to make good decisions.
Step 1: notice body cues that come before losing control.
Step 2: notice the risky thoughts pushing toward trouble.
Step 3: list coping options; Step 4: pick one that fits and do it.
Steps 1–3 are thinking; step 4 is thinking plus action. A facilitator who slips in a model stops, owns it and restarts.

items.stem: "My heart is pounding and my stomach feels sick." Which step of Using Self-Control is this?
options: Listing coping options, since he is about to choose what to do about it
Picking a strategy
Noticing risky thoughts
Noticing body cues
items.explain: Step one catches the physical early warnings that come before losing control.

items.stem: "I could breathe, take a walk, or do a quick double chain." Which step is this?
options: Listing coping options
Noticing risky thoughts
Picking one and doing it
Noticing body cues
items.explain: Step three reviews the available tools before choosing.

items.stem: Criticized unfairly by his supervisor, Ivan notices his body, catches "I'm always the one blamed," lists options, but never actually does one. What is the likely outcome?
options: The supervisor apologizes
He stays calm, because recognizing the problem is most of the work in self-control
He forgets the incident
The anger keeps building, since no tool was used
items.explain: Step four is where thinking becomes action. Without doing a strategy, the skill stops short.

items.stem: Which step of Using Self-Control includes visible action?
options: Step 2
Step 1
Step 3
Step 4
items.explain: The first three steps happen inside the head; the fourth is thinking plus doing.

items.stem: A firefighter feels heat through her glove, thinks "this door could flash," reviews options, and chooses to vent before entering. How does this map onto the skill?
options: Body cue, risky thought, options, then pick and act
Only steps 3 and 4 apply
It does not map, since firefighting is physical and the skill is about emotions
It is urge surfing
items.explain: The same four-step structure (notice, think, list, act) shows up in any high-pressure decision.

items.stem: Ming learns that his ears get hot about a minute before he yells. What does knowing that cue give him?
options: A window to use a tool before he loses control
Nothing, since by the time his ears get hot the outburst is already locked in
A reason to avoid all conflict
An excuse
items.explain: Early body cues are a warning light. Catching them buys time to choose.

items.stem: In your own words, why does Using Self-Control start with the body rather than thoughts?
items.explain: Body cues often show up first and are easier to notice than racing thoughts. Catching them early gives a warning before the feeling peaks.

items.stem: A member's go-to tool is pleasant imagery, but the moment is a tense standoff in the yard. Best guidance?
options: Pick a tool that fits, like leaving or breathing with eyes open
Do nothing
Use counting with eyes closed
Use imagery anyway, since practiced tools work in any situation
items.explain: Step four means choosing the strategy that fits the moment, not just the favorite.

items.stem: A chef has many techniques but a customer's allergy limits her options. Which step of the skill is she most like when she chooses?
options: Noticing risky thoughts
Picking the option that fits the situation
Noticing body cues
Listing every option she knows
items.explain: Choosing what fits the conditions, not just any tool, is the core of step four.

items.stem: Mid-demonstration, the facilitator skips step two by accident. What should he do?
options: Keep going so the group doesn't lose the flow of the scene
Explain step two afterward
Stop, say what happened, and restart from the beginning
Ask a member to finish for him
items.explain: Owning the mistake and restarting models the skill correctly and shows honesty.

items.stem: A member volunteers to act out the steps for the demonstration. What is the guidance?
options: Let him, since peer modeling is usually more convincing than staff modeling
The facilitator models, not a member
Let him if he has done it before
Ask the group to vote
items.explain: The demonstration is done by facilitators, rehearsed ahead, so the skill is shown accurately.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's chosen tool in his role play is "go to my cell and sleep it off." It works for him. Should the facilitator count it as a good step four?
items.explain: No single verdict. Sleep can calm intense feelings, but using it every time can become avoidance.
key_points: For: it removes him from risk and calms the body
Against: may become a way to avoid problems
Middle: accept it and add a tool for when sleep isn't possible

cbi-22.title: Managing Risky Feelings—Anger
summary: Anger is managed, not erased; even people conditioned to react aggressively can change.
Anger shows early in body sensations and body language.
Steps: name the trigger, identify thoughts, feelings and body signs, think through consequences, choose and use a strategy.
Anger moves fast; rehearsal slows it down so the steps can become automatic.
Anger usually reaches use through the chain: risky situation, risky thoughts, anger, urge.

items.stem: "I start pacing and grinding my teeth." What is he describing?
options: A consequence
A trigger
Thoughts that drive his anger and make it grow over time
Early warning signs in body language
items.explain: Body language like pacing and gritted teeth signals rising anger.

items.stem: Lamont's group helped him list his signs: hot cheeks, tight jaw, fists clenching. At work his jaw tightens during a meeting. What is likely now?
options: Nothing changes
He'll walk out
He has a chance to start the steps early
His anger will take over anyway, since body signs come on too fast to use
items.explain: Knowing personal signs lets a person catch anger before it peaks.

items.stem: "My friend borrowed my car overnight and wrecked it." Which step is this?
options: Thinking through consequences
Body signs
Choosing a strategy
Naming the trigger
items.explain: Step one identifies the risky situation setting off the anger.

items.stem: In the anger skill, a member starts with "My blood is boiling." What does step one ask him to name first instead?
options: The consequences of hitting back
A coping tool
The situation setting off the anger
His thoughts about the person who caused it, since thoughts drive anger
items.explain: Step one names the trigger, the risky situation, before moving to thoughts, feelings and body signs.

items.stem: Rafa pictures knocking out his friend: a brief rush, then arrest and a violation. He compares it with taking a walk and talking later. What does step three do here?
options: It increases his anger, because picturing the fight makes it feel more real
It replaces step four
It shows the costs before he acts
It forces him to forgive
items.explain: Weighing outcomes before acting is what interrupts the fast path to violence.

items.stem: Before a duel in the 1800s, a seconds' negotiation sometimes let both men withdraw with honor. Which step does that pause resemble?
options: Urge surfing
Thinking through the consequences before acting
Naming the trigger that started the quarrel in the first place
Noticing body cues
items.explain: A built-in pause to weigh outcomes is the same function as step three.

items.stem: In your own words, why is role play rehearsal especially important for anger?
items.explain: Anger moves so fast that people act before they think. Rehearsal slows the process down so each step can be practiced until it comes more automatically.

items.stem: During a role play, the actor rushes from "he wrecked my car" straight to "I walk away." Best move?
options: Praise him, since walking away was the right final choice and the rest is detail
Ask him to slow down and say each step aloud
Let him repeat it faster
Skip feedback
items.explain: The point of rehearsal is to slow anger down and practice every step.

items.stem: Lisa's sister insults her at dinner. Lisa thinks "She always disrespects me," feels furious, then thinks "I need a drink to deal with her." What does the lesson say about this sequence?
options: It is unusual, because anger and urges come from different parts of the brain
It shows she has no real substance problem
Anger and use are unrelated
It is the common route from anger to an urge
items.explain: Anger often reaches use through the chain: situation, risky thought, anger, urge.

items.stem: In your own words, why does managing anger matter for staying sober?
items.explain: Anger often leads to urges to use, especially when risky thoughts fuel it. Catching anger early interrupts that chain before it reaches the urge.

items.stem: A member says, "I've been fighting since I was eight. This is just who I am." Best response?
options: Agree, since temperament is mostly fixed by adulthood and the work is acceptance
Change the subject
Argue that he's choosing violence
Acknowledge the long habit and say change is still possible with practice
items.explain: The manual's message is that conditioned reactions can change. Acknowledging the history makes that message believable.

items.stem: Nelson Mandela described learning in prison to control his anger toward his jailers. What lesson idea does that support?
options: Anger is never justified
Even long-held reactions can be changed with deliberate effort
Anger always disappears with age and enough time, whatever a person does
Only famous people can change
items.explain: Long-practiced patterns can still be reshaped through effort.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says anger kept him alive inside and he worries that "managing it" will make him a target. Should the facilitator push the skill anyway?
items.explain: No single verdict. The skill aims at choice, not weakness, but his survival concern is real in his setting.
key_points: Push: managing anger is about control, not passivity
Validate: the environment shapes what is safe
Reframe: self-control as strength and strategy

cbi-23.title: Managing Risky Feelings—Stress and Anxiety
summary: Stress is usually tied to a situation and fades after; anxiety lasts longer and can come without a clear cause.
Change of any kind, good or bad, can set off stress.
Small daily hassles count as much as big events.
Long-term use changes how the brain handles stress, so stress stays a major relapse trigger early on.
Steps: name it as stress or anxiety and its cause, list options, pick one and do it. Mood surfing lets it pass.

items.stem: Selena is tense all day at work, but by dinner at home she's fine. Stress or anxiety, per the lesson?
options: Stress
Neither
Anxiety, since her tension follows a pattern that repeats every working day
Both equally
items.explain: Stress is usually set off by a situation and fades once you're out of it.

items.stem: For weeks Malik has felt uneasy and on edge, even on quiet days with nothing going on. Stress or anxiety?
options: Stress, since he is in reentry and reentry is stressful
More like anxiety
A craving
Neither
items.explain: Anxiety lasts longer and can show up without a clear trigger.

items.stem: A member says "I'm stressed" but doesn't know why. Which step does the facilitator help with first?
options: Listing every coping option
Picking a coping tool right away, since the reason does not matter for calming down
Sorting stress from anxiety and finding what's behind it
Skipping to mood surfing
items.explain: Step one figures out whether it is stress or anxiety and what is driving it.

items.stem: Darnell lands his first good job since release and his girlfriend moves in the same month. What does the lesson predict?
options: His stress will drop, because both changes are positive and solve problems
Nothing changes
His cravings will disappear
His stress may rise, since good changes stress too
items.explain: Stress responds to demands and change, good or bad.

items.stem: Holmes and Rahe's well-known life-events scale included marriage and outstanding personal achievement alongside losses. Which lesson idea does that reflect?
options: Only negative events are stressful; the positive ones were included as a control group
Marriage is the worst stressor
Positive changes can be stressful too
Stress cannot be measured
items.explain: Change itself, even welcome change, puts demands on the body.

items.stem: Rosa checks 12 items on the Daily Stressors list but says, "Nothing big is going on." What does the scoring suggest?
options: Her stress is low, since none of the items is a major life event
Her daily stress load is very high
She needs no plan
She misread the list
items.explain: Small hassles add up. Eleven or more checks puts her stress load in the very high range.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson count small daily hassles, not just big events?
items.explain: Small hassles, like bills, arguments and unstable housing, pile up and wear people down. Many unhealthy choices follow ordinary stress, not only crises.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's stress mostly comes from things outside his control: no ID, no housing, a curfew that blocks job interviews. Should the session focus on coping tools or on solving those problems?
items.explain: No single verdict. Coping tools help him survive the stress now, but practical barriers may need advocacy and problem solving.
key_points: Coping: tools lower the risk of using under stress
Solving: justice-involved people face real structural barriers
Both: pair a coping plan with a referral or problem-solving step

items.stem: In your own words, why is stress a bigger relapse risk early in recovery?
items.explain: Long-term use changes how the brain handles stress, so early recovery often feels more stressful and less manageable. That makes stress one of the strongest triggers in the first months.

items.stem: A runner coming back from an injury finds ordinary training loads feel heavier than before. Which lesson idea is this most like?
options: A system recovering from damage handles normal loads less well for a while
A cost-benefit analysis of whether to keep running or quit for good
Mood surfing
Positive events cause stress
items.explain: Like recovering tissue, a brain recovering from long use handles stress less well at first.

items.stem: Nina notices anxiety tightening her chest. Instead of reaching for a pill, she breathes and watches the feeling rise and fall. What is likely?
options: The anxiety peaks and eases without her using
The anxiety will keep building, since accepting it signals the brain that danger is real
It will vanish instantly
She'll panic
items.explain: Mood surfing applies urge-surfing logic to anxious moods: accept and let it pass.

items.stem: Which tool is the urge-surfing idea applied to anxious or stressed moods?
options: Grounding
Mood surfing
Taking a break
Counting backwards
items.explain: Mood surfing accepts the feeling and lets it pass without using to cope.

cbi-24.title: Dealing With Rejection and Failure
summary: Rejection and failure hit hard for people building a new life, and they come often in reentry.
Healthy handling: learn from it, don't take it too personally, keep it in proportion, work through it.
How someone defines themselves after a setback predicts whether they try again.
Steps: recognize the hit, think of ways to cope, choose one and do it, plan how to do better.
Step four turns a setback into learning rather than a reason to quit.

items.stem: After a third job rejection, Marco thinks, "I'm a failure. Nobody hires a felon." What is he most likely to do next?
options: Apply to more jobs with renewed energy, since anger at the rejection is motivating
Stop applying and drift toward old ways
Ask for feedback from the employer
Enroll in a training program
items.explain: Labeling oneself a failure predicts quitting. Self-definition shapes the response to setbacks.

items.stem: Same rejection, but Marco thinks, "That one didn't work. I'm someone who keeps going." What's more likely?
options: He applies again and adjusts his approach
He gets angry at the employer
He gives up just the same, since repeated rejection wears everyone down
He stops caring
items.explain: Seeing yourself as resilient makes trying again more likely.

items.stem: Carol Dweck's research on mindsets contrasts people who see ability as fixed with those who see it as growable. How does that connect to this lesson?
options: It shows failure has no effect on behavior
How people interpret failure shapes whether they keep trying
It only applies to children
It argues that rejection matters less than intelligence when it comes to persistence
items.explain: Both point to self-interpretation as a driver of persistence. Mindset studies have mixed replication results, so treat it as a useful frame, not settled law.

items.stem: "Next time I'll set my alarm an hour earlier so I'm not late to the interview." Which step is this?
options: Planning to do better next time
Recognizing the setback
Carrying out the strategy
Choosing a coping strategy
items.explain: Step four is planning what to do differently if it happens again.

items.stem: "I didn't get the apartment. I'm feeling rejected." Which step is this?
options: Doing the tool
Recognizing the rejection or setback
Planning for next time
Picking a tool
items.explain: Step one names the hit for what it is.

items.stem: In your own words, why is step four, planning for next time, the key step?
items.explain: Coping handles the feeling, but planning turns the setback into learning. It keeps the person pointed at the goal instead of treating the setback as a reason to quit.

items.stem: Paula copes with a rejected housing application by calling her sister, then plans to get a reference letter first next time. Six weeks later, a new application. What's likely?
options: She asks someone else to apply
She is better prepared and more likely to try
She doesn't apply
The same rejection, since housing decisions have nothing to do with what she does
items.explain: Planning ahead makes the next attempt stronger and keeps her in the game.

items.stem: "It's one 'no' from one landlord. It doesn't mean every landlord will say no." Which healthy response is this?
options: Keeping it in proportion
Being overly sensitive
Quitting
Learning from it, since she is drawing a lesson about landlords in general
items.explain: Keeping perspective prevents one setback from feeling like a total verdict.

items.stem: A member takes a peer's comment about his worksheet as a personal attack and shuts down. Which healthy response could help?
options: Quitting the group
Not taking it too personally, and looking for what is useful
Avoiding the peer for the rest of the program so it does not happen again
Responding with a comeback
items.explain: Healthy handling includes not being overly sensitive and learning from feedback.

items.stem: J.K. Rowling's first Harry Potter manuscript was turned down by many publishers before one accepted it. Which response from the lesson does persistence like hers illustrate?
options: Quitting early to save time
Taking each rejection personally until it builds enough anger to succeed
Avoiding risk
Keeping rejections in proportion and working through them
items.explain: Persisting through repeated rejection depends on keeping each no in perspective.

items.stem: A member says, "Every door gets shut on me since I came home." Best facilitator move?
options: Validate how often it happens, then practice the four steps on one example
Change the topic
Tell him rejection is all in his head and the doors are really open
Tell him to lower his goals
items.explain: Rejection is frequent in reentry. Validating that reality makes the skill credible.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member was rejected for a job explicitly because of his record. Should step four, "plan to do better," apply, or does it shift blame onto him?
items.explain: No single verdict. Planning gives him agency, but discrimination is real and not his fault.
key_points: Apply: he can plan strategies like targeting fair-chance employers
Caution: name the unfairness so he doesn't absorb blame
Both: separate what he controls from what he doesn't

cbi-25.title: Introducing Social Skills
summary: Risk comes from five areas: negative states, conflict, social pressure, positive moods or good news, and thinking.
No single fix holds, because risk comes from many areas at once.
Good news is risky too, because people want to celebrate.
On the chain, the situation is the trigger just before the choice; the risky act goes in the behavior box.
People slip from too much antisocial thinking or from lacking the skill to act on what they know; this module builds skills.

items.stem: Dwayne gets a good construction job after years of trouble. He then argues with his wife, uses, and fails a random test. What does the lesson draw from this?
options: The job was the wrong fix, so he should have found a different kind of work
Work causes relapse
He was never motivated
One fix rarely holds; risk comes from many areas
items.explain: A single improvement can't cover every risk area. Change takes many small adjustments.

items.stem: A city cuts crime in one district with more patrols, but problems shift to schools and housing. Which lesson idea does this mirror?
options: Risk comes from many areas, so one fix rarely holds
Patrols are the only intervention that has ever been shown to reduce crime reliably
Problems always disappear on their own
Housing has no link to risk
items.explain: Multiple risk areas need multiple changes; one lever rarely solves the system.

items.stem: "Got my GED results today, everyone wants to go out and celebrate." Which risk area?
options: Positive mood or good news
Negative state
Thinking
Conflict
items.explain: Good news can bring pressure to celebrate in risky ways.

items.stem: "My coworkers always do shots after Friday shifts and rib me if I leave." Which risk area?
options: Social pressure
Positive mood, since Friday is the end of the work week
Thinking
Negative state
items.explain: Pressure from friends, family and coworkers is the social pressure area.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson map risky situations across several life areas?
items.explain: Trouble can start in many places at once, from moods to conflict to peer pressure to good news. Mapping them shows that one change won't cover everything.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's family throws a welcome-home party with alcohol. Should he skip his own celebration?
items.explain: No single verdict. Skipping protects him, but the family's love and his reconnection matter too.
key_points: Skip: positive events are real triggers
Attend with a plan: leave early, bring a sober support
Ask: could the family host it without alcohol

items.stem: A member writes "situation: I robbed the store." What's the problem?
options: The robbery is behavior; the situation is what came just before
Nothing, since the robbery is the most important part of the story
It is a feeling
It should go under thoughts
items.explain: The situation is the trigger before the choice, not the offense itself.

items.stem: Helping a member fix his chain, what question best finds the real situation?
options: "What were the consequences?"
"What was happening right before you decided?"
"How did you feel after?"
"Why did you do it, and what were you thinking about your family at the time?"
