items.explain: Asking about the moment just before the choice locates the situation.

items.stem: A pair writes "one drink won't hurt" as a risky thought. Which counter fits best?
options: "Drinking is always wrong and I should be ashamed for thinking about it."
"One usually turns into five, and I have a test Monday."
"I'll never drink again."
"Nobody will know."
items.explain: A good counter is realistic and answers the specific thought.

items.stem: In your own words, why are counter thoughts called the first small change?
items.explain: They are a change anyone can make right away, and small thinking changes add up across many situations. They also open the way for the skills this module builds.

items.stem: Tanya knows she shouldn't go to her cousin's party, but when he pressures her she caves every time. What kind of problem is this?
options: A thinking problem, since she must be holding beliefs that support using at parties
No problem
A trauma problem
A skill problem
items.explain: Knowing better but caving to pressure points to a missing skill, which practice addresses.

items.stem: Vic believes "Rules are for suckers" and acts on it constantly. Which kind of work does he need most?
options: Skill practice, since role plays will fix the behavior without touching the beliefs
Only emotion regulation
Thought work on antisocial thinking
No work
items.explain: Lots of antisocial thinking calls for thought work; skills build on that.

cbi-26.title: Active Listening
summary: Hearing takes in sound; listening means the other person can tell you got their message.
Every skill step is labeled thinking (unseen) or action (visible).
Step 1, look at the speaker (action); Step 2, focus on what they say (thinking); Step 3, check you understood (action).
The check-back is a paraphrase, often followed by a question.
The skill is taught early partly so members listen to each other in group.

items.stem: Which shows listening, not just hearing?
options: Saying back the point in your own words
Waiting for a turn to talk
Nodding while scrolling a phone
Staying silent until they finish
items.explain: Listening means the speaker can tell you got their message.

items.stem: Kara tells her brother about her first week at work while he watches TV and says "uh huh." What is she most likely to feel?
options: Relieved
Unheard and less likely to share next time
Indifferent
Supported, since he is in the room and letting her talk without interrupting
items.explain: Hearing without listening leaves the speaker feeling dismissed.

items.stem: During a talk with his PO, Dev rehearses his reply instead of listening. What is likely?
options: He misses part of the message and replies to the wrong thing
His PO won't notice
He gives a better reply, because preparing ahead of time is usually more effective
Nothing
items.explain: Focusing means keeping attention on the speaker, not on your own response.

items.stem: Which step of Active Listening is a thinking step?
options: Check that you understood
None of them
Focus on what they're saying
Look at the speaker
items.explain: Focusing happens inside the head; looking and checking back are visible actions.

items.stem: Why does the skill label each step as thinking or action?
options: It has no purpose
So members know which steps are optional and which ones are required for the skill
To shorten the skill
So role players show thinking with a cue and observers can track it
items.explain: Labels tell members what happens inside versus outside, which matters for role plays.

items.stem: A member says eye contact feels aggressive where he grew up. Best adaptation?
options: Skip step one
Face the person and look toward them in a way that feels respectful to him
Have him close his eyes
Insist on eye contact, since it is required by the skill and he needs to adapt
items.explain: The step's purpose is showing attention and respect; cultural fit shapes how.

items.stem: Weigh it: in a prison unit, sustained eye contact can be read as a challenge. Should the facilitator still teach "look at the speaker" as written?
items.explain: No single verdict. The step signals respect, but in some settings it carries risk.
key_points: Teach as written: eye contact is a common sign of attention in many settings
Adapt: emphasize facing and attention over eye contact
Discuss: when and where each version fits

items.stem: "So you're saying a job gives me structure. Is there a placement program you'd suggest?" Which step is this?
options: Focus
Checking you understood
Asking for help
Look at the speaker
items.explain: A paraphrase plus a question is the check-back step.

items.stem: Air traffic controllers repeat back a pilot's instruction before acting. Which listening step does that resemble?
options: None
Checking that you understood
Focusing
Looking at the speaker, since controllers watch the radar screen closely
items.explain: The read-back confirms the message, the same function as paraphrasing.

items.stem: In a hostage negotiation, a negotiator says, "So you feel nobody's been listening to you." Which listening step is this?
options: Giving advice
Focusing, since the negotiator is paying full attention to the words being said
Checking back by paraphrasing
Looking at the speaker
items.explain: Paraphrasing shows understanding and builds trust, even in high-stakes settings.

items.stem: In your own words, why is active listening one of the first social skills taught?
items.explain: Members need to listen to each other for groups to work, and it is the base of every other communication skill. It also builds supportive relationships outside.

items.stem: A member skips the check-back step in a role play. What does feedback focus on?
options: Nothing
The topic he chose
Which steps observers saw, then what he might add
His tone of voice and whether he seemed confident while listening
items.explain: Feedback follows the steps, so missing ones become clear and fixable.

cbi-27.title: Understanding the Feelings of Others
summary: Empathy is a skill: read the other person's words and body cues, then name their most likely emotion.
Staying calm and open matters because the emotion shown is often about something deeper.
Checking the feeling with the person prevents acting on a misread.
Open questions get more than yes or no and show real interest.
Understanding loved ones' feelings helps rebuild the trust and accountability recovery depends on.

items.stem: Ray notices his daughter's arms are crossed, her voice is flat and she won't look up. Which step is he doing?
options: Checking the feeling with her by asking what is wrong
Asking an open question
Reading her words and body cues
Staying calm
items.explain: Step one takes in words, face, tone and posture before deciding anything.

items.stem: Which observation is most useful for step one?
options: "She's being dramatic again, like she always is."
"She probably wants money."
"She is wrong about this."
"Her voice is shaking and she keeps checking the door."
items.explain: Step one gathers cues without judging. Interpretations come later and are checked.

items.stem: Kenya snaps at her husband about dishes the night before his court date. If he stays calm and curious, what is he most likely to find?
options: That the dishes were the real issue and he should just do them more often
Nothing more
That she wants a divorce
That she's scared about the court date
items.explain: The emotion shown is often about something deeper; staying open lets you find it.

items.stem: A teacher notices a usually cheerful student picking fights all week. Using this lesson, what should she keep in mind?
options: The student has become a bully and needs immediate consequences to stop it
The student is tired
Ignore it
The anger may be covering something else, like trouble at home
items.explain: Shown emotion may mask a deeper issue. Calm openness helps discover it.

items.stem: Which line best checks a feeling, per step four?
options: "You're angry. I can tell."
"Sounds like you're under a lot of pressure. Is that right?"
"Why are you acting like this?"
"Calm down."
items.explain: Naming the feeling tentatively lets the other person correct you.

items.stem: Leo assumes his mother is angry and gets defensive. She was actually worried. What would step four have prevented?
options: Nothing, since anger and worry lead to the same kind of conversation in the end
Her worry
The need to talk
Acting on a misread and starting a fight
items.explain: Checking the feeling before reacting prevents responding to the wrong emotion.

items.stem: Which is an open question?
options: "Is it about money?"
"What can I do to help?"
"Did I do something?"
"Are you mad?"
items.explain: Open questions can't be answered yes or no, so they invite more information.

items.stem: A doctor asks, "What's been worrying you most about your health?" instead of "Any pain?" Why is that more useful?
options: It sounds friendlier only
It invites the patient to share what matters most
It avoids diagnosis
It is faster, since one broad question saves the doctor time with every patient
items.explain: Open questions bring out information a yes/no question would miss.

items.stem: In your own words, why do three thinking steps come before any action in this skill?
items.explain: Most of empathy happens inside: reading cues, naming the likely feeling and staying calm. Getting those right first makes the spoken steps accurate and less likely to escalate.

items.stem: After release, Andre keeps responding to his partner's worry with "Relax, I'm fine." What is likely over time?
options: She feels unheard and trust grows more slowly
She will relax, since steady reassurance builds trust faster than anything
She stops worrying
Nothing changes
items.explain: Understanding loved ones' feelings is part of rebuilding trust, which supports accountability.

items.stem: In your own words, why does understanding family members' feelings matter for recovery?
items.explain: Many members hurt loved ones while using. Showing understanding helps rebuild trust, and family support adds accountability that makes long-term success more likely.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says checking someone's feelings out loud ("Sounds like you're hurt") feels fake and his family would laugh. Should he use the step anyway?
items.explain: No single verdict. The step prevents misreads, but stiff wording can backfire.
key_points: Use it: confirming feelings prevents fights
Adapt: say it in his own natural words
Practice: role play until it sounds like him

cbi-28.title: Deciding to Say “No”
summary: Refusal is a planned skill: decide if it's risky, think of several ways to say no, pick one and say it, offer a safer option.
One excuse won't fit every person or setting, so have several ready.
Step three is both: decide inside, then say it out loud.
Offering an alternative keeps the relationship and gives the other person a yes.
Saying no is taking control, and it should be rehearsed across many situations.

items.stem: Before answering his boss's invite to a work happy hour, Carlos asks himself, "Does this put my goals at risk, and why for me?" Which step is this?
options: Thinking of ways to say no
Suggesting a non-risky alternative to the boss
Saying no
Deciding if it's risky for him
items.explain: Step one asks whether the situation threatens his goals, and why for him specifically.

items.stem: Nadia skips step one and agrees to "just drop by" a party. What is the likely problem?
options: She walks into a risk she never assessed
She'll enjoy it safely
She'll say no at the door
None, since dropping by briefly is a safe compromise for most people
items.explain: Without first judging the risk, people say yes on autopilot.

items.stem: A member has one refusal: "I'm on probation." Why build more?
options: More options confuse people
Probation is private
One excuse won't fit every person or setting
It is enough, since probation is a reason everyone will respect
items.explain: Different people and situations call for different ways to say no.

items.stem: A salesperson prepares several answers for common objections before a pitch. Which part of the refusal skill does this mirror?
options: Thinking of different options ahead of time
Saying the answer clearly and firmly once it has been chosen
Offering an alternative
Judging risk
items.explain: Having options ready is what lets you pick the best fit in the moment.

items.stem: Which step is both thinking and action?
options: Think of ways to say no
Decide if it's risky
Pick the best way and say it
Suggest something not risky
items.explain: You decide inside, then say it out loud.

items.stem: Jerome mumbles, "Uh, maybe not tonight, I don't know." What is his friend likely to do?
options: Accept the no, since any refusal is enough for a real friend
Push harder, sensing the no is weak
Get angry
Leave him alone forever
items.explain: A clear, confident no is harder to argue with than a hesitant one.

items.stem: A member's cousin keeps inviting him to drink. What step-four response fits?
options: "Maybe next time."
"I'll think about it."
"I'll pass on drinks, but let's watch the game Saturday."
"No, and stop asking me, because you know what I'm dealing with."
items.explain: An alternative keeps the relationship and gives the cousin something to say yes to.

items.stem: A diplomat refuses a treaty clause but proposes a joint commission instead. Which refusal step does that reflect?
options: Deciding if the clause is risky for her country
Saying no clearly
Suggesting a non-risky alternative
Brainstorming excuses
items.explain: Pairing a no with an alternative preserves the relationship.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson frame saying no as taking control?
items.explain: Refusing is an active choice about your own situation, not just dodging temptation. Framing it as control builds confidence and ownership.

items.stem: In your own words, why rehearse refusal across many situations?
items.explain: Skills practiced in one setting don't automatically transfer. Rehearsing with different people and pressures helps refusal show up wherever it's needed.

items.stem: Kai practiced saying no only to friends. At a family wedding, his uncle hands him a drink. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll leave the wedding
He refuses easily, because a skill learned with friends transfers to family automatically
His uncle won't insist
He may struggle, since this pressure is new
items.explain: Refusal needs rehearsal in many situations to generalize.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's old friend is a dealer. He wants to say no to deals but still offer an alternative to keep the friendship. Is offering an alternative wise here?
items.explain: No single verdict. Keeping the friendship has value, but continued contact may keep risk high.
key_points: Don't: the person himself may be the risk
Middle: offer only low-risk, public, time-limited plans

cbi-29.title: Communicating My Needs
summary: Two common failures: bottling it up until resentment builds, or blowing up while upset.
Step one, choose a calm time and place, is the only thinking step.
Asking permission to talk lowers defensiveness.
Describe the situation objectively, without blame, then share thoughts and feelings.
Make a request the other person can decline, and thank them either way.

items.stem: For months Dana says nothing about her brother borrowing her car without asking. One morning she screams at him. What does the lesson say happened?
options: He deserved it
Bottling up led to blowing up
She communicated her needs
She finally communicated assertively after waiting for the right moment
items.explain: Holding it in builds resentment until it explodes; both failures end in conflict.

items.stem: A pressure cooker without a release valve eventually bursts. Which pattern does that resemble?
options: Thanking them
Bottling up until it explodes
Choosing a calm time, since the cooker waits until it is ready before releasing
Asking permission
items.explain: The image matches resentment that builds unspoken until it blows.

items.stem: Which is the best moment to raise a need with a partner?
options: While she's rushing to work
A quiet evening when both are calm
Right after the argument, while the topic is still fresh
In front of her family
items.explain: Step one picks a calm time and private place.

items.stem: Rico raises his need for more help with bills right after his partner got bad news at work. What is likely?
options: She thanks him
She agrees immediately
She responds well because the topic is important and urgent
She gets defensive or shuts down
items.explain: The wrong timing makes even a fair request land badly.

items.stem: "Do you have a few minutes? There's something important I want to talk about." Which step?
options: Asking permission to talk
Thanking them
Describing the situation in neutral terms
Making the request
items.explain: Asking first gives the other person a say and lowers defensiveness.

items.stem: Which opening describes the situation objectively?
options: "We haven't had a night out together in two months."
"You clearly don't care."
"You're never home."
"You always ignore me and you're so selfish."
items.explain: Objective means what happened, without blame or labels, before sharing feelings.

items.stem: In a role play, a member opens with "You're lazy and you never help with the kids." Best coaching?
options: Tell him to skip it
Have the partner respond angrily
Rephrase as a fact, like "I've done drop-offs every day this month"
Let it go, since honesty about feelings matters more than wording
items.explain: Removing blame and labels keeps the listener from shutting down.

items.stem: Mia asks her landlord to fix a leak by Friday. He says it'll be next week. What does the skill expect her to do?
options: Withhold rent
Leave a bad review
Stay calm, accept or negotiate, and thank him
Insist on Friday, since a request that gets declined means the skill did not work
items.explain: A request can be declined. Staying calm with a no is part of the skill.

items.stem: In labor negotiations, a union proposal is rejected but talks continue respectfully. What lesson idea does this reflect?
options: A rejected proposal means communication failed and talks should end
Requests must be demands
Thanking is weakness
A request can be declined while the relationship stays intact
items.explain: Making a request, not a demand, allows a no without ending the relationship.

items.stem: In your own words, why thank someone even if they said no?
items.explain: It recognizes their effort to listen and leaves the relationship in good shape. That makes the next conversation easier.

items.stem: In your own words, how does this skill build on active listening and saying no?
items.explain: Listening helps you understand the other person's response, and refusal skills show that a no can be respectful. Together they make expressing needs a two-way exchange.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's need is urgent, his partner keeps bringing a using friend home, and there's never a calm moment. Should he wait for a calm time anyway?
items.explain: No single verdict. Calm timing improves the conversation, but delay may keep him at risk.
key_points: Wait: timing makes the request more likely to land
Act now: risk to recovery is immediate
Middle: ask permission for a short, focused talk soon

items.stem: Instead of launching in, Theo asks his sister, "Got ten minutes? Something's been on my mind." What is the likely effect?
options: She gets suspicious, since asking first makes it sound like bad news is coming
Nothing
She refuses
She feels respected and is more ready to listen
items.explain: Asking first gives the other person a say and lowers defensiveness.

items.stem: His girlfriend says she can't take the night off this week. Andre replies, "Okay. Thanks for hearing me out." Which step is this?
options: Asking permission
Making the request
Choosing a calm time
Thanking them for listening
items.explain: Ending with thanks, whatever the answer, keeps the relationship in good shape.

cbi-30.title: Engaging Social Supports
summary: Asking for help is hard: pride, not wanting to owe, fear of judgment, or past use of people.
Step 1: notice something's bothering you; Step 2: decide who can help and how.
Step 3: reach out and share thoughts, feelings and plans.
Step 4: ask their view and hear it without arguing, which is where people usually stumble.
Step 5: move from venting to planning together. Supporters need to know your risks and warning signs.

items.stem: In your own words, why is asking for help hard for many members?
items.explain: Some value independence or fear owing anyone; others feel weak, fear judgment, or have used people before. Naming these barriers makes them easier to work around.

items.stem: Tomas believes asking for help means he's weak. His job hunt stalls for a month. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll ask right away
He keeps struggling alone and stress builds
His PO will step in
He'll eventually succeed alone, since independence is a strength in reentry
items.explain: Beliefs about weakness keep people from support until problems grow.

items.stem: "I'm not sleeping, I'm snapping at people, and I keep staying in my room." Which step is this?
options: Asking for their view
Deciding who can help with the problem
Noticing something is bothering you
Making a plan
items.explain: Step one recognizes warning signs before a problem blows up.

items.stem: A member needs a ride to a job interview. Who fits step two best?
options: A safe person with a car and a free morning
His closest friend from the old block, since he is the most loyal
Whoever answers first
His sponsor, for any problem
items.explain: Step two matches a safe person to this kind of help.

items.stem: A researcher with a statistics question emails a methods expert, not her closest colleague. What lesson step is this?
options: Hearing the view without arguing, since experts know best
Thanking
Deciding who can help with this problem
Noticing the problem
items.explain: Match the helper to the kind of help you need.

items.stem: Rashad asks his aunt for advice, then rejects every suggestion with "That won't work." What is likely?
options: She stops offering help
She'll find a better idea, since pushback helps people think harder
He'll solve it himself
She'll take over
items.explain: Arguing with the answer is where people stumble; it shuts down support.

items.stem: In a role play, the actor asks for advice and immediately says, "Nah, I tried that." Best coaching?
options: Skip step four
Let the other actor argue back
Praise him for being honest about what he already tried before
Ask him to listen fully and reflect before responding
items.explain: Step four means really hearing the view before evaluating it.

items.stem: "Can you help me figure out a schedule so I'm not alone on weekends?" Which step?
options: Sharing thoughts and feelings with the person
Asking them to help solve it or plan
Deciding who
Noticing the problem
items.explain: Step five moves from talking about a problem to working out what to do.

items.stem: A manager tells a struggling employee, "I hear you. Let's figure out a plan together." What shift does this mark?
options: From listening to judging the employee's performance
From work to personal life
From venting to problem solving
From formal to informal
items.explain: Planning together stops the loop of complaining and creates action.

items.stem: In your own words, why should a support person know your risky situations and warning signs?
items.explain: They can't help prevent a relapse they can't see coming. Knowing triggers and slip signs lets them step in early.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member is willing to share his triggers with his new girlfriend but not his offense history. Should he share it now?
items.explain: No single verdict. Fuller disclosure helps support, but timing and safety in a new relationship matter.
key_points: Share: full information makes support effective
Wait: trust and safety need time
Middle: share what she needs for his plan and set a time for the rest

items.stem: A member's best support moved out of state. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Give up
Check in regularly and adjust the network as things change
Wait until the person moves back, since replacing support feels disloyal
Rely on phone only
items.explain: Networks need upkeep and adjustment when people move or prove a poor fit.

items.stem: Marcus ignores weeks of bad sleep and irritability. What does the lesson predict?
options: The signs fade by themselves, since most stress passes with time
The problem grows until it blows up
He'll ask for help right away
Nothing
items.explain: Step one is noticing warning signs early, before a problem explodes.

cbi-31.title: Communicating Assertively
summary: Assertive means honest and confident while respecting the other person; not passive, not aggressive.
Step 1: work out what about the moment might blow up, and why it bothers you.
Step 2: set your ultimate goal, which keeps the response from becoming a fight.
Step 3: list what you might say and weigh options against the goal.
Step 4: say it calmly, linking their action to your feeling and what you want.

items.stem: "When you smoke weed in my car, I feel worried about my probation. I need you to not bring it in." Which style?
options: Passive-aggressive
Passive
Aggressive, since he is telling his friend what to do
Assertive
items.explain: Honest, specific and respectful, with a clear request.

items.stem: Sam says nothing when his roommate keeps eating his food, then complains to others. Which style?
options: Direct
Passive
Aggressive
Assertive
items.explain: Staying quiet while resentment builds is passive.

items.stem: A nurse tells a surgeon, "When you skip the checklist, I worry about safety. I need us to finish it." Which style is this, and why does it matter in hospitals?
options: Aggressive, since nurses shouldn't challenge surgeons
Passive, since it's polite
None
Assertive; it raises a safety concern while keeping respect
items.explain: Assertiveness in medicine is often taught as a safety skill: clear, respectful and specific.

items.stem: A member wants to confront a friend who used in his car. Before speaking, what should he decide?
options: What the group thinks
His ultimate goal, like staying clean and keeping the friendship
The strongest thing to say so his friend never does it again
Whether to cut him off
items.explain: The goal keeps the response from turning into a fight.

items.stem: Javi skips step two and just reacts: "You're an idiot for doing that." What is likely?
options: Nothing
An argument and possibly a lost friendship
His friend thanks him
His friend apologizes, since blunt honesty usually works with close friends
items.explain: Without a goal, responses drift toward aggression.

items.stem: "I could kick him out, never drive him again, or talk it through." Which step?
options: Saying it
Setting the goal
Deciding why it could lead to conflict
Listing what he might say
items.explain: Step three lists options and weighs them against the goal.

items.stem: A member's only option is "never speak to him again." What should the facilitator prompt?
options: Tell him to forgive
Skip to step four
Accept it, since he knows his friend best and cutting off is safest
Ask him to list a few more and weigh each against his goal
items.explain: Comparing several options against the goal finds the strongest one.

items.stem: Which is a well-formed statement for step four?
options: "You always mess up my life."
"Whatever, forget it."
"When you're late picking me up, I feel stressed. I need a text if you're running behind."
"I hate when you do that."
items.explain: It names the behavior, the feeling, then what you want.

items.stem: Maya tells her mother, "When you criticize my parenting in front of the kids, I feel undermined. I'd like us to talk privately." What is a likely outcome?
options: Her mother escalates, since any challenge to a parent leads to a fight
Her mother cuts her off
Nothing changes
Her mother is more likely to listen without feeling attacked
items.explain: Linking a specific action to a feeling and a request lowers defensiveness.

items.stem: In your own words, how is assertiveness different from aggression?
items.explain: Assertiveness states what you think and want while respecting the other person; aggression ignores or attacks them. The goal is to be heard without causing harm.

items.stem: In your own words, why are there three thinking steps before speaking?
items.explain: Figuring out the conflict, the goal and the options first prevents reacting on impulse. It makes the final statement aimed and calm.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says that on the unit, if he pauses to think through three steps, others will see hesitation as weakness. Should he still use the full skill there?
items.explain: No single verdict. Thinking first prevents escalation, but the setting may reward quick responses.
key_points: Use it: rehearsal makes the steps fast enough to be invisible
Adapt: a shortened version for high-pressure moments
Context: some situations call for leaving instead

cbi-32.title: Responding to Criticism
summary: You can't control what others say, only your response.
Constructive criticism aims to help; derogatory criticism aims to put you down. Keep the first, let go of the second.
Step 1: listen to the message, not the tone; Step 2: stay calm and decide what's useful.
Step 3: repeat it back and ask about anything unclear; Step 4: thank them.
Step 5: make changes that help you succeed. Learning from criticism beats learning from failure.

items.stem: "Your reports are late, and that slows the whole team. Can we set an earlier draft date?" Which kind of criticism?
options: Neither
Derogatory, since it points out a problem in front of the team
Bullying
Constructive
items.explain: It aims to help improve, with a specific suggestion.

items.stem: "You'll never be anything but a junkie." Which kind?
options: Derogatory
Advice
Constructive
Feedback
items.explain: It's meant to put down, not help; the skill is to let it go.

items.stem: A coworker yells, "You were rude to that customer!" Pablo focuses on the yelling and fires back. What does he miss?
options: A promotion
An apology
Nothing, since the tone shows the coworker isn't worth listening to at all
A possibly valid point about how he treated the customer
items.explain: Tone can be harsh even when the point is valid; step one separates them.

items.stem: A drill sergeant shouts that a recruit's rifle is dirty. Which response matches step one?
options: Shout back
Focus on the content: the rifle needs cleaning
Report him
Ignore it, since shouting means the criticism is personal and derogatory
items.explain: Listening for the message, not the delivery, is the first step.

items.stem: A member's PO criticizes his job search harshly. What does step two ask?
options: Defend himself right away so the PO knows the criticism is unfair
Agree with everything
Calm down, then decide what part is true or helpful
Ignore it
items.explain: Calming skills come first, then sorting the useful from the hurtful.

items.stem: Lia's boss says, "You're careless, and you've made three errors this week." Lia stays calm and sorts it. What's the most likely useful takeaway?
options: That her boss dislikes her and nothing in the comment can be used
She should quit
The three errors are worth fixing; "careless" can be let go
She should argue the label
items.explain: Keep the useful part (specific errors) and let go of the put-down (label).

items.stem: "So you're saying I need to be more patient with customers who complain. What should I do when they yell?" Which step?
options: Repeating the message back and asking about anything unclear
Thanking them for raising it in the first place
Staying calm
Making changes
items.explain: Repeating back shows understanding; the question clears up confusion.

items.stem: In your own words, why thank someone for criticism?
items.explain: It sounds odd, but thanks calm the exchange and show you're open. People become more willing to help you in the future.

items.stem: Rene thanks his supervisor for pointing out a mistake. What is a likely effect?
options: Nothing
The conversation cools and she's more willing to help
The supervisor sees it as sarcasm and gets angrier at him
Rene looks weak
items.explain: Thanking lowers tension and builds goodwill.

items.stem: After criticism about handling angry customers, what fits step five?
options: Avoid angry customers by switching shifts without telling anyone
Ask a coworker how they handle difficult customers, then try it
Promise to never upset anyone
Ignore it
items.explain: Acting on the useful part turns criticism into improvement.

items.stem: An author revises a chapter after an editor's notes. Why does the lesson say this beats learning from failure?
options: Acting on feedback early prevents the costlier lesson of failing
Editors are always right
Failure is a better teacher, since public mistakes are more memorable
Revision is optional
items.explain: Learning from criticism is cheaper than learning from consequences.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's father says, "You're a disappointment, and you need to get a job." Part of it is derogatory, part useful. Should the member engage with it at all?
items.explain: No single verdict. The job point may be useful, but the put-down can be painful and repeated.
key_points: Engage: take the useful part, like the job, and act on it
Protect: set a boundary on the put-downs
Both: thank him for caring about the job and name the hurt separately

items.stem: His supervisor says, "Your safety checks are sloppy." Before reacting, what does step three suggest Jorge say?
options: "That's not true, I've done them every single day this month without a problem."
"Fine."
"So the checks aren't thorough enough. Which part should I tighten?"
"Who complained?"
items.explain: Repeating the message and asking about unclear parts confirms understanding before responding.

cbi-33.title: Avoiding Trouble with Others
summary: Avoiding risky people helps, but many members won't or can't end long-standing relationships.
Step 1: decide if a plan or offer could lead to trouble.
Step 2: call up your goals, which is what's new compared with the basic refusal skill.
Step 3: line up several ways to say no; Step 4: tell them you can't take part, offering a safer version.
The refusal can keep the relationship while removing the risky part.

items.stem: Luis's brother uses and lives two doors down. Luis plans to "just avoid him." What does the lesson predict?
options: Luis will cut off the family
Contact will happen anyway, and he'll need refusal skills
Avoidance will work, since the brother will stop coming around once he gets the hint
The brother will move
items.explain: Many relationships can't simply be avoided, so refusal inside the relationship is needed.

items.stem: In your own words, why isn't avoidance enough for many members?
items.explain: Family and longtime friends who use are often people members won't or can't cut off, and people who use often want company. So members need ways to refuse while staying connected.

items.stem: "I'm six weeks sober and two months from finishing probation." Which step is this?
options: Telling them
Listing ways to say no
Deciding if it's risky
Calling up his goals
items.explain: Recalling goals gives a reason to refuse that's bigger than the moment.

items.stem: When his friend shows up with a bottle, Omar thinks about his daughter's graduation next month. What does that do for his refusal?
options: Makes him angry at his friend
Nothing
Makes it harder, since thinking about family stirs emotions that trigger drinking
Gives him a stronger reason to say no
items.explain: Goals provide motivation that outweighs the pull of the moment.

items.stem: An Olympic swimmer turns down late nights with teammates by thinking of the trials in six weeks. What step does this mirror?
options: Calling up goals before refusing
Deciding if it's risky
Offering an alternative
Listing ways to say no to teammates without hurting them
items.explain: Recalling a goal is what makes the no feel worth it.

items.stem: "My buddy wants to come over tonight with a bottle." Which question starts the skill?
options: What are my goals?
Could this lead to trouble for me?
What will I offer instead?
How can I say no without hurting him and losing a friend I care about?
items.explain: Step one decides whether the plan puts him at risk.

items.stem: A member's only plan is to tell his cousin "Don't come over." What should he add?
options: More options, like asking him to bring food instead, or just being honest
A lie
Nothing, since one clear answer is always better than having several ready
A threat
items.explain: Several options help when the first one doesn't work.

items.stem: Which response fits step four best?
options: "Sure, just one."
"Get out of here with that."
"I appreciate it, but I can't drink. Come over and we'll grill instead."
"Maybe later."
items.explain: Saying clearly you can't take part, plus a safer version, keeps the relationship.

items.stem: Teo tells his old friend, "I can't smoke anymore, but I'm down to play ball Sunday." What's a likely result?
options: The friend cuts him off, since any refusal ends a friendship built on using
Nothing changes
The friendship continues without the risky part
He gets pressured more
items.explain: The refusal removes the risk while keeping the connection.

items.stem: In Shakespeare's Hamlet, Polonius advises "neither a borrower nor a lender be." A modern reader wants to refuse a loan but keep a friend. What does this lesson suggest?
options: Follow Polonius strictly and end the friendship to avoid all risk
Say clearly no to the loan and offer another kind of help
Avoid the friend
Lend the money anyway
items.explain: The skill keeps the relationship while removing the risky part.

items.stem: In your own words, why does this skill have three thinking steps before the one action step?
items.explain: Most of the work is deciding the risk, recalling goals and planning ways to refuse. That prep makes the spoken refusal clear and firm in the moment.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's mother drinks every night and expects him to join her at dinner. Should he keep eating with her?
items.explain: No single verdict. Family dinners matter for connection, but nightly exposure is a real risk.
key_points: Keep: refuse the drink but keep the meal
Limit: fewer dinners or a different meal time
Talk: ask her for a drink-free dinner once a week

cbi-34.title: Getting Involved in a Positive Activity
summary: A lack of prosocial activities and supports is itself a risk factor.
Avoiding risky people and places is half the job; filling the time is the other half.
Many feel awkward in social settings because they're used to being under the influence; practice reduces it.
Steps: identify an activity, think of ways in, pick the best time and route, then get involved.
New activities bring new, non-using people into a member's life.

items.stem: Ken has cut off his old crew but has nothing to replace them. What does the lesson predict?
options: Empty time and loneliness, which raise risk
No change
Lower risk, since cutting off the crew removes the main danger in his life
He'll find new friends automatically
items.explain: Avoiding is half the job; filling the time is the other half.

items.stem: In your own words, why is a lack of positive activities a risk factor?
items.explain: Empty time and few prosocial connections leave space for old habits and old friends. Positive activities fill that space and bring new supports.

items.stem: At his first sober community event, Darius feels stiff and out of place. What does the lesson say about this?
options: He should drink to relax
It's normal and eases with practice
He should leave immediately
It means he isn't suited to social events and should skip them
items.explain: Many feel awkward because they're used to socializing under the influence.

items.stem: A public speaker who always used notes feels lost without them at first. What does the lesson suggest about her discomfort?
options: Practice will make the new way feel more natural
It proves she needs notes forever and should not try to change
She should quit speaking
It's permanent
items.explain: Discomfort with a new way of doing something shrinks with repetition.

items.stem: "I could ask someone who already goes, or check the community board." Which step?
options: Picking the best time
Getting involved
Identifying a positive activity to try
Thinking of ways to get involved
items.explain: Step two lists routes into the activity.

items.stem: "Is your volunteer group taking new people?" Which step?
options: Identifying an activity
Getting involved
Thinking of ways in
Picking the best time
items.explain: Step four is the action of actually following through.

items.stem: Marisol plans to join a church choir, picks Wednesday rehearsals, but never goes. What does the lesson say about this?
options: Step four is where people stall; the plan needs action
She should choose a new activity
The plan alone is progress, since thinking about joining counts as involvement
She doesn't like singing
items.explain: The only action step is where the change actually happens.

items.stem: A member says he'll "get around to" joining the rec league. Best facilitator move?
options: Sign him up yourself
Accept it, since pushing creates resistance and he will join when ready
Drop it
Help him pick a day and practice asking how to sign up
items.explain: Turning the plan into a specific action and rehearsing it helps him follow through.

items.stem: A member's plan reads: "Join something healthy." What does step three call for?
options: A list of 10 options
A deadline only
A specific activity, time and route, like Tuesday's 6 p.m. class
Keep it open-ended so he can pick whatever feels right in the moment
items.explain: Step three is a concrete plan with action steps, like earlier goal setting.

items.stem: After two months of Saturday volunteering, Rachel has met several people who don't use. What else does the lesson predict?
options: Her support network widens
She'll lose interest
Her risk goes up
Nothing beyond the activity itself, since volunteering does not build friendships
items.explain: New activities bring new, non-using people into a member's life.

items.stem: Sociologist Robert Putnam's "Bowling Alone" argued that joining clubs and leagues builds social ties. How does that relate to this lesson?
options: Group activities create new connections that can support change
It proves isolation is healthy
It shows bowling is risky
It suggests clubs mainly matter for entertainment and have little effect on behavior
items.explain: Shared activities create social networks, which the lesson relies on for new supports.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member wants to join a dance class but every social dance event in his area serves alcohol. Should he pursue it?
items.explain: No single verdict. Dance is a positive activity, but the setting may expose him to drinking.
key_points: Pursue: classes are structured and he can leave before social time
Avoid: early recovery may not handle that exposure
Adapt: find a class at a community center or gym

cbi-35.title: Celebrating a Positive Event
summary: Good news is a high-risk situation, especially with pressure from others to celebrate.
Step 1: decide if an accomplishment is worth celebrating, big or small.
Step 2: pick a healthy reward that moves a goal forward, not just one that avoids harm.
Step 3: follow through; skipping the reward leaves the win unmarked.
It is the shortest skill in the module, three steps, followed by the goal readiness check.

items.stem: Victor finishes probation. His old friends want to take him out "for one night." What does the lesson predict?
options: No risk at all
His friends will celebrate sober
A low-risk night, since celebrating a real achievement is good for recovery
One of his best days could turn into one of his worst
items.explain: Using to celebrate can turn a milestone into a setback. Good news is a high-risk situation.

items.stem: Some lottery winners report new problems after the win, like pressure from relatives and old friends. Which lesson idea does that echo?
options: Only bad events are risky
Money always causes harm, so big rewards should be avoided by everyone
Good luck guarantees happiness
Positive events can bring new risks and pressures
items.explain: Positive events carry their own risks, especially with outside pressure.

items.stem: "I made it 90 days clean." Which step is this person doing?
options: Deciding the accomplishment is worth celebrating
Rating confidence
Following through
Picking a healthy reward that moves a goal forward
items.explain: Step one recognizes a win, big or small, as worth marking.

items.stem: A member says, "Thirty days is nothing, why celebrate?" Best response?
options: Move on
Agree, since only long stretches like a year deserve celebrating in recovery
Say small wins count and help him name one he's proud of
Tell him he's being negative
items.explain: Small wins are worth marking; recognizing them builds motivation.

items.stem: Which reward best fits step two?
options: Buying new sneakers
Sleeping in
A park day with his son, which supports his goal of being a present father
A night of video games alone
items.explain: The reward should move a goal forward, not just avoid harm.

items.stem: A member picks "buy a new phone" as his reward. What should the facilitator explore?
options: A cheaper option
How the reward could also move one of his goals forward
Whether he can afford it
Nothing, since any reward that does not involve using is a good enough choice
items.explain: The skill asks for a reward tied to a goal, like a phone for job applications.

items.stem: A graduate student celebrates finishing her thesis by attending a conference where she'll meet future employers. Which step does this reflect?
options: Avoiding risk
Deciding it's worth celebrating, since finishing a thesis is a big deal
Choosing a reward that also moves a goal forward
Following through
items.explain: The reward does double duty: it marks the win and advances a goal.

items.stem: Kyle plans to celebrate with a dinner with his mother but never calls her. What does the lesson say?
options: He'll celebrate later
No harm, since thinking about the reward is enough to mark the win
Nothing
The win goes unmarked and motivation can fade
items.explain: Skipping the reward leaves the win unmarked.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the skill insist on actually following through on the reward?
items.explain: A planned reward that never happens doesn't mark the win. Following through makes the success feel real and reinforces the effort behind it.

items.stem: In your own words, what does the goal readiness check at the end of the module do?
items.explain: Members rate importance and confidence for their short-term goal and list steps taken. It shows progress over time and prompts a new goal if one is met.

items.stem: At the module's end, Rosa's confidence rating jumps from 4 to 8, and she has met her goal. What comes next?
options: She stops setting goals, since meeting one means she has finished the work
She repeats the old goal
Nothing
She sets a new short-term goal
items.explain: When a goal is met, a new one is set to keep momentum.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's family insists on toasting his release at a big dinner. He wants to celebrate with them. Should he attend?
items.explain: No single verdict. Family celebration matters, but a toast is a direct trigger.
key_points: Attend: plan a non-alcoholic toast and an exit line
Skip: the risk may be too high this early
Adjust: ask the family for a dry dinner and a separate party

cbi-36.title: Introduction to Problem Solving
summary: Three steps: identify the problem and goal, brainstorm and pick the best option, plan and try the solution.
Problem solving is a healthy alternative to ignoring or numbing problems.
"Now" problems demand an instant response; "later" problems leave time to plan.
Delaying a now problem buys time to think and get help, even though the problem remains.
Good practice problems have no single obvious fix, involve other people, and ideally connect to use.

items.stem: Riding with friends, Isiah sees them start to smoke weed. Which kind of problem?
options: Not a problem
A long-term problem
A later problem, since he can figure out what to do after the ride ends
A now problem
items.explain: It demands an immediate response; that's a now, or in-your-face, problem.

items.stem: Ana just got fired and has a week of savings. Which kind of problem?
options: A later problem, with time to plan
Not a problem
A crisis only
A now problem, since losing a job is urgent
items.explain: She has time to think and plan, so it's a time-to-think problem.

items.stem: A friend offers Isiah a hit in the car. Isiah says, "Hold up, I need to make a call first," and steps out at the next stop. What has he done?
options: Avoided all risk forever
Lied
Solved the problem for good, since stepping out means the friend will not ask again
Turned a now problem into a later one
items.explain: Delaying gives him time to think and plan, even though the problem itself remains.

items.stem: A negotiator facing a sudden demand says, "Let me take that to my team and get back to you tomorrow." What lesson tool is this?
options: Setting a goal
Avoiding the problem
Buying time on a now problem
Brainstorming options with the team before giving any answer at all
items.explain: Stalling gives room for a cooler, planned response.

items.stem: Which line best buys time in a pressure moment?
options: "Never ask me that again."
"Fine, whatever, let's just go."
"I'm good for now, let me grab a soda and think."
"You're a bad influence."
items.explain: A neutral stall creates space to respond with a cooler head.

items.stem: Kim ignores a growing pile of unpaid fines, hoping they'll go away. What does the lesson predict?
options: Nothing
They'll be forgotten, since courts often drop old fines if nobody follows up
The problem usually grows
Her PO will handle it
items.explain: Ignoring or numbing a problem usually makes it bigger. Problem solving offers a structured alternative.

items.stem: In your own words, why is problem solving called a healthy alternative to avoiding?
items.explain: Many people ignore problems or numb them with substances, and the problems grow. A structured method gives a way to face them without trouble.

items.stem: Which is the correct order of the problem solving steps?
options: Identify problem and goal, brainstorm and pick, plan and try
Plan, try, identify
Brainstorm, identify, plan
Pick, plan, brainstorm
items.explain: The skill starts with defining the problem and goal before generating options.

items.stem: Which makes the best practice problem for this module?
options: Remembering a birthday
Choosing a lunch
Replacing a lost Social Security card, which has a set list of steps
A roommate who keeps using in the apartment
items.explain: Good problems have no single checklist fix, involve others, and ideally connect to use.

items.stem: In your own words, why should practice problems involve other people and no obvious fix?
items.explain: Problems with set procedures don't need the skill. Problems involving people and tradeoffs give real practice, and they're reused through the next four lessons.

items.stem: In your own words, why is problem solving treated as an advanced social skill?
items.explain: It bundles earlier skills: reading feelings, communicating needs, refusing and managing emotions. Each step draws on those, so it comes after they're in place.
key_points: Draws on emotion and social tools

items.stem: Weigh it: in a car with friends who start smoking, a member says stalling isn't possible; he can't get out until they reach the house. What's the best course?
items.explain: No single verdict. Delay tools may be limited, but some response is still possible.
key_points: Speak: a clear no and window down
Plan: ask to be dropped at the next stop
Prevent: in future, drive himself or check plans first

items.stem: A member jumps straight to "I'll just move out" before saying what the problem is. Which step did he skip?
options: Brainstorming
Nothing; moving is a fine first step
Identifying the problem and goal
Planning and trying, since he has not worked out how he will move
items.explain: The skill starts by defining the problem and goal; jumping to a solution skips the step that guides everything else.

cbi-37.title: Identifying the Problem and Goal
summary: Step 1 has two halves: an objective problem statement and a specific goal.
Objective means facts, without feelings, biases or assumptions; subjective means opinion or interpretation.
Opinion clue words like best, worst, awful or "I think" flag a subjective statement.
Many conflicts begin with a wrong guess about what someone else is thinking.
Goals must be within the member's control and should weigh what others think and feel.

items.stem: Which statement is objective?
options: "My roommate is the worst."
"I think he wants me to relapse."
"My roommate has used in the living room three times this week."
"My roommate is disrespectful and lazy."
items.explain: It sticks to facts without interpretation.

items.stem: "He looked at me like he wanted to fight." Objective or subjective?
options: Objective, since it describes exactly what she saw
Neither
Subjective; it assumes his intent
Objective, since it's a feeling
items.explain: Claiming to know someone's intent is an interpretation.

items.stem: Which word flags an opinion?
options: Apartment
Awful
Three
Tuesday
items.explain: Words like awful, best or terrible signal interpretation.

items.stem: A news editor cuts "a disastrous policy" from a straight news story and writes "a policy that cut funding by 20 percent." What is she doing?
options: Adding bias
Making the article more persuasive for readers who agree
Hiding the truth
Replacing a subjective term with an objective one
items.explain: Removing opinion words leaves only verifiable facts.

items.stem: "I feel uneasy about how he's looking at me." Is this objective, per the lesson?
options: No, because all feelings are subjective by definition
Yes; reporting your own feeling counts as objective
Only if he agrees
No, it assumes intent
items.explain: Stating your own feeling is a fact about you. Claiming to know his intent is not.

items.stem: Rashida assumes her coworker's silence means he's angry at her. She confronts him. He was just tired. What does the lesson say?
options: Her instinct was right, since silence usually signals anger
She should avoid him
It doesn't matter
Many conflicts start from a wrong guess about someone's thoughts
items.explain: Misreading another's intent is a common start to conflict.

items.stem: In Othello, Iago persuades Othello that Desdemona is unfaithful, and Othello acts on the false belief. Which lesson idea does this tragedy illustrate?
options: Opinion words help clarify
Goals must be in your control
Acting on a misread of someone else's intent leads to conflict
Objective statements can still lead to conflict between people
items.explain: The play turns on a wrong guess about another person's thoughts, the trap the lesson warns about.

items.stem: Which goal is within the member's control?
options: "Get my ex to apologize."
"Show up prepared to my next PO meeting."
"Make my roommate stop using."
"Get a different probation officer."
items.explain: A goal must be something the member can actually do.

items.stem: A member's goal is "My boss stops picking on me." Best reframe?
options: "Ignore the boss"
Something he controls, like "Ask for a private meeting to clarify expectations"
"Quit"
Keep it, since the boss's behavior really is the problem to be solved
items.explain: Reframing to an action in his control makes the goal workable.

items.stem: Setting a goal about a roommate who uses, what should the member consider after picturing his ideal outcome?
options: What the roommate thinks and feels
Nothing more
His own feelings only, since this is his problem and his goal
What the landlord wants
items.explain: Considering the other person's view leads to a goal that respects everyone involved.

items.stem: In your own words, why should a goal account for what others involved think and feel?
items.explain: Goals that ignore others often spark conflict and fail. Considering their perspective leads to goals that are more realistic and respectful, building on the empathy skill.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member insists, "My PO is racist," and backs it with several incidents. Should the facilitator push him to rewrite it "objectively"?
items.explain: No single verdict. Facts strengthen his case and his planning, but demanding neutrality can feel like denying a real experience.
key_points: Push: listing incidents objectively is powerful and actionable
Respect: his interpretation may be accurate
Middle: keep both, the facts and how he reads them

items.stem: Kiara tells her roommate, "I feel anxious when there's weed in the apartment," instead of "You're trying to make me relapse." What is the likely difference?
options: The roommate will move out
The roommate is less likely to get defensive
None, since both statements carry the same message about the weed
Kiara loses credibility
items.explain: Reporting your own feeling is objective and lands better than claiming to know someone's intent.

cbi-38.title: Brainstorming Options
summary: Step 2: brainstorm many options without judging, then weigh each and pick the best.
Keeping generating separate from judging lets more options surface.
Weigh realistic positives and negatives for yourself and others, and whether each option meets the goal.
Best option: closest to the goal, keeps you out of trouble, doesn't hurt others.
Tunnel vision, believing there's only one way, keeps people stuck.

items.stem: During brainstorming, a member says, "That idea's stupid, cross it off." What rule is broken?
options: Weighing consequences for others involved in the problem
Generate first, judge second
Plan and try
Pick the best option
items.explain: Judging during generating shuts down options early.

items.stem: A group lists 12 ideas, some unrealistic, before evaluating. Another group judges each idea as it comes and lists 3. What does the lesson predict?
options: The second group finds better solutions, since judging early saves time and effort
Neither works
Both equal
The first group has better odds of finding one that works
items.explain: More options mean better chances one fits.

items.stem: Design firms often run "no bad ideas" sessions before critique. Which lesson principle does that mirror?
options: Weighing consequences for each design before any sketches are drawn
Separating generating from judging
Picking the best
Tunnel vision
items.explain: Keeping phases apart lets unusual options surface.

items.stem: A member's option is "Move out tomorrow." What does weighing consequences require?
options: List realistic positives and negatives for him and others, then mark if it meets the goal
Mark it as good or bad based on the facilitator's experience with moving
Skip it
Ask the group to vote
items.explain: Each option gets real pros and cons for everyone involved, plus a goal check.

items.stem: In your own words, how does weighing consequences here connect to the Behavior Chain?
items.explain: It works like the consequences link of the chain: look ahead at what each choice is likely to bring before acting. It's the same habit of thinking forward.

items.stem: Which option best fits the rule for choosing?
options: Asking the landlord about a room transfer, which meets the goal without harm
Moving in with an old using friend
Telling the roommate off loudly, which feels good but starts a fight
Doing nothing
items.explain: Best = closest to the goal, keeps you out of trouble, and respects others.

items.stem: Jamie picks an option that meets his goal but would hurt his sister. What should he do?
options: Ask her permission later
Go ahead, since meeting the goal is what matters most in problem solving
Ignore the harm
Return to the list and choose another
items.explain: If the chosen option harms self or others, choose again.

items.stem: "The only way to deal with my roommate stealing is to beat him up." What is this?
options: A good option
Objective thinking
Weighing consequences quickly and honestly
Tunnel vision
items.explain: Believing there is only one way keeps people stuck and in trouble.

items.stem: Historians note that before World War I, some generals had only one mobilization plan and felt locked into it. What lesson idea does that resemble?
options: Weighing consequences
Choosing the best option
Generating options freely, since the generals had studied many plans
Tunnel vision: one plan leaves no room to choose
items.explain: Having only one way forward narrows choices and can escalate a crisis.

items.stem: A member insists, "There's nothing else I can do." Best facilitator move?
options: Tell him he's wrong
Move on
Agree, since some problems really have only one solution available
Invite him and the group to brainstorm, even wild ideas
items.explain: Brainstorming breaks tunnel vision by surfacing new options.

items.stem: After brainstorming alone, a member has only two ideas. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Choose randomly
Pick the better of the two, since more options only make choosing harder
Run ideas past others to add more
Start over tomorrow
items.explain: Good problem solvers seek input to widen their options.

items.stem: Weigh it: the option closest to a member's goal is to report his roommate's use to the landlord, which could get the roommate evicted. Should he choose it?
items.explain: No single verdict. It protects his sobriety and housing, but harms the roommate and may carry social risk.
key_points: Choose: his recovery and lease are at stake
Reconsider: harm to others counts in the rule
Middle: talk to the roommate first, then escalate if needed

cbi-39.title: Planning and Trying Your Solution
summary: Step 3 means planning the chosen option and then actually trying it.
What, when, where and how is the fallback when a plan won't come together.
Anticipating barriers and naming helpers raises the odds the plan works.
Rehearse plans that involve other people; non-social plans need a step list.
Members with weaker skills may need exact scripted words, not just a skill name.

items.stem: "I'll text him Thursday after work and tell him I'm not coming to the party." What has this plan answered?
options: Nothing specific
Only the barriers he expects his friend to raise
What, when and how
Only the goal
items.explain: A concrete plan states what you'll do, when, where and how.

items.stem: A member's plan is "Be honest with my friend." Group is stuck. Best facilitator move?
options: Walk through what he'll say, when, where and how
Move to a new problem
Accept it, since honesty is the core of the plan and details can come later
Pick a plan for him
items.explain: The four questions turn a vague intention into an executable plan.

items.stem: Isiah expects his friend may get angry. He plans to stay calm and remind him he values the friendship. If the friend does get angry, what's likely?
options: Isiah handles it better because he planned for it
The plan fails anyway
The friend apologizes
Isiah is caught off guard and gives in, since anger is hard to plan for
items.explain: Naming likely barriers in advance prepares a response.

items.stem: Mountaineers plan for storms, altitude sickness and gear failure before a summit push. Which planning element is this?
options: Choosing what, when and where for the climb
Brainstorming
Rewarding success
Anticipating barriers
items.explain: Planning for what could go wrong is what makes plans survive contact with reality.

items.stem: "My sponsor will check in with me after, and I'll use Deciding to Say No." Which part of the plan is this?
options: Anticipating barriers
Evaluating
The goal
Naming helpers and the skill to use
items.explain: Plans name who can help and which practiced skill fits.

items.stem: One member's plan is to ask his boss for his job back; another's is to start a job search online. Which needs a role play?
options: The boss conversation; the search needs a step list
Only the job search
Neither
Both, since every plan in this module must be role played
items.explain: Rehearsal is for interpersonal plans; non-social plans need concrete steps.

items.stem: Tavo role-plays asking his mom for a place to stay three times before the real call. What does the lesson predict?
options: No difference
He changes his mind
He sounds scripted and the call goes worse than if he had improvised
The real call goes more smoothly
items.explain: Practicing the words builds fluency and confidence for the real moment.

items.stem: A member with limited reading skills writes "talk to mom." What help fits?
options: Assign a different problem
Leave it, since he knows what he means and writing more is a burden
Help him script the exact words, like "Mom, can I stay two weeks while I find work?"
Have someone else talk to his mom
items.explain: Some members need help writing exact words, not just naming a skill.

items.stem: In your own words, why does naming a skill sometimes fall short in a plan?
items.explain: Knowing a skill's name doesn't mean you know what to say under pressure. Exact words give members with weaker skills something concrete to fall back on.

items.stem: In your own words, why does problem solving need a concrete plan at the end?
items.explain: Without a plan, defining the problem and choosing an option don't change anything. The plan turns an intention into specific actions.

items.stem: A city council votes to "improve parks" but never sets a budget, timeline or owner. What does the lesson predict?
options: The council is dissolved
The parks improve anyway, since public support is enough to make it happen
Little changes, because there's no concrete plan
Parks get worse
items.explain: A decision without a what/when/who plan rarely becomes action.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's plan is to confront his abusive father about past harm. Should the group role-play it?
items.explain: No single verdict. Rehearsal builds confidence, but role-playing trauma in group can overwhelm him.
key_points: Rehearse: practice reduces fear and improves outcome
Caution: trauma content may need a counselor
Middle: rehearse only the opening lines and plan support afterward

cbi-40.title: Putting It all Together
summary: This is guided practice of the full model, with little new content.
Every scenario starts by sorting it as a now or later problem.
A social or emotion regulation skill can sometimes resolve a now problem outright.
On a member's real problem, the group offers ideas but the member decides.
Evaluating a plan includes rating it, rewarding yourself and figuring out what to change.

items.stem: Before any brainstorming, what question starts every scenario?
options: What's the goal?
What is the best option for everyone involved?
Who can help?
Does this need an answer right now?
items.explain: The now/later sort decides whether to buy time or work all three steps.

items.stem: Scenario: a coworker offers a pill on break. The group starts filling the brainstorming chart. Best move?
options: Skip the scenario
Assign it as homework
Let them continue, since a full brainstorm always produces the best result
Sort it first: it's a now problem, so name a skill to use right away
items.explain: Now problems call for a quick skill or stall, not a full chart in the moment.

items.stem: Offered a drink at a barbecue, Ray uses his refusal skill and the host drops it. What does the lesson say about this case?
options: He avoided the problem
He still needs to brainstorm and plan, since every problem needs all three steps
It was not a real problem
A skill can resolve a now problem outright
items.explain: Sometimes a social or emotion regulation skill finishes the problem in the moment.

items.stem: A member brings a real problem about his partner. The group strongly favors one option he dislikes. Who makes the final call?
options: The member
The facilitator
A vote
The group, since consensus is the rule for every step in this lesson
items.explain: On real problems the group offers ideas, but the member decides.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the member, not the group, choose the solution to his own problem?
items.explain: He knows his life and has to carry out the plan. Ownership raises follow-through and respects his autonomy.

items.stem: Mario skips step one and goes straight to brainstorming about "my brother." What is likely?
options: He'll find the perfect fix
Better ideas, since skipping definitions saves time for creativity
Emotional, scattered options aimed at no clear goal
No difference
items.explain: Skipping the objective problem and goal invites emotional reactions.

items.stem: Which mistake comes from skipping step two?
options: Having no concrete plan
Reacting with feelings instead of facts about the problem
Going with a gut reaction that may cause trouble
Forgetting the goal
items.explain: Without brainstorming, people tend to act on the first impulse.

items.stem: Aviation checklists exist because skipping one routine item can cause disaster. Which lesson idea does that support?
options: Each step guards against a specific kind of error
Steps can be skipped when confident
Checklists are only for beginners and experts can rely on judgment
Planning slows things down
items.explain: Each step of problem solving prevents a different failure.

items.stem: "It went okay. Telling him in person worked; texting first would have been better. I told my sponsor and treated myself to a movie." What is this?
options: Buying time
Setting a goal
Evaluating a plan, with a reward
Brainstorming new options for the next problem
items.explain: Evaluating means rating it, noting what worked, rewarding yourself and planning changes.

items.stem: In your own words, why reward yourself after trying a plan, even if it only partly worked?
items.explain: Rewards reinforce the effort of trying, which makes it more likely you'll use the skill again. Partial success still deserves credit while you plan changes.

items.stem: At the end of Module 6, Kim's importance rating stays at 9 but confidence rises from 5 to 8. What does this suggest?
options: Her motivation has dropped, since importance did not go up
Skill practice is building her confidence
Nothing
Her goal should be dropped
items.explain: Rising confidence with steady importance suggests skills are working.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member chooses an option the facilitator thinks is likely to fail, though it is legal and harms no one. Should the facilitator step in?
items.explain: No single verdict. Letting him try respects autonomy and teaches through evaluation, but a predictable failure could discourage him.
key_points: Let him: the evaluation step turns failure into learning
Step in: name concerns with an open question
Both: voice the concern once, then support his choice

cbi-41.title: Developing a Plan
summary: The Success Plan is a personal relapse prevention plan, where relapse means sliding back into whatever gets the person in trouble.
It looks for repeating behavior patterns and the triggers, thinking, emotions and beliefs that travel with them.
Eight steps run from life history and lifestyle factors to transferring skills after group.
Life history factors are past and largely fixed; lifestyle factors are current and changeable.
High risk situations are specific prompting events, narrower than lifestyle factors.

items.stem: In your own words, describe the Success Plan.
items.explain: A personal relapse prevention plan built from the whole program. It pins down a person's risky patterns and pairs each with concrete ways to cope.

items.stem: In the Success Plan, "relapse" refers to what?
options: Sliding back into whatever gets the person in trouble
Only returning to drug or alcohol use after a period of sobriety
Missing a group
Being rearrested
items.explain: The plan defines relapse broadly as returning to the behavior that causes trouble.

items.stem: Across four Behavior Chains, Leon's risky choices all follow a fight with his partner and the thought "Nobody respects me." What does the plan target?
options: Only the fights, since they are the visible part of the pattern
The repeating pattern of trigger, thought and behavior
Nothing; patterns are random
His partner's behavior
items.explain: The plan looks for unhealthy behaviors that repeat and what travels with them.

items.stem: An epidemiologist maps where outbreaks keep recurring and what conditions they share. How is this like the Success Plan?
options: Both only study the past
Both look for repeating patterns and their shared conditions
It's not, since disease spreads randomly while behavior is chosen
Both ignore triggers
items.explain: Spotting recurring patterns and their conditions is the basis for prevention.

items.stem: "My parents both used when I was a kid." Which plan category?
options: Coping skill
Life history factor
High risk situation
Lifestyle factor, since it shapes how he lives now
items.explain: It's past and largely out of his control.

items.stem: "Most of my free time is with guys who think stealing is fine." Which category?
options: High risk situation
Lifestyle factor
Life history factor
Belief
items.explain: It describes how he lives now, which can change.

items.stem: Which is a high risk situation for the plan?
options: "I hang out with users"
"Friday night, my cousin texts that he's outside with a bag"
"I grew up poor"
"I'm stressed a lot"
items.explain: A high risk situation is a specific prompting event right before a risky choice.

items.stem: A member lists "my neighborhood" as a high risk situation. What should the facilitator do?
options: Remove it
Accept it, since a neighborhood can be the most important risk in someone's life
Move it to life history
Help him name specific moments there, like a particular corner at a particular time
items.explain: Lifestyle factors produce situations; the plan needs the specific events.

items.stem: In your own words, why are the Success Plan's steps built from earlier worksheets?
items.explain: Most of the content already exists in members' Behavior Chains and practice work. Pulling it together makes the plan personal and evidence-based rather than generic.

items.stem: A pilot's preflight plan combines weather data, maintenance logs and route charts collected earlier. How does that compare to building the Success Plan?
options: Both assemble earlier information into one working plan
It differs, since flight plans are made from scratch each time
Both are optional
Neither needs approval
items.explain: Like a flight plan, the Success Plan is assembled from work already done.

items.stem: Dee submits a plan with vague coping skills like "stay strong." What is likely?
options: It's rejected outright
The facilitator asks for more specific detail before approving
It is approved, since motivation is what matters most at this stage
Nobody reads it
items.explain: Facilitators must approve each plan and push for specific, realistic content.

items.stem: Weigh it: the plan is adapted from a correctional relapse prevention model. A member says it treats him "like a criminal, not a person in recovery." How should the facilitator respond?
items.explain: No single verdict. The model's structure works, but the framing can feel stigmatizing.
key_points: Explain: the structure targets risk patterns, not identity
Adapt: use language that fits his goals
Listen: his reaction is information about engagement

cbi-42.title: Getting to the Source
summary: Step 3: a Behavior Chain for every high risk situation in the plan.
Step 4: specific thinking-based and action-based coping skills for each situation.
Coping by Thinking replaces risky thinking; the chain itself is a thinking tool.
Coping by Doing uses a practiced skill to act; vague answers like "go to a meeting" aren't enough.
Thinking tools fit when there's time; doing tools fit when a trigger hits fast.

items.stem: "I'll remind myself the urge will pass, then tell myself I've made it 60 days." Which coping type?
options: Neither
Lifestyle change
Coping by Doing, since he is taking action against the urge
Coping by Thinking
items.explain: Urge reminders and self-talk work on thoughts.

items.stem: "I'll use Avoiding Trouble with Others to tell my cousin I can't come." Which coping type?
options: A barrier
Coping by Thinking
Coping by Doing
Lifestyle change
items.explain: Using a practiced skill to act is Coping by Doing.

items.stem: A fight starts brewing in the dayroom within seconds. Which kind of tool fits first?
options: A full cost-benefit analysis, since big decisions deserve careful thinking
A doing tool, like breathing or leaving, to calm enough to think
Nothing
Writing a Behavior Chain
items.explain: Fast triggers call for doing tools first; thinking tools fit when there's time.

items.stem: A firefighter first gets out of a burning room, then later reviews what went wrong. How does that map onto the lesson?
options: Act first in the fast moment, reflect when there is time
Only doing matters
Thinking first, then doing, since good decisions need analysis
Only thinking matters
items.explain: The fit depends on time: act fast in emergencies, reflect afterward.

items.stem: A member's coping for "friends pushing me to use" is "play ball." What should the facilitator ask for?
options: A different activity
A list of five activities
Nothing, since healthy activities are always good coping for any situation
A practiced skill that fits, and how he'll use it there
items.explain: Coping by Doing should be a skill matched to the situation, explained in detail.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the final plan require explaining how each skill will be used?
items.explain: Naming a skill doesn't show the member can use it in that moment. Describing exactly what they'll do makes the plan usable under pressure.

items.stem: Jace rewrites his chain: same situation, but new thoughts. What does the lesson predict for the rest of the chain?
options: The situation changes
Feelings, action and outcome change too
Only the thoughts change; the feelings and actions stay the same
Nothing changes
items.explain: Coping by Thinking swaps risky thoughts, which changes everything downstream.

items.stem: In Roll a Role, a die picks a thinking skill and the member applies it to one of his six situations. What does the random pairing train?
options: Speed only
Using different skills flexibly across situations
Memorizing which skill goes with which situation so the answers are fixed
Luck
items.explain: Random pairings force members to apply skills in new combinations, building flexibility.

items.stem: Jazz musicians practice improvising over random chord changes. What does that share with Roll a Role?
options: Both avoid structure
Both mainly reward memorizing one perfect answer ahead of time
Both build flexible use of skills in unpredictable combinations
Neither involves practice
items.explain: Practicing in varied, unplanned pairings makes skills hold up when situations change.
