items.stem: In your own words, why does each high risk situation need its own Behavior Chain?
items.explain: Different situations spark different thoughts and feelings. A chain for each reveals the specific pattern so coping can be matched to it.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member relies only on doing tools, like leaving or breathing, and says thinking tools "never come fast enough." Should his plan require thinking tools too?
items.explain: No single verdict. Doing tools handle fast moments, but thinking tools address the patterns behind them.
key_points: Require: thought change prevents repeated triggers
Respect: doing tools may be what works for him now
Both: add one thinking tool for calmer moments after

cbi-43.title: Reinventing My Life
summary: Step 5: drop or manage risky lifestyle factors and build healthy ones with action steps.
Lifestyle change is a coping strategy of its own.
Unstructured free time is a known risk, so leisure is a big lever.
Past activities sort three ways: not risky, risky but fixable, risky and better left alone.
Use often crowds out diet, exercise, spiritual growth and mental health care.

items.stem: Kevin is released with no job and spends afternoons on the porch watching the block. What does the lesson predict?
options: No effect
Rising risk, since unstructured time is a known danger
Lower risk, since staying home keeps him away from trouble
He'll find work faster
items.explain: Empty, unstructured time is a known risk factor.

items.stem: Watching the game at a friend's house where nobody drinks. How would it sort?
options: Not an activity
Risky and better left alone, since watching games used to involve drinking
Risky but fixable
Not risky
items.explain: Activities without risky elements can stay as they are.

items.stem: Watching the game at a sports bar where he always drank. How might it sort?
options: Not risky, since watching sports is a healthy activity
Risky but fixable, such as watching at home instead
Neither
Always fine
items.explain: Some activities can be made safe by changing them.

items.stem: A member's old weekend activity is running dice games behind a club. Which sort fits?
options: Risky and better left alone
Risky but fixable, since he could play somewhere else
Fixable by playing for less
Not risky
items.explain: Some activities carry risk at their core and need to go.

items.stem: Which question is part of screening a new activity?
options: Is it the cheapest?
Will it impress people?
Whether his friends from before would enjoy it too
Does it fit my values?
items.explain: Screening asks about trouble risk, fit with values, and practical access.

items.stem: Before taking a job offer, a nurse asks: is it safe, does it fit what I care about, and can I get there? What lesson tool is this?
options: The three-way sort of past jobs
A Behavior Chain
Screening an option before choosing it
A lapse plan
items.explain: Screening checks risk, values and access before committing.

items.stem: Tanya starts regular meals and walking after work. What does the lesson suggest beyond physical health?
options: Less free time is the only effect
More cravings
Little else, since diet and exercise mostly affect weight
Better mood and stress, plus a way to ride out urges
items.explain: Diet and exercise connect to mood and stress, and exercise can help ride out urges.

items.stem: Which counts as mental health care in this lesson?
options: Watching motivational videos online
Working overtime
Avoiding people
Couples therapy or a peer self-help group
items.explain: Mental health care includes counseling, family or couples therapy and peer self-help.

items.stem: A member writes "get in shape." What does step five need?
options: A bigger goal, like running a marathon by spring, to keep him motivated
A gym membership
Nothing more
A concrete first move, like walking 30 minutes after work three days a week
items.explain: Each healthy activity needs a specific action step.

items.stem: In your own words, why is changing how you live a coping strategy, not just background?
items.explain: Thinking and doing skills handle moments, but lifestyle shapes how often risky moments happen. Changing who you spend time with and how you fill time cuts risk at the source.

items.stem: Public health experts note that redesigning streets can lower accidents more than warning drivers. How does this connect to the lesson?
options: Drivers should be blamed
Streets cause addiction
It suggests individual skills are useless and only environment matters
Changing the environment can cut risk at the source
items.explain: Lifestyle change works upstream, reducing how often risky situations arise.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's main social outlet is a motorcycle club where some members use. Should he leave it?
items.explain: No single verdict. The club offers identity and support, but exposure to use is real.
key_points: Fix: ride with the sober members only
Decide: weigh how central use is to the club's culture

cbi-44.title: Staying on Track
summary: Step 6: update social supports and empower them to give corrective feedback.
A lapse is any thought, feeling or action that sets someone on the path back; relapse is lapsing again into the old pattern.
Reactions like "I'm no good" or "it was only a lapse, so it's fine" both push toward relapse.
Getting back on track: stop right away, review chains, practice with support, update the plan.
Step 8: plan how to keep skills going after group, since unpracticed skills fade. Never imply relapse is inevitable.

items.stem: "It's only weed, it's not like I'm on heroin." What kind of lapse is this?
options: A behavior lapse
Not a lapse, since no use has happened yet
A feeling lapse
A thinking lapse, comparing to minimize
items.explain: Lapses include thoughts like comparing or justifying, not only use.

items.stem: Ellen starts skipping meetings and stops answering her sponsor. What kind of lapse?
options: A behavior lapse
No lapse, since she hasn't used
A feeling lapse
A thinking lapse
items.explain: Behavior changes that move toward old patterns are lapses even without use.

items.stem: After one drink, Hank thinks, "I've blown it. Treatment doesn't work for me." What is likely next?
options: He'll call his sponsor
He gets back on track quickly, since admitting failure is the first step
Nothing
He's more likely to keep drinking
items.explain: Self-condemning thoughts push a lapse toward relapse.

items.stem: After one drink, Hank thinks, "It's fine, I didn't fully relapse." What does the lesson warn?
options: It's a risky reaction that downplays the lapse
This is the healthy response, since it avoids shame and keeps him calm
It shows insight
It guarantees recovery
items.explain: Minimizing a lapse is itself risky; the healthy response takes it seriously without condemning.

items.stem: Marlatt and Gordon described the "abstinence violation effect": after a slip, people who feel total failure often binge. How does this lesson apply it?
options: It recommends strict punishment after a slip so it does not happen again
It targets the all-or-nothing reaction so a lapse doesn't become relapse
It says slips are fine
It ignores slips
items.explain: The lesson coaches responses to a lapse that avoid both despair and minimizing.

items.stem: A member lapses on a weekend. What does the lesson suggest first?
options: Start the program over
Stop the pattern right away, then review his chains to find what failed
Wait until next group to talk about it, since slips are best handled in session
Hide it
items.explain: Getting back on track starts with interrupting the pattern and reviewing what happened.

items.stem: In your own words, why review Behavior Chains after a lapse?
items.explain: They show which coping skill failed or was never tried. That turns the lapse into information for updating the plan.

items.stem: A member's brother points out he's been isolating. The member snaps, "Stay out of my business." What does the lesson say supports need?
options: Nothing
Less involvement, since unrequested feedback usually harms recovery
Tools and permission to give feedback, and the member needs to hear it
Training as counselors
items.explain: Supports need permission to give corrective feedback, and members need to take it without hearing an attack.

items.stem: Jo finishes the program and stops practicing her skills. A year later, what does the lesson predict?
options: Her skills remain strong, since anything learned well stays with a person
She'll forget everything
Her skills may fade without practice
She'll be fine regardless
items.explain: Even motivated people lose skills they don't practice; step eight plans for that.

items.stem: In your own words, why should a facilitator never imply relapse is inevitable?
items.explain: Saying relapse is inevitable can become a self-fulfilling excuse. Nearly everyone lapses or wants to quit sometimes, and the point is that recovery is about bouncing back.

items.stem: Which describes a lapse rather than a relapse, in this lesson?
options: Finishing the program
A slip that sets someone on the path back, caught early
A new charge
Returning to daily use for several months
items.explain: A lapse is a step toward old patterns; relapse means falling back into them.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's wife wants to check his phone weekly as part of being a support. He feels it's controlling. Should it go in the plan?
items.explain: No single verdict. Monitoring can add accountability, but it may strain trust and autonomy.
key_points: Include: transparency can rebuild trust after harm
Exclude: support shouldn't feel like surveillance
Negotiate: agree on what she checks and for how long

cbi-45.title: Responding to Roadblocks
summary: Short lapses often come before a full relapse, so handling a roadblock helps head off the bigger fall.
Step 1: identify the roadblock and why, objectively.
Step 2: find ways past it and add the best one to the Success Plan.
Step 3: practice the updated plan, often by telling someone.
Lapses are not presented as inevitable or as always involving use.

items.stem: "I skipped two meetings because I started a night shift and didn't adjust my schedule." Which step is this?
options: Practicing the updated plan by telling someone
Adding fixes to the plan
Identifying the roadblock and why
Nothing
items.explain: Step one names what happened and why, without feelings or opinions.

items.stem: "I'll switch to the morning meeting and add it to my plan under Step 7." Which step?
options: Practicing the plan
Identifying the roadblock
Finding ways past it and adding them to the plan
Evaluating
items.explain: Step two brainstorms fixes and writes the best into the Success Plan.

items.stem: Nico admits his lapse to his sister, shares his new plan, and asks her to check in. Which step is this, and what is likely?
options: It is not part of the skill
Brainstorming
Identifying the roadblock, which helps him feel better
Practicing the updated plan; support makes follow-through likelier
items.explain: Step three acts on the new plan, often by telling someone who can help.

items.stem: A member's step one reads: "I messed up because I'm weak and stupid." Best coaching?
options: Ask him to describe what happened and why, leaving out self-judgment
Accept it, since honesty about feelings is what matters most in step one
Agree he messed up
Skip to step two
items.explain: Step one should be objective, which keeps shame from blocking problem solving.

items.stem: In your own words, why should step one be objective?
items.explain: Feelings and judgments cloud what actually happened. Sticking to facts makes the real cause visible and easier to fix.

items.stem: In your own words, why teach a skill for roadblocks near the end of the program?
items.explain: Short lapses often come before full relapse, so a ready way to respond helps prevent the larger fall. It's a just-in-case tool members carry out of the program.

items.stem: Airlines train crews for emergencies they hope never happen. How is that like this skill?
options: Both assume failure is certain
Both prepare a response in advance for a setback that may come
Neither is needed
It's different, since airline emergencies are random and lapses are always predictable
items.explain: Preparing for a possible setback makes recovery from it faster.

items.stem: Introducing the skill, a co-facilitator says, "Everybody relapses, so you'll need this." What's the problem?
options: It implies relapse is inevitable, which can become an excuse
It's off-topic
Nothing, since realism about relapse helps members prepare for it
It's too long
items.explain: Lapses shouldn't be presented as certain or as always involving use.

items.stem: During the role play, the main actor taps his head. Which steps is he doing?
options: Steps one and two, the thinking steps
None
Step three only, since it is the step where he talks to someone
All three
items.explain: Tapping the head marks thinking steps so observers can follow.

items.stem: After a role play, what comes before observers' comments?
options: The facilitator's corrections of what the actor got wrong
The actor's self-rating
Asking the co-actor what it felt like on the receiving end
A vote
items.explain: The protocol starts with the co-actor's experience, then observers on assigned steps.

items.stem: The co-actor says, "When he admitted the lapse calmly, I wanted to help him." What does that feedback teach the actor?
options: To hide lapses
That his calm honesty invites support
That he should have been more upset to show he took it seriously
Nothing useful
items.explain: Hearing the receiver's side shows how the approach lands in real relationships.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member lapsed but fears that telling his PO will mean a violation. Should step three include telling his PO?
items.explain: No single verdict. Honesty with the PO may build trust and get help, but the legal stakes are real.
key_points: Tell: officers often respond better to self-report than discovery
Wait: tell a sponsor or counselor first and get advice
Know: what his supervision terms require

cbi-46.title: Rehearsing My Plan
summary: This is a working session to finish every part of the Success Plan before presenting.
Delivering a complete, detailed plan is required to complete the program.
The Packet checklist shows at a glance which pieces are done.
Each coping skill must say how it will be used in that specific situation, not just its name.
Members who finish early help others, which sharpens their own understanding.

items.stem: Drew's plan lists high risk situations but no coping skills for two of them. What happens before he presents?
options: He fails automatically
He presents anyway, since partial plans are fine at this stage
He skips those situations
He must fill the gaps; a complete plan is required
items.explain: A full, detailed plan is a completion requirement.

items.stem: A member doesn't know what's missing from his plan. Which tool helps most?
options: The Packet checklist, by step number
Asking a friend
Rewriting the whole plan from the beginning so nothing is missed
Waiting for feedback
items.explain: The checklist lists each piece by step so members see what's done and what isn't.

items.stem: Which entry meets the detail standard?
options: "Avoid trouble."
"Be strong."
"Use Deciding to Say No."
"When my cousin offers, I'll say, 'I'm good, I've got work early,' and suggest breakfast instead."
items.explain: Each skill should say how it will be used in that situation.

items.stem: A member's coping for anger is "Coping by Doing." What should the facilitator ask?
options: For a longer list
Which skill, and exactly how he'll use it in that situation
Nothing, since naming the category shows he knows the material
To pick a different situation
items.explain: Labels aren't plans; details make the plan usable.

items.stem: A recipe that says "cook until done" versus one that gives time and temperature. Which matches the lesson's standard?
options: Both equal
Neither
The second, because specifics make it usable
The first, since experienced cooks prefer flexibility over instructions
items.explain: Specifics are what let someone follow a plan under real conditions.

items.stem: Ali finishes early and helps Ben write his coping details. What does the lesson predict for Ali?
options: He loses focus on his own plan, since helping others takes his attention
His own understanding sharpens
He gets credit for Ben's plan
Nothing
items.explain: Teaching others deepens your own grasp and keeps the group together.

items.stem: Educators describe a "protégé effect," where students learn more when they teach. Which session practice relies on it?
options: Facilitator review
Members who finish early helping others
The Packet checklist, since checking items is a kind of teaching
Homework
items.explain: Explaining material to someone else strengthens the explainer's understanding.

items.stem: In your own words, when is this working session most useful?
items.explain: Mainly in outpatient settings, where one-on-one plan reviews are hard to schedule, or when members are stuck. It gives guided time to finish before presenting.

items.stem: In your own words, why require a complete, detailed plan to finish the program?
items.explain: A partial plan leaves gaps exactly where risk may hit. Requiring completeness ensures every high risk situation has a usable response.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member who finished early wants to help others, but he tends to give them his own answers. Should the facilitator let him help?
items.explain: No single verdict. Peer help sharpens understanding, but copied answers make other plans less personal.
key_points: Allow: with guidance to ask questions, not give answers
Limit: steer him to review his own plan deeper
Pair: with a member who needs structure, not content

cbi-47.title: Presenting My Plan
summary: Every member must present a Success Plan to complete the program; the facilitator decides final approval.
Plans are judged on detail and on how realistic they are in the member's real life.
After presenting, the member role-plays a high risk situation from the plan with a peer.
Peers rate each plan from 1 (sketchy) to 4 (practical and detailed) and name strengths and additions.
Final plans go to the supervision officer and support people, making them a working tool.

items.stem: Which plan is most likely to pass?
options: A plan with specific situations, matched skills and realistic details
A plan written in very polished language
A long plan that lists every skill from the program but no situations
A plan with only goals
items.explain: Plans are judged on detail and realism in the member's actual life.

items.stem: Sam's plan says he'll go to the gym every day, though he has no transport and works doubles. What feedback is likely?
options: A note that the plan isn't realistic for his life
Automatic failure
Praise for ambition, since high goals show commitment
No comment
items.explain: Realism matters as much as detail.

items.stem: For the role play, a member picks a situation he's sure he can handle easily. What does the session call for?
options: A situation from the plan played as close to real life as possible
A made-up situation
No role play
Accept it, since success builds confidence before release
items.explain: The practice should be realistic, using a peer co-actor.

items.stem: Before a real game, a team scrimmages under game-like conditions. Which session element is this like?
options: Peer rating
The realistic role play after presenting
Facilitator feedback
Sharing the plan
items.explain: Practicing under conditions close to reality prepares for the real thing.

items.stem: A peer rates a plan "4." What does that mean?
options: Missing parts
Poor and sketchy, needing major revision
Excellent, practical and detailed
Average
items.explain: The scale runs from 1, sketchy, to 4, practical and detailed.

items.stem: In your own words, why have peers rate each plan?
items.explain: Peers often spot what's unrealistic in each other's lives. Rating and naming strengths keeps everyone engaged and sharpens their own plans too.

items.stem: Which is part of the facilitator's feedback form?
options: A list of the member's offenses
A pass/fail stamp only
A ranking of all members from best plan to worst plan
Strong areas, unclear areas and skills to keep working on
items.explain: The form names strong areas, thin areas and skills to practice.

items.stem: Marco's final plan goes to his PO and his two supports. What does the lesson expect?
options: His PO uses it against him
The plan stays in a file and is rarely used again
His supports can help, because they know his risks and plan
Nothing
items.explain: Sharing turns the plan into a working tool for life after the program.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member is willing to share his plan with his supports but not with his supervision officer, fearing it will be used against him. Should he be required to share it?
items.explain: No single verdict. Sharing with the officer can align support and supervision, but his fear reflects real power differences.
key_points: Share: officers can reinforce the plan and connect resources
Limit: share a version without sensitive details
Discuss: what the officer can and can't do with it

items.stem: In your own words, why does the facilitator, not the peers, decide final approval?
items.explain: Peers add useful feedback, but the facilitator knows the program standards and each member's full record of work. Keeping the decision there keeps standards consistent.

items.stem: Peers rate Lou's plan 4, but the facilitator sees a missing high risk situation from his chains. What happens?
options: The facilitator asks him to add it before approval
The peers are overruled and scolded
The plan passes, since peer ratings decide approval
Lou repeats the program
items.explain: The facilitator makes the final rating and approval.

lib-1.title: Definitions, Terms, and Self-Assessment
summary: A substance use disorder is use of mood-altering drugs that harms a person's life; DSM-5 rates it mild to severe.
Addiction is primary, chronic and progressive: fixing other problems does not cure it.
Loss of control shows up over amount, over stopping, and over behavior while using.
Denial is usually an unconscious defense, not deliberate lying.
Dependence, tolerance and withdrawal are body adaptations; withdrawal tends to mirror the drug in reverse.

items.stem: Rosa's husband says, "Once we fix our marriage, she won't need to drink." What does the lesson say?
options: He is right, since drinking is usually a symptom of relationship stress
The marriage caused the addiction
Addiction is primary; fixing the marriage alone won't cure it
Drinking will stop on its own
items.explain: Addiction is its own condition. Other problems matter, but solving them does not remove it.

items.stem: Over five years, Mike's drinking went from weekends to most nights, with growing consequences. What does the lesson's model predict without treatment?
options: It will level off at most nights, since people find a stable amount
It depends only on willpower
It tends to keep progressing
It will reverse on its own
items.explain: Addiction is described as progressive: it tends to get worse over time.

items.stem: "I only meant to have two, but I ended up closing the bar." Which kind of lost control is this?
options: Over stopping entirely
Over behavior while drinking, since closing the bar is a behavior
Not lost control
Over how much he uses
items.explain: Using more than planned is impaired control over amount.

items.stem: "When I'm high I do things I'd never do sober, like steal from my mom." Which kind of lost control?
options: Over stopping
Preoccupation
Over amount
Over behavior while using
items.explain: Acting out of character while intoxicated is the third kind of lost control.

items.stem: Kevin genuinely believes his drinking is "normal" despite two DUIs. What is this, in the lesson's terms?
options: Lying to avoid consequences, since he knows the DUIs happened
Cross-tolerance
Denial, an unconscious defense
Tolerance
items.explain: Denial usually works without the person knowing it, which is why it differs from lying.

items.stem: A member insists, "I don't have a problem. I just got unlucky." Best facilitator approach?
options: Confront him directly with his record so he can no longer deny it
Have the group call him out
Ignore it
Approach gently, exploring consequences without labels
items.explain: Because denial is usually unconscious, gentle exploration works better than confrontation.

items.stem: A hospital patient on morphine for two weeks has withdrawal when it's stopped, but no cravings or compulsion. What does she have?
options: Denial
Physical dependence without addiction
Addiction, since withdrawal shows the drug has taken hold
Tolerance only
items.explain: Dependence means the body adapted; addiction involves compulsion and harm.

items.stem: After weeks of heavy Xanax use, what withdrawal symptoms does the lesson's rule predict?
options: Euphoria
Sleepiness and calm, since the drug's effects linger for weeks
Anxiety and agitation
Increased appetite only
items.explain: Withdrawal tends to mirror the drug in reverse: off a downer, the body swings up.

items.stem: A coffee drinker skips her morning cups and feels sluggish and foggy. Which lesson principle explains it?
options: Withdrawal mirrors the drug in reverse: off a stimulant, energy drops
Primary addiction
Denial
Cross-tolerance between caffeine and other stimulants
items.explain: Caffeine is a mild stimulant; its withdrawal swings toward fatigue.

items.stem: Tony quits cocaine but keeps drinking "since alcohol was never my problem." What does the lesson predict?
options: No effect
He'll quit drinking too
His recovery from cocaine will be fine, since alcohol is a different drug
A higher chance of drifting back to cocaine
items.explain: Keeping another mood-altering drug often leads back; abstinence means all of them.

items.stem: At a party, Jay mixes cocaine with heavy drinking and feels fine. Later the cocaine wears off. What is the danger?
options: The full alcohol load hits at once, risking overdose
The alcohol wears off first
He crashes into a deep but safe sleep and wakes up hungover
No danger
items.explain: A stimulant masks intoxication, so people drink more; when it fades, the full depressant effect lands.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson separate dependence from addiction?
items.explain: Dependence is the body adapting to a drug and can happen in medical use without compulsion. Addiction adds compulsion: losing control and using even as harm piles up.
key_points: Medical use can cause dependence alone

items.stem: Weigh it: a member scores "mild" on the eleven-item self-assessment but has a long criminal record tied to use. Should the facilitator challenge his score?
items.explain: No single verdict. The tool reflects his answers, which may be honest or shaped by denial, and the record suggests more harm.
key_points: Accept: the self-rating is his starting point
Explore: ask about items like failed attempts to cut down
Revisit: scores often rise as denial lowers

items.stem: The self-assessment's eleven statements are based on what?
options: A sponsor's opinion
The member's legal history and the number of arrests
The diagnostic criteria for substance use disorder
Family reports
items.explain: The items follow the diagnostic criteria, such as using more than planned and craving.

lib-2.title: Alcohol and Other Drug Education
summary: Stimulants act alike; strength, dose and route make the difference, and smoking reaches the brain fastest.
Hallucinations see what isn't there; illusions misread what is.
Some depressant combinations add up; others potentiate, totaling more than the sum.
Sedative-hypnotic withdrawal, including alcohol, can cause seizures and death; opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely fatal.
Fentanyl is far stronger than heroin, and brain recovery after heavy use can take months.

items.stem: At a low dose of a stimulant, Ana feels alert. She keeps increasing the dose through the night. What does the lesson predict?
options: Growing anxiety and agitation, then paranoia and overdose risk
Steady alertness, since stimulants have the same effect at every dose
Relaxation
Sleepiness
items.explain: Stimulant effects climb with dose from alert to anxious, agitated and paranoid.

items.stem: Which route usually gets a drug to the brain fastest?
options: Swallowing
Snorting
Skin patch
Smoking
items.explain: Smoking reaches the brain in seconds, faster than snorting; only injecting rivals its speed and strength.

items.stem: Nicotine gum works more slowly than a cigarette. Which lesson principle explains the difference?
options: Gum causes cross-tolerance
Route of use changes how fast and strongly a drug hits
Gum is a different drug, with different effects on the brain
Cigarettes are weaker
items.explain: Route affects speed and strength; that is why delivery method matters for both risk and treatment.

items.stem: High on meth, Victor thinks a coat on a chair is a man watching him. Hallucination or illusion?
options: An illusion, misreading something real
Neither
A hallucination, since he is seeing a person who is not there
A flashback
items.explain: An illusion distorts something real; a hallucination perceives something not there.

items.stem: Alone in his room, Victor hears voices calling his name. Which is it?
options: Paranoia only
An illusion
A hallucination
Withdrawal
items.explain: Hearing something with no real source is a hallucination.

items.stem: Darnell stops using meth. When does the lesson suggest his withdrawal is likely to peak?
options: Around day three or four
Never
On the first day, since withdrawal always starts and peaks immediately
After a year
items.explain: Stimulant withdrawal tends to peak around day three or four and may linger about two weeks.

items.stem: A member a week off cocaine says he's been thinking life isn't worth it. What fits the lesson?
options: Take it seriously and connect him with mental health care now
Wait until next group
Reassure him it's just withdrawal and will pass on its own
Tell him to exercise
items.explain: Suicidal thinking can appear during stimulant withdrawal; it needs prompt professional attention.

items.stem: Lou takes one Valium with a beer, thinking it's "like two drinks." What does potentiation predict?
options: No interaction
A weaker effect
About two drinks' worth of effect, since depressant effects simply add
A combined effect larger than the sum
items.explain: Some depressants potentiate each other; most depressant overdoses involve more than one drug.

items.stem: Two medications each mildly lower blood pressure, but together they cause fainting. Which lesson concept fits?
options: Route
Cross-tolerance
Additive effect, since the two effects are simply added together
Potentiation, where the combination exceeds the sum
items.explain: Potentiation describes interactions where the total is greater than the parts.

items.stem: A member who drank a fifth a day says he'll quit cold turkey on his own this weekend. What does the lesson say?
options: Encourage him, since stopping completely is always the safest way
No action
Suggest tapering with beer
Refer him to medical care, since alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures
items.explain: Sedative-hypnotic withdrawal can be fatal and needs medical supervision.

items.stem: Which withdrawal does the lesson describe as miserable but rarely fatal?
options: Opioid withdrawal
Alcohol, since most people survive it without help
Benzodiazepine withdrawal
GHB withdrawal
items.explain: Opioid withdrawal feels like a bad flu; sedative-hypnotic withdrawal is the dangerous one.

items.stem: Marisol buys what she's told is a pressed Xanax. What risk does the lesson highlight?
options: It may contain fentanyl, which is far stronger than heroin
Low risk, since pressed pills are made to standard doses
It will be weaker than real Xanax
No risk
items.explain: Fentanyl is sold as, or mixed into, other drugs, which drives overdose risk.

items.stem: In your own words, what do the brain scans in this lesson suggest about recovery?
items.explain: Drug-related brain changes can last months after use stops, and cues alone can light up craving areas. Recovery takes time, so early cravings are not a sign of failure.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member asks about carrying naloxone in case a friend overdoses, but worries it means he's "planning to be around drugs." Should the facilitator encourage it?
items.explain: No single verdict. Naloxone saves lives and is widely recommended, but he is right that the setting matters for his own recovery.
key_points: Encourage: it can reverse opioid overdose and save a life
Explore: what situations he expects to be in
Both: carry it and plan to avoid using settings

items.stem: Which effect does the lesson tie to all stimulants, whatever the dose?
options: Deep, restful sleep afterward, since the body is worn out
Less sleep and less appetite
Calm and sedation
Lower heart rate
items.explain: All stimulants cut sleep and appetite; dose shifts the rest from alert to agitated.

items.stem: Ninety days off cocaine, Jamal watches a movie scene with people using and feels a sudden strong craving. What does the lesson suggest?
options: The movie caused a new addiction
His recovery has failed, since cravings should be gone by now
Cue-driven craving can last months as the brain heals
He was never addicted
items.explain: Brain changes and cue reactivity can persist for months; a craving is not proof of failure.

lib-3.title: Triggers, Cravings, and Avoiding Relapse
summary: A trigger is anything linked with past use; longer use makes triggers stronger and more numerous.
Triggers are internal (feelings), external (people, places, things, times) or sensory, and usually work together.
The chain runs trigger, thought, craving, use; once craving has physical signs, clear thinking drops.
The chain is easiest to break at the start, yet most people wait until the craving.
Handle triggers by identifying, avoiding, interrupting and talking about them; thought-stopping tools help.

items.stem: "Every Friday at 5 I want a drink." Which kind of trigger?
options: Internal, since the craving comes from inside him
Not a trigger
Sensory
External, a time
items.explain: Times, like Friday or payday, are external triggers.

items.stem: The smell of a certain cologne reminds Ray of the guy he used with. Which trigger type?
options: Internal
Sensory
Emotional
External
items.explain: Smells, sounds and tastes tied to past use are sensory triggers.

items.stem: "When I get lonely, I start thinking about using." Which type?
options: Internal
A belief
Sensory
External
items.explain: Feelings like loneliness, boredom or even celebration are internal triggers.

items.stem: Jo walks past her old corner (trigger), thinks "just one" (thought), and her heart starts racing (craving). What does the lesson predict about her thinking now?
options: The craving will vanish
It is at its sharpest, since physical arousal increases focus
Clear thinking is dropping, making use more likely
No effect
items.explain: Once craving brings physical signs, clear thinking drops and use gets more likely.

items.stem: Two people face the same payday trigger. One schedules a dinner with a sober friend for payday; the other waits to see if a craving comes. Who is more likely to stay sober?
options: The second, since waiting avoids overthinking it
The first, who acted at the start of the chain
Neither
Both equal
items.explain: The chain is easiest to break at the trigger, before thoughts and cravings build.

items.stem: Firefighters say it is easier to stop a fire at the spark than at full blaze. Which lesson idea is this?
options: Breaking the chain at the start is easiest
Denial
Sensory triggers, since fire is something people see and smell
Thought-stopping
items.explain: Early interruption is easier than stopping something once it has built.

items.stem: A member says he has "no triggers anymore." Best facilitator move?
options: Tell him he's lying
Invite feedback from peers and supports, since many triggers are invisible to us
Move on
Accept it, since he knows himself best after a long time clean
items.explain: Others' feedback helps because many triggers aren't noticed by the person.

items.stem: A member's trigger is payday, which he can't avoid. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Have someone else collect his pay so he never sees the money
Schedule a healthy activity ahead, ideally with sober people
Ignore it
Quit his job
items.explain: Unavoidable triggers are handled by planning healthy activities in advance.

items.stem: Clara pictures flipping a switch and immediately brings up a prepared image of her daughter at the beach. Which tool?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation
Urge surfing
The mental switch
Snapping a rubber band
items.explain: The mental switch replaces a using thought with a prepared calming image.

items.stem: A pianist who catches herself thinking "I'll miss this note" snaps her attention to the next phrase. What does this resemble?
options: Avoidance
A sensory trigger response, since music is a sound
Denial
Thought-stopping, interrupting a thought early and switching
items.explain: Interrupting a risky thought early and redirecting attention is the shared move.

items.stem: In your own words, why do longer years of use mean more and stronger triggers?
items.explain: Every time use happens around a person, place, feeling or object, the link strengthens. Years of use create many links that fire automatically.

items.stem: Weigh it: snapping a rubber band works for one member, but another says it feels like self-punishment. Should the facilitator keep teaching it?
items.explain: No single verdict. It's a quick interrupter for some, but for others it may echo harm or shame.
key_points: Keep: it's offered as one option among several
Adapt: suggest the mental switch or a different physical cue
Check: ask each member how it feels

lib-4.title: Planning for Sobriety
summary: Addiction, sobriety and relapse are processes built from small steps, not single moments.
Relapse usually starts with seemingly unimportant decisions long before the substance is in hand.
Warning signs often show to others before the person sees them.
Dropping recovery activities is one of the most common signs relapse is coming.
A full recovery program includes abstinence, frequent meetings, sober friends, a sponsor and a crisis plan.

items.stem: Ray calls in sick, skips his meeting "just this once," and takes the long way home past his old block. What does the lesson say about these choices?
options: They are only bad luck
They may be early steps of a relapse already underway
They prove he's fine
They are unrelated small things that happen to everyone
items.explain: Relapse decisions are often made through choices that look harmless.

items.stem: Investigators of a bridge collapse find a string of small skipped inspections over years. Which lesson idea does that resemble?
options: Many small, harmless-looking choices adding up to disaster
Denial
A single dramatic failure that nobody could have predicted
Primary addiction
items.explain: Like relapse, the collapse grew from small decisions that each seemed unimportant.

items.stem: "Sobriety isn't one promise; it's what I choose every morning." Which idea is this?
options: A relapse warning sign
Denial
Sobriety as a process of daily choices
A control fantasy
items.explain: Sobriety is built from many daily choices, not a single vow.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson describe relapse as a process instead of an event?
items.explain: Relapse builds through small choices and warning signs long before use. Seeing it as a process shows many points where it can be interrupted.

items.stem: Which is a warning sign on the relapse checklist?
options: Getting irritated with supports and dropping meetings
Going to extra meetings
Talking openly about cravings
Calling his sponsor more often than usual
items.explain: Irritation with supports and dropping meetings are classic warning signs.

items.stem: Gina's sponsor notices she's isolating and talking about "doing it my way." Gina doesn't see it. What does the lesson say?
options: Warning signs often show to others first, which is why feedback matters
Isolation is healthy
Gina knows herself best, so the sponsor is probably overreacting
The sponsor should stay quiet
items.explain: Others often spot warning signs before the person does.

items.stem: Six months sober, Tom says meetings are boring and stops going. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll go back when needed
No change
Little risk, since he has proven he can stay sober on his own
A raised risk of relapse; dropping activities is a common sign
items.explain: Dropping recovery activities, often with boredom as the reason, is among the most frequent signs of coming relapse.

items.stem: A member's plan is "I'll just stay away from drugs." What does the lesson add?
options: Moving away
Medication only
Nothing more, since willpower alone is the core of recovery
The building blocks: meetings, sober friends, a sponsor, a crisis list, avoiding triggers
items.explain: A full program has many parts beyond simply avoiding drugs.

items.stem: Which is one of the building blocks of a full recovery program in the lesson?
options: Keeping old phone numbers just in case
Moving to a new city where nobody knows his history
Working more hours
Getting rid of paraphernalia
items.explain: Removing paraphernalia is one of the practical steps the lesson lists.

items.stem: A year sober, Luis thinks, "I can handle a few drinks now." What does the lesson call this?
options: A healthy goal
A control fantasy and a red flag
A thinking error with no risk
A sign of real progress and strength after a year sober
items.explain: Thoughts of being able to handle it now are a classic red flag for relapse.

items.stem: In your own words, why does planning ahead matter, given the lower and upper brain idea?
items.explain: Triggers and urges come from the emotional lower brain, which can overwhelm the thinking upper brain during a craving. Plans made calmly ahead do the thinking before it's hard to think.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says the full program sounds like "trading drugs for meetings" and wants a lighter plan. Should the facilitator insist on all the parts?
items.explain: No single verdict. A full program offers many supports, but a plan he resents may not last.
key_points: Insist: each part guards against a known relapse path
Negotiate: start with the parts he'll actually do
Revisit: add pieces as his confidence grows

items.stem: In the middle of a strong craving, Ana tries to reason her way out and can't think straight. What does the lower/upper brain idea predict would have helped more?
options: Waiting for the craving to get stronger
Thinking harder in the moment, since willpower grows with effort
A plan made earlier, while she was calm
Nothing helps
items.explain: Cravings come from the emotional brain and drown out planning, so decisions made in advance do the heavy lifting.

lib-5.title: Alcohol and Tobacco
summary: Legal doesn't mean safe; the CAGE questions screen for a drinking problem, with two or more yeses a likely concern.
Alcohol is a sedative-hypnotic that gives confidence not matched by real skill.
Alcoholism tends to progress through tolerance, memory lapses, loss of control and binges, often over years.
Alcohol harms directly and indirectly; no amount is known to be safe in pregnancy.
Staying off alcohol matters even when another drug was the problem; nicotine is a drug, and quitting with other drugs is linked to better sobriety.

items.stem: Rick says he's felt he should cut down, and he's needed a drink first thing in the morning. How many CAGE yeses, and what does it suggest?
options: Zero
One, which means no concern
Four, which means severe addiction
Two, which suggests a likely drinking problem
items.explain: Two or more yeses on CAGE point to a likely problem worth assessing.

items.stem: What does the "A" in CAGE ask?
options: Whether he drinks Alone most of the time
Whether people have Annoyed him by criticizing his drinking
Whether he drinks Alcohol daily
Whether he has been Arrested
items.explain: Annoyed at criticism is the A in CAGE.

items.stem: After a few drinks, Dee feels sure she can drive home fine. What does the lesson predict about her actual skill?
options: It is better than usual
It is worse than she thinks
It is about the same, since she feels confident and alert
It is unaffected by a few drinks
items.explain: Alcohol gives confidence not matched by real skill.

items.stem: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes people overestimating their skill in areas where they know little. How is alcohol's effect similar?
options: It is identical, since alcohol makes people less intelligent
Alcohol increases skill
Neither involves confidence
Both involve confidence running ahead of actual ability
items.explain: In both cases, felt confidence outpaces real competence, which is why it is dangerous. The Dunning-Kruger findings themselves are debated, but the general pattern is widely discussed.

items.stem: Over years, Tom's tolerance rises, then he starts having blackouts. Which stage might come next, per the lesson's model?
options: No further stage
Recovery, since blackouts scare people into quitting
Total abstinence
Loss of control
items.explain: The stages (tolerance, memory lapses, loss of control, binges) often overlap and progress.

items.stem: In your own words, why do people often miss the stages of alcoholism?
items.explain: They overlap and can unfold over many years, so changes feel gradual and normal. There is no single moment that announces the problem.

items.stem: Which is an indirect way alcohol harms the body?
options: Replacing food with empty calories, leading to poor nutrition
Damaging the liver
Raising cancer risk
Harming the heart
items.explain: Direct harms hit organs; indirect harms include poor nutrition and toxic byproducts.

items.stem: A pregnant member asks if one glass of wine a week is safe. What fits the lesson?
options: Say only beer is risky
Say an occasional glass is fine after the first trimester
Let her decide alone
No amount is known to be safe in pregnancy; refer her to her doctor
items.explain: There is no known safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy.

items.stem: Marco's drug was heroin. He thinks a couple of beers at a cookout are harmless. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll lose interest in heroin
No risk, since alcohol was never his problem
Lowered inhibitions and links to old use raise relapse risk
No effect
items.explain: Alcohol lowers inhibitions and is often tied to other drugs, endangering any recovery.

items.stem: "I smoke because I need something to do with my hands when I'm on the phone." Which reason is this?
options: Craving
Stimulation
Tension reduction
Handling
items.explain: Each smoking reason calls for a different replacement; handling needs something for the hands.

items.stem: Lara wants to quit cigarettes at the same time as drugs but fears it's "too much at once." What does the lesson suggest?
options: Smoking helps sobriety
Quitting both is linked to better sobriety
Wait, since quitting both increases relapse risk for the main drug
It makes no difference
items.explain: Quitting smoking alongside other drugs is linked to better outcomes; a doctor can advise on aids.

items.stem: Weigh it: in a prison unit, cigarettes are currency and a main stress reliever. Should a member trying to get sober also quit smoking now?
items.explain: No single verdict. The evidence favors quitting together, but the setting may make it harder and stress may rise.
key_points: Quit now: linked to better sobriety
Wait: stress and social pressure may be too high
Middle: set a quit date with medical help and a plan for stress

items.stem: A member whose drug was meth says, "I'll still drink socially; that was never my thing." Best response?
options: Say nothing
Tell him to switch to weed
Agree, since abstinence only applies to his drug of choice
Explain that alcohol lowers inhibitions and links to old use, so it threatens any recovery
items.explain: The lesson holds that staying off alcohol matters even when another drug was the problem.

lib-6.title: Spirituality
summary: Spirituality here means everyday living and connection to something beyond yourself, not a specific religion.
Addiction slowly shrinks a person's world to self and drug, with the belief "I can control it alone."
HOW stands for honesty, open-mindedness and willingness; recovery needs willingness more than willpower.
A Higher Power is self-defined and many paths exist: meditation, prayer, service, study, forgiveness.
Spiritual change is usually gradual, and others often notice it first.

items.stem: Jamal, an atheist, says spirituality "isn't for me." According to the lesson, what could spirituality mean for him?
options: Nothing, since spirituality requires belief in God
How he lives each day and connects to something beyond himself
Attending religious services regularly, since that is how most people practice spirituality
Reading scripture
items.explain: The lesson separates spirituality from religion and respects every view.

items.stem: A climber describes feeling small and connected on a mountaintop, though she isn't religious. How would the lesson classify the experience?
options: Intellectualization
Not spiritual, since no prayer, ritual or belief in a deity was involved in it
A spiritual experience in the lesson's broad sense
Religious, since awe always points to faith
items.explain: Connection to something beyond oneself counts as spiritual, with or without religion.

items.stem: Over years of use, Chris's world narrowed to his next score and the belief he could handle it alone. What does the lesson say about reversing this?
options: It never reverses
It tends to reverse slowly, just as it grew slowly
Only medication helps
It flips quickly once he stops using, since the drug was what shrank his world
items.explain: Self-centeredness grows gradually in addiction; spiritual recovery grows gradually too.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson link addiction to self-centeredness?
items.explain: Use gradually shrinks life to the person and the drug, along with a belief that they can manage alone. Reaching beyond oneself is the counterweight.

items.stem: What does HOW stand for in this lesson?
options: Honesty, Open-mindedness, Willingness
Humility, Order and Willpower, the three supports of a disciplined recovery
Hope, Obedience, Work
Help, Openness, Wisdom
items.explain: These three qualities are described as the carriers of spiritual growth.

items.stem: Tito relies on gritting his teeth through every craving and refuses help. Ana is willing to try meetings and advice she doesn't fully trust yet. Who does the lesson favor?
options: Both equally
Ana; willingness matters more than willpower
Tito, since willpower is what keeps people sober in the long run
Neither
items.explain: Recovery depends more on openness to help than on solo force.

items.stem: A rookie surgeon is skilled but won't take advice; another is less gifted but asks questions and adapts. Which lesson value predicts the second does better over time?
options: Willingness, being open to help and change
Willpower
Self-reliance
Honesty, since asking questions is a way of being honest
items.explain: Willingness keeps learning possible; it outlasts raw effort.

items.stem: A member wants to "be totally honest" by telling his ex every hurtful thing he's thought about her. What does the lesson's view of honesty suggest?
options: Go ahead, since full honesty is the foundation of HOW
Honesty should serve growth, not become a weapon to hurt others
Write every thought down in a letter and mail it, so it is honest but not face to face
Never be honest
items.explain: The manual warns that honesty used to wound is not the honesty HOW means.

items.stem: A member says his Higher Power is "the group." Is that acceptable in the lesson?
options: No, a Higher Power must be God
Only if he also commits to a Twelve Step group, since the idea comes from AA
Yes; it is self-defined, ideally loving and bigger than oneself
No, groups are human
items.explain: The lesson allows the group, nature, God or another meaningful source.

items.stem: A Muslim member and a Buddhist member both feel uncomfortable with "God" language in group. Best facilitator approach?
options: Avoid the topic entirely
Use only Christian examples
Ask them to set their own beliefs aside for the session so the group can share one common language
Affirm that each person defines spirituality and Higher Power for themselves
items.explain: The program takes no side; each person's path is respected.

items.stem: Six months in, Dina feels nothing "spiritual" has happened, but her sister says she's calmer and more patient. What does the lesson say?
options: Her sister is being polite, since spiritual change is felt from inside first
Spiritual change is often gradual and noticed by others first
She should try harder
Nothing has changed
items.explain: Most spiritual experiences are slow changes others see before the person does.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says the Twelve Steps' spiritual language feels like religion forced on him in a prison program. Should the facilitator keep using it?
items.explain: No single verdict. The language connects to a well-known recovery tradition, but required spirituality raises fairness concerns in a mandated setting.
key_points: Keep: the steps help many and terms can be self-defined
Adjust: offer secular framings and alternatives
Respect: participation in the spiritual part is his choice

lib-7.title: Sex, Alcohol, and Other Drugs
summary: Alcohol's sexual effect depends on dose: a little lowers inhibition; heavier or chronic use dulls arousal and performance.
Stimulants may briefly raise desire but reduce it over time; opioids usually lower desire.
Drugs lower inhibitions and can raise aggression, increasing risky sex and sexual violence.
For people whose sex life centered on getting high, sex can become a powerful trigger.
Go slow in early recovery; sexual problems are common and treatable; sex can become a way to escape returning feelings.

items.stem: Over years of heavy drinking, Hector develops erection problems. What does the lesson say?
options: It's purely psychological
Chronic heavy drinking is a leading cause of impotence in middle-aged men
It's mostly anxiety about performance, which tends to fade once he relaxes more
It's just aging, unrelated to alcohol
items.explain: Alcohol's effect on sex depends on dose; chronic use dulls arousal and performance.

items.stem: Shakespeare's porter in Macbeth jokes that drink "provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance." Which lesson point does this match?
options: Alcohol may lower inhibition but impairs sexual function
Alcohol mainly affects mood, and its effects on sex are mostly in a person's head
Alcohol improves sex at any amount
Alcohol has no sexual effects
items.explain: The line captures the dose effect the lesson describes: more desire, less ability.

items.stem: Which drug class does the lesson say usually lowers sexual interest?
options: Hallucinogens only
Caffeine
Opioids
Stimulants, since they speed up the body and burn out desire
items.explain: Opioids usually reduce desire; stimulants may give a brief burst that fades.

items.stem: Trey used meth partly because it made sex feel intense. After months of use, what does the lesson predict?
options: Interest and performance decline, and sex gets tied to craving
No change
Desire stays high, since meth reliably boosts sex
Desire disappears the day he stops, then comes back stronger than it was before
items.explain: Stimulants may briefly boost desire, but over time they reduce interest and impair performance.

items.stem: In your own words, how do drugs increase risky sex and sexual violence?
items.explain: They lower inhibitions and can raise aggression and impair judgment. That makes unprotected sex, unwanted sex and violence more likely.

items.stem: Marcus always used cocaine during sex. Sober now, he meets an old partner. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll feel nothing
Little risk, since sex and drugs are different urges
The encounter may set off a strong craving
It will strengthen his recovery
items.explain: When sex was tied to getting high, sex itself can become a trigger.

items.stem: A smoker who always lit up after meals craves a cigarette after dinner even years later. How does that relate to sex as a trigger?
options: Only places and people can become triggers, while activities like sex are too personal to be cues
Any activity repeatedly paired with use can become a trigger
It doesn't; meals and sex are unrelated
Smoking is not a drug
items.explain: Repeated pairing turns ordinary activities, including sex, into cues for craving.

items.stem: Two weeks out, a member says he's "falling hard" for someone he just met. What does the lesson suggest discussing?
options: Encourage him, since love is the best support in early recovery
Breaking it off immediately
Nothing; it's personal
Going slow on new relationships early, and why
items.explain: The manual suggests holding off on new sexual relationships early in recovery.

items.stem: Early in sobriety, a flood of guilt and sadness hits Nia. She jumps into an intense new romance. What does the lesson warn?
options: It may stall recovery or become a substitute addiction
The romance will heal the feelings
Nothing
It is a healthy outlet, since romance releases the same feelings in a safer way than drugs
items.explain: Using sex or romance to avoid returning feelings can block recovery.

items.stem: In your own words, why might someone in early recovery use sex or romance to escape?
items.explain: Feelings numbed by use come flooding back. Intense romance or sex can mute them the way the drug did, which delays dealing with them.
key_points: Sex can numb like a drug

items.stem: A member quietly mentions recurring pain during sex. Best response?
options: Say it will pass once she has been sober longer
Discuss it in detail in group
Ignore it, since it's off-topic
Normalize it and encourage her to see a doctor
items.explain: Recurring pain needs medical attention; many sexual problems are treatable.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's long-term partner wants to resume their sex life right after release, and he fears it's a trigger. What should guide the decision?
items.explain: No single verdict. Intimacy can support the relationship, but if sex was tied to use it may raise risk.
key_points: Resume: the relationship and closeness matter
Wait: give recovery time to settle
Talk: be open with the partner about cravings, as the lesson suggests

lib-8.title: Stress and Emotional Well-Being
summary: A stressor is a demand from the world; stress is your reaction, and not every stressor stresses everyone.
Stressors come as frustrations (blocked goals), pressures (pushes to hurry or meet expectations) and conflicts (opposing goals).
Stress hits harder depending on the stressor's size, length and pile-up and the person's perception and resources.
Defenses like repression, emotional insulation, intellectualization and regression ease tension automatically.
Ongoing stress moves through alarm, resistance and exhaustion; a stress plan is relapse prevention.

items.stem: A loud dayroom makes Kev tense but doesn't bother his cellmate. What does that illustrate?
options: His cellmate is in denial
Noise isn't a stressor
Kev is less resilient than his cellmate and needs to toughen up to handle unit life
The same stressor doesn't stress everyone
items.explain: A stressor is the demand; stress is the individual reaction.

items.stem: Leo is denied an apartment because of his record. Which stressor type?
options: A frustration: an obstacle to a goal
Not a stressor
A conflict
A pressure, since he needs housing fast
items.explain: Frustrations block goals; this one is external.

items.stem: Maya wants to see her kids this weekend but also wants to keep a double shift she was offered. Which type?
options: Conflict between two goals
Regression
Pressure
Frustration
items.explain: A conflict is a pull between opposing goals, here two good options.

items.stem: "My family wants me fixed in a month." Which type?
options: Frustration
Insulation
Conflict
Pressure
items.explain: Pressures push you to hurry or meet expectations.

items.stem: Jorge's sponsor pushes him to attend a meeting every day for a month. How does the lesson classify that?
options: A pressure that can be good, pushing toward recovery
A bad pressure, since all pressure raises stress
A conflict
A frustration, since daily meetings block his other goals
items.explain: Pressure isn't always harmful; it depends on what it pushes toward.

items.stem: Ann faces one large stressor with strong family support. Ben faces several small stressors at once with no support. Who is more likely to feel overwhelmed?
options: Ann, since one large stressor always outweighs several small ones put together
Neither
Ben, since pile-up and few resources raise the impact
Equal
items.explain: Impact depends on pile-up and resources as much as size.

items.stem: Two cities get the same snowstorm. One has plows ready; the other doesn't. Which lesson idea does this mirror?
options: Snow is not a stressor
Preparation and resources shape how much a stressor hurts
The stressor alone determines the outcome
Both cities suffer about equally, since the size of the storm decides most of the damage
items.explain: The person's or system's resources change the impact of the same stressor.

items.stem: Talking about his son's death, Ray calmly lists statistics about grief and shows no emotion. Which defense?
options: Emotional insulation only
Repression, since he has pushed the memory away
Intellectualization
Regression
items.explain: Intellectualizing handles painful material by turning it into abstract ideas.

items.stem: Under stress, a grown man starts throwing tantrums like a child. Which defense?
options: Insulation
Repression
Intellectualization
Regression
items.explain: Regression returns to an earlier, more childlike way of coping.

items.stem: Under months of reentry stress, Tom tightens up, becomes rigid, and drops his meetings. Which stage, and what comes next if nothing changes?
options: Alarm, the first stage, which usually passes once a person adjusts to the change
Resistance, which can lead to exhaustion
No stage
Exhaustion, followed by alarm
items.explain: The stages run alarm, resistance (often rigid, dropping supports), then exhaustion or collapse.

items.stem: In your own words, why is a stress plan also relapse prevention?
items.explain: Stress is a major driver of relapse, especially when it piles up and supports drop away. Planning for stress protects sobriety.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member uses emotional insulation, staying flat and detached, to get through a violent unit. Should the facilitator try to break it down?
items.explain: No single verdict. The defense may protect him now but could block recovery work later.
key_points: Respect: it may be adaptive where he lives
Explore: when it helps and when it costs him
Plan: practice safe ways to feel in group or one-on-one

lib-9.title: Skills for Reducing Stress
summary: Disorganization adds stress and creates openings for relapse.
Three priority levels: must do this week, should do but can slide a week, nice to have.
Support feels like pressure if you resist recovery and like help if you accept it.
Rate supports as definitely, possibly, not supportive, or possibly harmful; don't recover alone.
The Relaxation Response (Benson): quiet place, repeated word, passive attitude, comfortable position, 10–20 minutes once or twice a day.

items.stem: Hector's first week home is a blur of appointments he keeps forgetting. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll get organized on his own within a couple of weeks as the routine sinks in
Stress fades as he adjusts
Rising stress and more openings to relapse
No effect
items.explain: Disorganization increases both stress and relapse opportunities.

items.stem: A member schedules eight recovery activities in his first week and feels overwhelmed. Best guidance?
options: Balance: schedule key activities, but not so many they create stress
Add more
Drop all but one, so he can focus completely and avoid stress in his first week
More activities mean more protection; keep all eight
items.explain: New recovery activities need scheduling, but too many create stress.

items.stem: "Meet my PO Tuesday; it can't be skipped." Which priority level?
options: Priority 3
Priority 2
Priority 1
Not a priority
items.explain: Priority 1 is what must happen this week for recovery.

items.stem: "Clean out the garage." It'd be nice, but nothing bad happens if it waits a month. Which level?
options: Priority 3, nice to have
Not a task
Priority 1
Priority 2
items.explain: Anything that's merely nice to have falls below the first two levels.

items.stem: An emergency room sorts patients by urgency so the sickest are seen first. How does that relate to this lesson?
options: It's an example of conflict
Both sort tasks by urgency so essentials happen first
Both make sure every task gets equal attention so nothing important is neglected
It doesn't; medicine has different rules
items.explain: Triage and the three priority levels share the same logic.

items.stem: Leah resists recovery; her mother's daily check-ins feel like nagging. Six months later, Leah is committed to sobriety. How might the same check-ins feel?
options: The same
Even more annoying
Like a threat
More like help
items.explain: Support feels like pressure when you resist recovery and like help when you embrace it.

items.stem: A member wonders what to tell an old using friend who keeps calling. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Meet him to explain in person at his place
Tell him clearly you're not using and won't be around him if he is
Avoid answering and hope he stops
Block everyone from his past, including family, so nobody can pull him back
items.explain: Clear statements to old using contacts protect recovery.

items.stem: A cousin who doesn't use but often brings up "the good old days" of partying. How might a member rate her?
options: Possibly harmful or not supportive, depending on her effect
Irrelevant
Definitely supportive, since family who stay sober themselves are the safest supports
Definitely supportive, since she doesn't use
items.explain: The four levels sort people by their actual effect on recovery.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson say to let sober time show change after apologizing to people you hurt?
items.explain: Words alone rarely rebuild trust after addiction. Consistent sober behavior over time is what makes an apology believable.

items.stem: Three weeks sober, Kyle falls into an all-consuming romance and stops going to meetings. What does the lesson warn?
options: It's unrelated to recovery
He'll be fine, since a healthy relationship is a better support than meetings
Intense early romance can stand in for the drug
Love is the best support
items.explain: Early intense romance can replace the drug and pull focus from healing.

items.stem: Which is part of Benson's Relaxation Response?
options: Doing it right after a big meal, when the body is naturally ready to rest
Vigorous exercise to tire the body
Silently repeating a word like "one" with a passive attitude
Listening to loud music
items.explain: It needs a quiet place, a repeated word, a passive attitude and a comfortable position.

items.stem: Many contemplative traditions use a repeated phrase or prayer to quiet the mind. How does that relate to Benson's method?
options: Benson drew on a shared core: a repeated focus word and a passive attitude
It requires religious belief
Contemplative traditions use repetition for worship only, which has nothing in common with relaxation
It is unrelated; Benson's method is purely medical
items.explain: Benson described a common element across meditative practices and made it secular and simple.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member rates his mother "possibly harmful" because she enables him, but she's his only housing. What should his plan do?
items.explain: No single verdict. Her home meets a basic need, but enabling may undermine recovery.
key_points: Set limits: talk about what support he needs
Plan B: line up alternatives in case it slides

lib-10.title: Negative Emotions
summary: Sadness is shorter and lets you function; depression lasts weeks or longer, makes daily life hard, and is treatable.
Drugs and depression feed each other; withdrawal-related depression is expected.
Antidepressants restore brain chemistry, aren't intoxicating, and can support sobriety.
Guilt is a useful signal; overwhelming, lasting guilt calls for help; childhood guilt often blames the child for what he couldn't fix.
Powerlessness explains how use took over but doesn't erase responsibility; sharing feelings increases control.

items.stem: After his brother's move, Omar feels down for a few days but keeps working and seeing friends. Sadness or depression?
options: Neither
Depression, since he feels down
Sadness: shorter, and he still functions
Depression, since any low mood after a loss counts as a depressive episode
items.explain: Sadness is a normal reaction that passes while you keep functioning.

items.stem: For six weeks Lena can barely get out of bed, has stopped eating well and feels hopeless. Sadness or depression?
options: Sadness
Likely depression, which needs evaluation and is treatable
Laziness
Withdrawal only, which will lift by itself once her body adjusts
items.explain: Longer, more severe low mood that disrupts daily life suggests depression.

items.stem: Carl uses alcohol to lift his low moods. What does the lesson predict over time?
options: His mood improves for a while, since alcohol is a proven way to lift low mood
Drinking deepens the depression, which drives more drinking
No effect
His mood improves
items.explain: Depressants and stimulant crashes cause depression, and self-medicating feeds the cycle.

items.stem: Sara was depressed before she started using. After she stops, what does the lesson predict?
options: Her depression lifts at once
No depression, since her low mood was caused by the drugs and will leave with them
A longer, deeper episode is possible, and she may need treatment for both
Only physical withdrawal
items.explain: People with prior depression often face a deeper post-use episode and need integrated care.

items.stem: A member refuses an antidepressant: "I'm not trading one high for another." What does the lesson say?
options: Antidepressants aren't intoxicating and can support sobriety
He's right; all psychiatric medication is a relapse
He's partly right, since antidepressants work by producing a mild, steady high
Stop talking about it
items.explain: Antidepressants help restore brain chemistry without getting a person high.

items.stem: A diabetic takes insulin daily. A friend says she's "dependent on a drug." How does the lesson's view of antidepressants answer that?
options: Medicine is weakness
The friend is right; any medication is addiction
Taking medicine to restore normal function differs from using to get high
The friend is right in a technical sense, so the comparison actually supports his worry
items.explain: Treating a medical condition is different from intoxication.

items.stem: Kim feels bad about missing her son's game, apologizes, and makes the next one. Which kind of guilt?
options: Overwhelming guilt, since she is still thinking about it after the game
No guilt
Healthy guilt, working as a signal
Overwhelming guilt
items.explain: Healthy guilt flags a harm and prompts repair.

items.stem: Years after sobriety, Tom still can't stop punishing himself for the past and can't function. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Overwhelming guilt calls for counseling and group support
That's normal and will fade alone
He deserves to feel it, since lasting guilt is what keeps people from repeating mistakes
He should hide it
items.explain: Long-lasting, crushing guilt is unhealthy and needs support.

items.stem: As an adult, Ana apologizes for everything, even things she didn't do. She grew up with a parent who drank. What does the lesson suggest?
options: She has no guilt
She's simply a polite, considerate person, and it has nothing to do with her childhood
She's just polite
A childhood habit of taking blame for what she couldn't fix
items.explain: Children in troubled homes often blame themselves and over-apologize as adults.

items.stem: A member says, "Step One says I'm powerless, so I'm not responsible for what I did." Best response?
options: Agree, since powerlessness removes responsibility
Agree in part, since responsibility only applies to choices made while sober
Powerlessness explains how use took over but doesn't erase responsibility for harm
Change the subject
items.explain: The lesson separates explanation from excuse; healing includes amends.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson say sharing feelings increases control?
items.explain: Many believe hiding feelings keeps them in charge, but bottled feelings tend to drive behavior unseen. Sharing them makes them manageable.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member wants to make amends to a woman he harmed, but she has a no-contact order. Should he pursue direct amends?
items.explain: No single verdict. Amends matter to healing, but contact may hurt her and break the law.
key_points: No contact: her safety and the order come first
Indirect amends: changed behavior, letters not sent, restitution through proper channels
Discuss: with a sponsor or counselor before acting

items.stem: What order does the lesson suggest for forgiveness?
options: Acknowledge harm, take responsibility, ask forgiveness, forgive others, then yourself
Forgive yourself first, then others
Wait for others to apologize first, then forgive them, then make amends to the people you hurt
Skip it
items.explain: The sequence follows the spirit of Steps Eight and Nine.

lib-11.title: Anger and Communication
summary: Anger has a strong physical side like fear; prolonged anger harms health.
Unhealthy patterns: stuffing, delaying without resolving, shifting to a safer target, diluting out of guilt, attacking.
Cooling off is fine, but the underlying problem still needs addressing.
Expressing anger aims at being understood, not at wounding.
Assertiveness rests on basic rights; "I feel" statements name the feeling and a specific incident, without "you" openers or mind-reading.

items.stem: "My heart pounds, my breathing speeds up and my fists clench." What is this?
options: Anger's physical alarm, similar to fear
A panic attack
A craving, since the body is preparing to use
Relaxation
items.explain: Anger triggers a body alarm much like fear.

items.stem: Luis is furious at his boss but takes it out on his kids at home. Which pattern?
options: Delaying
Stuffing
Diluting
Shifting
items.explain: Shifting moves anger to a safer target, often without the person realizing.

items.stem: Maria pretends she isn't angry about her sister's comments, month after month. Which pattern?
options: Stuffing, since she is pushing her anger down
Assertiveness
Attacking
Shifting
items.explain: Stuffing pushes anger down so it builds.

items.stem: Dev keeps waiting for "a better time" to discuss a problem with his roommate, and it never comes. What does the lesson predict?
options: The problem fades
The roommate eventually notices and brings it up himself, which solves it
No effect
He eventually blows up over something small
items.explain: Delaying without resolving tends to end in blow-ups.

items.stem: After hurting people while using, Nate says his anger at his father "doesn't count" because he did worse. Which pattern?
options: Attacking
Stuffing
Diluting anger out of guilt
Shifting
items.explain: Diluting blocks healing; accepting anger is separate from choosing how to express it.

items.stem: A member walks away from an argument to cool off and never brings it up again. What does the lesson say?
options: He should have stayed and argued it out, since walking away leaves the other person feeling dismissed
Cooling off is fine, but the problem still needs to be addressed
Perfect; walking away solves it
He should apologize
items.explain: Cooling off is a first step, not the resolution.

items.stem: "Oh great, thanks a lot for remembering," said with an eye roll. Which hurtful style?
options: Pouting
Sarcasm
Yelling
An "I feel" statement
items.explain: Sarcasm is on the manual's checklist of hurtful ways to express anger.

items.stem: Which is a well-formed "I feel" statement?
options: "I feel hurt when you come home an hour late without calling."
"You make me angry."
"I feel like you're selfish and don't think about anyone but yourself."
"You never call, you don't care."
items.explain: It names a feeling and ties it to a specific incident, without accusing.

items.stem: A member's statement is "I feel that you're trying to disrespect me." Best coaching?
options: Point out it's mind-reading; name the feeling and the specific action instead
Make it louder
Add more examples of times he felt disrespected so the point is clearer
Accept it; it starts with "I feel"
items.explain: "I feel that you're trying to disrespect me" is an accusation in disguise; the skill needs a real feeling and a specific event.

items.stem: Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication pairs observations with feelings and needs. How does it relate to this lesson?
options: It's only for children
It's opposite: it avoids feelings
It shares the idea of naming feelings tied to specific observations without blame
It is the opposite: it avoids feelings and sticks only to facts and requests
items.explain: Both approaches separate observation from judgment and name feelings directly.

items.stem: In your own words, what should expressing anger aim for, according to the lesson?
items.explain: To be understood, not to hurt or upset the listener. That goal shapes which words and tone actually work.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson ground assertiveness in basic rights?
items.explain: Everyone has rights like stating needs, saying no, changing their mind and making mistakes. Knowing those rights gives people permission to speak up without aggression.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says that inside, "answering criticism" from a CO can get him written up. Should he still exercise the right to respond?
items.explain: No single verdict. The right exists, but in a correctional setting expressing it carries real consequences.
key_points: Respond: calmly and through proper channels like grievances
Hold: choose timing and venue that keep him safe
Discuss: how rights apply differently in different settings

lib-12.title: Relapse Prevention Basics
summary: Being drug-free is the start of recovery; recovery means changing lifestyle, attitudes, people and places.
The chain runs trigger, automatic thought, craving, relapse; brain changes make people more vulnerable.
Triggers are internal, external or sensory.
Five ways to defuse triggers: identify, avoid, interrupt, talk about, thought-stop; avoiding before exposure is strongest.
