Daily test: is this choice good or bad for my recovery? If relapse starts, stop fast, skip self-punishment, return to treatment.

items.stem: Sixty days clean, Raul still spends evenings with the same crew, in the same spots, with the same attitudes. What does the lesson predict?
options: He should stop treatment
He'll stay clean for sure
He's drug-free but not yet in recovery, and risk stays high
He is in solid recovery, since sixty clean days is the main proof that matters
items.explain: Recovery means changing lifestyle and attitudes, not only stopping use.

items.stem: A company stops a fraud but keeps the same culture and incentives that produced it. What does the lesson's logic predict?
options: Culture doesn't matter
Fraud becomes impossible
The old pattern is likely to return without deeper change
Problem solved
items.explain: Stopping a behavior is a start; changing the conditions that produced it is the recovery.

items.stem: Trigger, automatic thought, craving, then what?
options: Relapse
Withdrawal
Denial
Recovery
items.explain: The chain ends in relapse unless interrupted earlier.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson say brain changes make people more vulnerable to the chain?
items.explain: Drug-related brain changes make triggers fire more automatically and cravings stronger. That's why planning and early interruption matter so much.

items.stem: A pipe left in a drawer. Which trigger type?
options: Internal
External: paraphernalia
Sensory only
Not a trigger
items.explain: External triggers include people, places, times and paraphernalia.

items.stem: The sound of a lighter flicking. Which trigger type?
options: Internal, since it brings up a feeling
Sensory
None
External
items.explain: Sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touch tied to use are sensory triggers.

items.stem: A member's apartment is on the block where he used to buy. What does the lesson consider the strongest option?
options: Talk about it in group only
Ignore it
Avoid it before exposure, which can mean moving
Practice walking past daily so the trigger loses its power over time
items.explain: Avoiding before exposure is the strongest option, even when that means moving.

items.stem: "Triggers stay powerful when they're kept secret, so I tell my sponsor every one." Which defusing step?
options: Interrupt
Talk about them
Identify
Avoid
items.explain: Talking about triggers weakens their hold.

items.stem: A personal trainer tells a client to ask before each food choice, "Does this help my goal?" How does that mirror the lesson?
options: Both use a simple daily test question for small choices
Both rely on willpower
It doesn't; food and drugs are different
Both forbid all treats
items.explain: Small choices add up; a quick test question keeps them aimed at the goal.

items.stem: Kyla applies "good or bad for my recovery?" to small daily choices, like which route home and who to call. Over months, what is likely?
options: Little effect, since small choices don't matter much compared with big decisions
Many small choices add up toward recovery
No change
She'll become anxious
items.explain: Many minor choices lead toward or away from triggers; the test steers them.

items.stem: A member uses once after six months and says, "I'm a failure, I might as well keep going." What does the lesson recommend?
options: Stop it fast, skip self-punishment, take responsibility and return to treatment
Start over alone
Agree he should take a break from treatment until he feels ready
Hide it
items.explain: Ending a relapse quickly and returning to treatment, possibly at a higher level, limits damage.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member relapsed and fears telling his treatment team will lead to a sanction. Should he disclose?
items.explain: No single verdict. Honesty opens the way to more help, but the consequences in a justice setting are real.
key_points: Disclose: early help limits the relapse and builds trust
Seek advice: talk to a counselor about how disclosure works
Weigh: the risks of hiding it if it's discovered later

lib-13.title: Introduction to Self-Help Groups
summary: Keeping use secret and trying to quit alone are among the top reasons early recovery fails.
Twelve Step fellowships have no dues, leaders or membership lists; the only requirement is a desire to stop.
Meeting types differ (speaker, topic, Step/Tradition, Big Book), so try several.
A sponsor answers questions, is available, keeps confidences and pushes more meetings after a slip.
Secular alternatives include SOS, SMART Recovery (CBT tools) and Women for Sobriety.

items.stem: Dan tells no one he's quitting and plans to "handle it himself." What does the lesson predict?
options: No effect
A strong chance of success, since private efforts avoid outside pressure
He'll succeed if motivated
Higher odds the attempt fails
items.explain: Hiding the problem and quitting alone are among the most common reasons early sobriety fails.

items.stem: In your own words, why does secrecy undermine early recovery?
items.explain: Shame keeps people quiet, so no one can support them or spot warning signs. Going it alone removes the mutual help that fellowship provides.

items.stem: What is the only requirement for Twelve Step membership?
options: Paying monthly dues
A religious belief
Having a sponsor
A desire to stop using
items.explain: There are no dues, leaders or membership lists; desire to stop is the only requirement.

items.stem: AA began when two men found they could stay sober only by helping each other. Which concept does that origin explain?
options: Why the groups are called fellowships
The Steps
The Big Book
The sponsor's role as an expert who instructs newcomers
items.explain: Mutual support is the core of fellowship.

items.stem: A member went to one speaker meeting, disliked it, and says "meetings aren't for me." Best response?
options: Tell him to go anyway
Drop it
Suggest trying other types, like topic or Step meetings, and different groups
Agree, since one meeting shows whether the format fits
items.explain: Groups and meeting types differ; trying several is recommended.

items.stem: In this meeting, one person tells their story while others listen. Which type?
options: Step/Tradition
Topic
Big Book
Speaker
items.explain: In a speaker meeting, one person shares their history.

items.stem: Which is part of a sponsor's role in the lesson?
options: Prescribing medication
Answering questions, keeping confidences and pushing more meetings after a slip
Reporting to the PO
Paying for treatment and supervising the member's day-to-day life
items.explain: A sponsor is a guide with long sobriety who is available and trustworthy.

items.stem: After a slip, Teo calls his sponsor. What is the sponsor most likely to suggest, per the lesson?
options: More meetings
Ending the sponsorship
Cutting back on meetings to reduce the pressure he is under
Keeping it quiet
items.explain: Sponsors push for more meetings after a slip.

items.stem: Which group uses CBT tools, teaches self-reliance and doesn't use sponsors?
options: SOS
SMART Recovery
Women for Sobriety
Narcotics Anonymous
items.explain: SMART Recovery is CBT-based, avoids labels and sponsors, and members may stop once stable.

items.stem: A member says he can't accept any Higher Power and won't attend AA. What fits the lesson?
options: Argue about religion
Tell him to attend AA anyway, since nothing else works as well
Offer secular options like SOS or SMART, and note agnostic AA meetings exist
Excuse him from support groups
items.explain: The lesson presents non-spiritual alternatives and agnostic meetings.

items.stem: A public health planner wants several recovery support options rather than one model. What does the lesson suggest about why?
options: Because one model is clearly best but people need choices to feel free
Because Twelve Step groups don't work
People differ, and a fit they'll actually attend matters
Because alternatives cost less
items.explain: Different groups suit different people; engagement depends on fit.

items.stem: Weigh it: a court order requires "AA attendance," but the member is an atheist who prefers SMART Recovery. What should the facilitator advise?
items.explain: No single verdict. Following the order protects him legally, but a better-fitting group may help recovery more.
key_points: Comply: attend AA, perhaps agnostic meetings
Advocate: ask the court or PO if SMART can count
Both: attend both while seeking approval

lib-14.title: The Twelve Steps
summary: The Steps are suggestions from early AA experience, practiced continually, not finished one at a time.
Step 1 is humility: losing control was not a willpower failure; Step 2's "insanity" means the compulsive pattern.
Steps 4–7 are inventory and change; Step 5 is usually shared with a sponsor or clergy person.
Steps 8–10 repair harm, skipping amends that would injure; Steps 11–12 are contact and service.
Seven principles: admit, fellowship, surrender, inventory, restitution, service, one day at a time. Surrender means quitting an unwinnable fight, not giving up hope.

items.stem: "Admitting I couldn't control it was a relief. It wasn't just that I was weak." Which step?
options: Step 9
Step 12
Step 1
Step 4, since he is looking honestly at his past
items.explain: Step 1 is humility: control was lost to the drug, not a simple willpower failure.

items.stem: In your own words, why do many people find Step 1 a relief?
items.explain: It reframes years of failed attempts as the nature of the problem, not a personal weakness. That lifts shame and opens the door to help.

items.stem: In Step 2, what does "insanity" refer to?
options: Legal insanity
Anger
A diagnosed mental illness requiring medication
The compulsive, self-destructive pattern of use
items.explain: Insanity here means repeating a harmful pattern, not mental illness.

items.stem: Which step is usually done with a sponsor or clergy person, as a release after the inventory?
options: Step 10
Step 3
Step 4
Step 5
items.explain: Step 5 shares the inventory aloud, which works as a release valve.

items.stem: Lorenzo wants to make amends to an ex-partner, but contact could reopen trauma for her. What does Step 9 guide?
options: Skip direct amends where they would injure her
Send a long letter
Make direct amends anyway, since amends are always required
Ask her family
items.explain: Amends are made except where they would harm the person or others.

items.stem: Truth and reconciliation commissions after civil conflicts sometimes pair acknowledgment of harm with repair. How does that echo Steps 8 and 9?
options: It doesn't; nations differ from people
Both avoid responsibility
Both punish offenders
Both name harm done and then seek to repair it
items.explain: Naming harm and making restitution are the shared moves.

items.stem: Which is one of the seven principles behind the Steps?
options: Self-reliance at all times
Punishment
Avoid feelings
One day at a time
items.explain: The seven: admit, fellowship, surrender, inventory, restitution, service, one day at a time.

items.stem: A member says, "Surrender means giving up, and I'm no quitter." Best response?
options: Explain that surrender means stopping a fight he can't win alone, not giving up hope
Skip the topic
Agree that surrender is giving up, and say he can skip that principle
Tell him he'll fail
items.explain: Surrender here is giving up a losing battle for control, not giving up on himself.

items.stem: A swimmer caught in a rip current is told not to fight it head-on but to swim parallel to shore. How does that reflect the lesson's idea of surrender?
options: Stopping a losing fight lets you find a way out
It's unrelated
It shows that resistance is always the right response to danger
It's about fitness
items.explain: Surrender in recovery means ending an unwinnable struggle so a better path appears.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson say the Steps are practiced continually, not finished one by one?
items.explain: They're suggestions drawn from experience, and their principles keep applying as life changes. People return to them again and again.

items.stem: Five years sober, Ana starts sponsoring newcomers. Which step and principle is she living, and what does the lesson suggest it does for her?
options: Step 4; it's an inventory
Step 12, service, which also strengthens her own recovery
No step
Step 1; it reminds her she's powerless
items.explain: Carrying the message to others is service, which supports the helper's sobriety too.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says Step 3, turning will over to God "as we understood Him," still sounds religious to him. Should he skip it?
items.explain: No single verdict. The Steps are suggestions and the Higher Power is self-defined, but some find the language a barrier.
key_points: Adapt: define the Higher Power as the group or principles
Skip for now: the Steps are suggestions
Explore: secular groups or agnostic meetings

items.stem: How does the lesson distinguish spirituality from religion?
options: They are the same thing described with different words
Spirituality means prayer
Religion is optional, spirituality required
Spirituality is awareness of something bigger than yourself; religion is a specific belief system
items.explain: The Steps rest on spirituality broadly defined, open to members of any faith or none.

lib-17.title: Nutrition and Exercise
summary: Stimulants suppress appetite and speed metabolism; alcohol calories have no nutrition; long, heavy use carries the highest risk.
Protein supplies amino acids the body needs to rebuild neurotransmitters.
Favor good carbs (whole grains, beans, produce); limit added sugar, saturated fat and salt.
Sugar and caffeine swings can affect mood, anxiety and sleep in recovery.
Aerobic exercise helps restore brain chemistry; target about 150 minutes moderate or 75 vigorous a week.

items.stem: After a year of daily meth use, what nutritional pattern does the lesson predict for Rico?
options: No change
Weight loss from suppressed appetite and faster metabolism
Better nutrition
Weight gain from late-night eating, since meth keeps people up
items.explain: Stimulants kill appetite and speed metabolism.

items.stem: Which drug does the lesson tie to weight gain and junk food cravings?
options: Cocaine
Heroin
Marijuana
Meth
items.explain: Marijuana tends to bring weight gain and junk food.

items.stem: In your own words, why does protein matter especially in early recovery?
items.explain: Protein supplies amino acids the brain uses to rebuild neurotransmitters depleted by use. Eating enough supports mood and repair.

items.stem: A builder can't repair a wall without bricks. How does that analogy fit the lesson?
options: Bricks are like sugar
Amino acids from protein are the raw material for rebuilding brain chemistry
Walls are like fat
Food is mainly about energy, so the analogy fails
items.explain: The brain needs building blocks to restore neurotransmitters.

items.stem: Which is a good carbohydrate in the lesson's terms?
options: Soda
Pastries
Candy
Lentils
items.explain: Whole grains, beans and lentils, and unsweetened produce are good carbs.

items.stem: Early in recovery, Jess drinks four sodas a day and feels shaky and irritable between them. What does the lesson suggest?
options: She needs more caffeine
It's withdrawal only
The sodas are helping by giving her energy she would not otherwise have
Sugar highs and lows may be affecting her mood and recovery
items.explain: Sugar swings can bring highs and lows that affect recovery.

items.stem: A member drinks coffee all day and complains of anxiety and poor sleep. Best suggestion?
options: Add an energy drink in the afternoon to push through the tiredness
Nothing
Cut back on caffeine, a stimulant that worsens anxiety and sleep
Stop eating
items.explain: Caffeine is a stimulant; cutting it can ease anxiety and improve sleep.

items.stem: Why does the lesson call high blood pressure "the silent killer," and which food item raises it?
options: Because it's rare; fiber
Because it's harmless; water
Because it has few symptoms; salt raises it
Because it causes loud symptoms; sugar
items.explain: Salt holds fluid and raises blood pressure, which often has no symptoms.

items.stem: Which type of exercise does the lesson tie to restoring neurotransmitter balance?
options: Stretching only
Aerobic
Isotonic
Isometric
items.explain: Aerobic exercise acts like a natural antidepressant.

items.stem: Darnell starts brisk 30-minute walks five days a week. What does the lesson predict besides fitness?
options: Weight gain
Little change, since walking is too light to affect the brain
More cravings
Better mood, partly from restored brain chemistry
items.explain: Aerobic exercise supports mood and acts like a natural antidepressant.

items.stem: What weekly target does the book give for adults?
options: 30 minutes total
10 hours of weights
150 minutes moderate or 75 vigorous, spread over 3 or more days
Daily marathons
items.explain: That target spreads aerobic activity across the week.

items.stem: A credit card lets you spend more now and leaves you short later. How does the lesson use a similar idea to compare drugs and exercise?
options: Drugs push brain chemicals far beyond normal, leaving a shortfall after; exercise gives a smaller, healthier lift
Neither affects the brain
Both are equal
Exercise borrows more than drugs do
items.explain: Drugs "borrow" heavily from the brain's reward chemistry, which is why the crash follows.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member wants to eat better, but commissary food is mostly salty and sugary. Should he focus on diet now or wait for release?
items.explain: No single verdict. Small changes are possible inside, but options are limited and stress is high.
key_points: Now: choose the better options available and drink water
Later: plan a fuller change after release
Both: start with one change, like cutting soda

lib-18.title: Physical Wellness
summary: Addiction is biopsychosocial; some part of the body is usually out of balance early on, which calls for checkups, not panic.
Several conditions are silent but testable: high blood pressure, diabetes, TB, hepatitis.

Hepatitis B spreads through blood, sex and from mother to baby; shared needles are the main route among people who inject drugs, and hepatitis D only infects people who already carry B. Neither is curable; vaccines exist for A and B.
Stimulants, heavy drinking, smoking, salt, obesity and stress raise heart risk.
Insomnia is common early and raises relapse risk; a steady sleep schedule is the core fix.

items.stem: A member is overwhelmed: "Everything in my body is broken." Best response, per the lesson?
options: Tell him he's fine
Normalize early imbalance and encourage checkups to sort out what needs care
Refer only for emergencies
Agree that the damage is likely permanent and focus only on staying clean
items.explain: Some imbalance is normal early on; testing and care beat panic.

items.stem: Which condition usually has no symptoms and is caught only by checking?
options: High blood pressure
A migraine
A broken arm, since it is obvious
The flu
items.explain: High blood pressure is silent but easy to measure.

items.stem: Terry feels fine and skips medical screening after release. He used needles for years. What does the lesson warn?
options: Only TB matters
Conditions like hepatitis can be present without symptoms
He's fine if he feels fine
Screening is pointless
items.explain: Several serious conditions give little warning; testing catches them.

items.stem: According to the lesson, which route spreads hepatitis B and D among people who inject drugs?
options: Through shared needles
Through coughing
Through handshakes
Through contaminated food and water, like hepatitis A
items.explain: Shared needles are the main route for people who inject drugs. B also spreads sexually and from mother to baby, and D only infects people who already have B; neither is curable.

items.stem: A member asks if any hepatitis can be prevented. What does the lesson say?
options: Only with antibiotics
No, all forms can only be treated after infection
Only by avoiding food
Vaccines exist for hepatitis A and B
items.explain: Vaccines for A and B are a key prevention step.

items.stem: Luis uses cocaine, smokes, eats salty food and is under constant stress. What does the lesson predict?
options: Only lung problems
Low risk
Higher blood pressure and heart-attack risk
His heart is protected, since stimulants strengthen the heart muscle over time
items.explain: Stimulants, smoking, salt and stress all push heart risk up.

items.stem: What does the book recommend for early-recovery constipation and diarrhea?
options: Fasting
Fiber, fluids and exercise, with a doctor if it persists
More coffee
Laxatives and anti-diarrhea pills, since they work fastest
items.explain: The book favors fiber, fluids and exercise over medicines.

items.stem: Early in sobriety, Mia sleeps three hours a night for a week. What does the lesson predict?
options: No effect
She'll adapt and need less sleep, which helps her stay busy
Better focus
She becomes more vulnerable to relapse triggers
items.explain: Lack of sleep raises vulnerability to triggers.

items.stem: When does the lesson say insomnia may show up weeks later rather than right away?
options: Never
For people who used depressants
For people who used stimulants, since their sleep was disrupted most
For coffee drinkers
items.explain: Withdrawal insomnia usually eases in about a week, but depressant users may get it later.

items.stem: A member can't fall asleep, so he lies in bed for two hours scrolling his tablet. What does the sleep plan suggest?
options: Sleep pills nightly
If not asleep in about half an hour, get up and do something calm, keep the bed for sleep
Nap during the day
Keep scrolling, since screens help him relax before sleep
items.explain: Bed only for sleep, no daytime naps, a steady schedule, and getting up if sleep won't come.

items.stem: Sleep researchers often call keeping a fixed wake time "anchoring" the body clock. Which part of the lesson's plan is that?
options: Avoiding naps during the day
The same bedtime and alarm every day
Taking sleep medication
Using the bed only for sleep
items.explain: A consistent schedule is the core fix.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member in early recovery asks his doctor for sleeping pills. Some are habit-forming. Should he take them?
items.explain: No single verdict. Sleep loss raises relapse risk, but some sleep medicines carry their own dependence risk.
key_points: Consider: a non-habit-forming option under medical guidance
Avoid: habit-forming pills in early recovery
First: try the sleep plan consistently

lib-19.title: Problem Solving
summary: Addiction hides problems through distorted thinking and denial, shifts blame and lets problems pile up.
Early recovery reactions: feeling buried, exaggerating, resenting problems, using them as relapse excuses.
Problem solving starts with willingness: accept problems exist, believe they're solvable, and change yourself.
Six steps: identify one problem, own it, list all solutions, think through outcomes, plan with a backup, learn from the result.
Tools: prioritize, break it down, ask for help, brainstorm, and weigh benefits and risks.

items.stem: During years of use, Gene kept telling himself his debts and family conflicts "weren't his problem." What does the lesson predict at the start of sobriety?
options: No problems
A pile of problems that feels overwhelming
Instant solutions
A clean slate, since sobriety makes old problems fade on their own
items.explain: Denial and blame let problems pile up during use.

items.stem: "With all these problems, why bother staying sober?" Which early-recovery reaction is this?
options: Exaggerating
Using problems as a relapse excuse
Willingness
Owning a problem
items.explain: Resenting problems and using them as excuses is a common early-recovery trap.

items.stem: "Everything is falling apart and nothing will ever work out." Which reaction?
options: Owning
Prioritizing
Brainstorming
Exaggerating and feeling buried
items.explain: Feeling buried and exaggerating are common reactions to the pile.

items.stem: In your own words, why does problem solving start with willingness?
items.explain: Without accepting that problems exist and believing they can be solved, no method gets used. Willingness also includes changing yourself, not just the situation.

items.stem: "I got the ticket because I let my registration lapse, and I can set a reminder next year." Which step?
options: Owning the problem
Making a plan with a backup
Listing all solutions
Learning from the result
items.explain: Owning it means understanding your part without beating yourself up.

items.stem: A member's plan has one solution and no fallback. What does the six-step method add?
options: A longer list of problems
More options are unnecessary if the first plan is good
A backup plan in case the first doesn't work
Someone else to solve it
items.explain: Step five is a plan with a backup.

items.stem: NASA engineers review every mission afterward to improve the next. Which step of the method is that?
options: Identifying one problem
Owning the problem
Learning from the result
Thinking through outcomes before acting
items.explain: The last step turns results into lessons for next time.

items.stem: A member owes a $50 police ticket and a 50-cent library fine. Which first?
options: Both at once
Neither
The police ticket, since it carries bigger consequences
The library fine, since it is the easiest and quickest win
items.explain: Prioritizing means sorting what must be handled now from what can wait.

items.stem: A novelist facing a 400-page draft sets a goal of one scene a day. Which tool is she using?
options: Asking for help
Owning it
Breaking a big problem into pieces
Weighing benefits and risks
items.explain: Breaking a big problem down makes it manageable.

items.stem: Kara believes asking for help is weak and struggles alone with a housing problem for months. What does the lesson suggest?
options: She should give up
Asking for help is strength, and most people like helping
Struggling alone builds the strength she needs, so it pays off later
Help would make it worse
items.explain: The book treats asking for help as maturity, not weakness.

items.stem: In the benefit/risk tool, how is each option scored?
options: 0 to +10 for benefit and 0 to −10 for risk
1 to 5 stars
Yes or no
By group vote
items.explain: Each option gets a benefit score and a risk score.

items.stem: A member and his sponsor sit down to brainstorm, but the member rejects each idea as it comes. What rule is broken?
options: Brainstorm alone
Hold judgment and write everything down; more ideas are better
Weigh the risk of each idea right away, before writing down the next one
Limit ideas to three
items.explain: Brainstorming works by generating freely for about fifteen minutes before judging.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's eviction happened partly because of his use and partly because the landlord broke the law. How much should he "own"?
items.explain: No single verdict. Owning his part builds change, but taking all the blame ignores real wrongdoing.
key_points: Own: his missed payments and choices
Name: the landlord's violations and seek legal aid
Balance: understanding his part without self-blame

lib-20.title: Attitudes and Beliefs
summary: A stressor makes a demand; stress is your reaction, and beliefs about the event make the difference.
The chain runs event, belief, emotional consequence, much like Ellis's ABC model.
Irrational beliefs hide in words like must, should, ought, always and never.
Disputing means recognizing a belief is wrong and replacing it, which changes the feeling.
The inner critic is irrational but self-protective; test it for evidence and accept what can't be changed.

items.stem: Two women get the same court order to attend NA for a year. One thinks, "I don't have a problem, this is unfair." The other thinks, "I need help and this gives it to me." What does the lesson predict?
options: Both feel relieved
Both feel angry
Both feel the same, since the order and its demands are identical for each of them
The first feels angry and stressed; the second feels calmer
items.explain: Same event, different beliefs, different emotional consequences.

items.stem: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus taught that people are disturbed not by things but by their views of things. Which lesson idea does that anticipate?
options: That events never matter at all to how people feel
That beliefs about an event shape the emotional reaction
That stress is purely physical
That feelings can't change
items.explain: Ellis credited the Stoics; the belief step in the chain carries the same insight.

items.stem: Event: "My PO adds a curfew." Belief: "He's out to get me." Feeling: rage. Which link most decides the feeling?
options: The event, since curfews are frustrating for anyone
The belief
None
The feeling itself
items.explain: The belief between event and feeling is what makes the difference.

items.stem: A member says, "My boss made me furious." How would the facilitator use the chain?
options: Tell him to quit
Agree that the boss caused the anger and move on to coping
Ask what he told himself about what the boss did
Ask the group if the boss is bad
items.explain: Pulling out the belief shows where change is possible.

items.stem: Which belief carries a classic irrational marker?
options: "I'm working on rebuilding trust."
"I'd like my family to trust me again."
"Trust takes time."
"My family must forgive me right away."
items.explain: "Must" turns a preference into a rigid demand, which breeds stress and anger.

items.stem: "I always mess everything up." What makes this irrational?
options: "Always" overgeneralizes from some events to every event
It's too short
It describes a past mistake
It's a feeling
items.explain: Absolute words like always and never are flags of irrational thinking.

items.stem: After a missed bus makes her late for work, Tara thinks, "I'm going to get fired, I can't do anything right." She disputes: "I've been on time for weeks; one late day is unlikely to cost my job." What happens to the feeling?
options: Her panic eases toward manageable worry
It gets stronger, because disputing draws attention to the worry
She feels guilty
Nothing
items.explain: Disputing replaces the stressful belief, which changes the emotional consequence.

items.stem: A scientist treats her hunch as a hypothesis and looks for disconfirming data before accepting it. How does that mirror disputing?
options: It's unrelated; science has no feelings
Both ignore data
Both assume the hunch is true
Both test a belief against evidence instead of accepting it
items.explain: Disputing treats beliefs as claims to test, the core of cognitive approaches.

items.stem: "You're stupid. Don't even try for that job, you'll embarrass yourself." What does the lesson say this voice is doing?
options: Protecting him from embarrassment in an irrational way
Giving accurate, healthy feedback
Nothing
Motivating him
items.explain: The inner critic is irrational but self-protective: it avoids challenge and disappointment.

items.stem: A member says his inner voice tells him he's worthless. Which challenge test fits?
options: Agree with it
Argue with it loudly
Ignore the voice completely, since paying attention to it gives it more power
Ask whether there's evidence it's true and evidence it's exaggerated
items.explain: Testing the claim usually shows it's overblown.

items.stem: In your own words, how does healthy self-criticism differ from the irrational kind?
items.explain: Healthy criticism targets a specific behavior and points to a fix. Irrational criticism condemns the whole person, which breeds hopelessness.

items.stem: Which is healthy self-criticism?
options: "I'm a total loser."
"I snapped at my daughter; I'll apologize and take a breath next time."
"I'm hopeless."
"I can't do anything right."
items.explain: It names a specific behavior and a change.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member has a lifelong chronic illness and says, "Acceptance just means giving up." How should the facilitator frame accepting what can't be changed?
items.explain: No single verdict. Acceptance can free energy for what can change, but pushed too early it can feel like dismissal.
key_points: Frame: acceptance redirects effort to what's in his control
Respect: his grief about the illness is real
Practice: separate the fixed facts from the choices still open

lib-21.title: Human Needs and Social Relationships
summary: Needs stack from biological to safety, belonging, esteem and self-actualization, based on Maslow.
In addiction, the drive to use acts like a basic need but can never be satisfied, crowding out real needs.
Using circles rest on getting drugs and exploitation; recovery circles rest on mutual care.
Healthy relationships share qualities like vulnerability, empathy, respect, trust and honesty; recovery aims for interdependence.
Children need care, protection, love, firm but kind limits and teaching; harm from a parent's addiction can be repaired with consistent care.

items.stem: Housing and a steady job fall at which level of needs?
options: Biological
Belonging
Safety
Esteem
items.explain: Safety covers stable housing, steady food and work.

items.stem: During his addiction, Hal knowingly lost his apartment and job to keep using. What does the lesson say about this?
options: It was bad luck
The drive to use acted like a basic need and pushed real needs aside
He didn't care about housing
He simply made a bad but rational trade between his priorities
items.explain: Addiction mimics a basic need but can never be satisfied, so it crowds out others.

items.stem: A historian describes a gold rush town where people abandoned farms and families chasing gold that rarely paid. How does that echo the lesson?
options: A pursuit that feels essential can crowd out basic needs
It's unrelated
It shows that gold is a basic biological need for people
It shows greed is good
items.explain: Like addiction, an all-consuming pursuit can override safety and belonging.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the levels-of-needs idea matter for recovery planning?
items.explain: Higher goals like esteem and potential are hard to reach while basics like housing and safety are unmet. Plans often start by rebuilding the lower levels.

items.stem: A friendship that mostly involved scoring together and covering for each other. Which kind of circle?
options: A recovery circle, since they looked out for each other
A healthy interdependent tie
A support network
A using circle
items.explain: Using relationships rest on getting drugs and often exploitation.

items.stem: Paulo stays close to his old using friends "just to hang out." What does the lesson predict?
options: No effect
He'll recruit them to recovery
Little risk, since he has decided not to use with them
A raised relapse risk, since ties to using friends rank high among causes
items.explain: Staying close to using friends is among the most common relapse causes.

items.stem: Which is one of the healthy-relationship qualities the book draws from Janet Woititz?
options: Independence at all costs
Control, so each person knows what to expect from the other
Vulnerability
Secrecy
items.explain: The list includes vulnerability, empathy, respect, trust, acceptance and honesty.

items.stem: Early in recovery, a member feels guilty that he takes more support than he gives. What does the lesson say?
options: He should stop asking
He should give back equally from day one
He owes everyone
Early on it's fine to take more than you give
items.explain: Recovery aims for interdependence over time; early imbalance is acceptable.

items.stem: In a jazz trio, each player listens, leaves space and builds on the others. Which lesson idea fits?
options: Interdependence: open exchange and joint action
Independence, since each musician plays a separate part
Codependence
Isolation
items.explain: Interdependence means shared decisions, trust and mutual concern.

items.stem: Which is on the lesson's list of what children need?
options: Total freedom
Expensive gifts
Kind but firm limits without physical punishment
Physical punishment to set clear and memorable limits
items.explain: Children need care, protection, love, attention, firm limits without physical punishment, and teaching.

items.stem: After years of absence due to use, Jamal shows up for his son every weekend for a year. What does the lesson predict?
options: Little change, since early harm to children is permanent
His son will reject him forever
His guilt fixes it
Consistent care can repair much of the harm
items.explain: Harm can be repaired with consistent care; guilt alone doesn't fix it.

items.stem: In your own words, what does the orphanage example in the book show?
items.explain: Babies who were fed but never held or played with wasted away. It shows love and attention are needs, not extras, which is why consistent presence matters in repair.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's only friends from childhood are in his using circle, and he fears total isolation if he cuts them off. What should he do?
items.explain: No single verdict. Distance lowers relapse risk, but isolation is also a risk factor.
key_points: Distance: the evidence on using friends is strong
Build first: add recovery friends before cutting ties
Limit: see old friends only in safe, sober settings

lib-22.title: Family Matters
summary: Healthy families run on open talk and flexible, fair rules; dysfunctional ones are closed, rigid and inconsistent.
Codependence means bending yourself around the addicted person until your own identity and self-esteem fade.
Four unspoken rules in addicted families: act rigidly, keep silent, deny, feel isolated. Claudia Black's famous three for children of alcoholics: don't talk, don't trust, don't feel.
Survival roles: hero, placater, lost child, scapegoat; roles help short-term but limit feeling and communication later.
Unexpressed hurt comes out as self-medicating or hurting others; forgiveness and reconciliation may take years.

items.stem: In Rita's family, rules change depending on Dad's mood and nobody discusses it. Which kind of system?
options: Codependent only
Interdependent
Dysfunctional: closed, rigid and inconsistent
Healthy, since rules are flexible
items.explain: Inconsistent rules nobody can talk about mark a dysfunctional system.

items.stem: Marisol organizes her whole life around her husband's drinking, hides it from family, and no longer knows what she wants. What is this?
options: Codependence
Independence
Enabling only
Healthy loyalty and devotion to a spouse
items.explain: Codependence involves obsession with the user, pleasing at your own expense and lost identity.

items.stem: In literature, the wife in Ibsen's A Doll's House organizes her life around her husband's approval until she realizes she has no self. Which lesson concept resonates?
options: Healthy interdependence
Scapegoating, since she is blamed by her husband
Losing one's identity by bending around another person
Grief
items.explain: The play explores self-erasure in a relationship, a theme close to codependence, though it involves no addiction.

items.stem: "In our house, we never mentioned Mom's drinking. Ever." Which unspoken rule?
options: Keep silent
Feel isolated
Act rigidly
Deny only
items.explain: Silence about the problem is one of the four rules.

items.stem: Kevin grew up under "don't talk, don't trust, don't feel." In group he struggles to share. What does the lesson suggest?
options: He has nothing to share
He's just shy and it has nothing to do with his family
He doesn't want to change
Childhood rules may still shape how he communicates
items.explain: Family rules learned in childhood often carry into adulthood.

items.stem: As a child, Tasha cooked, cleaned and got her siblings to school. Which role?
options: Scapegoat
Lost child
Placater
Hero
items.explain: The hero becomes a little adult who keeps things running.

items.stem: Andre was the kid who always got in trouble and took the blame for the family's chaos. Which role?
options: Lost child
Hero
Placater
Scapegoat
items.explain: The scapegoat acts out the family's confusion and gets blamed.

items.stem: Lucy stayed in her room, never asked for anything and was barely noticed. Which role?
options: Lost child
Hero
Placater
Scapegoat
items.explain: Staying invisible and making no demands is how this role gets by.

items.stem: Grown up, the family hero runs a crew at work but can't relax or admit any struggle. What does the lesson say?
options: The role brought skills but now blocks feeling and honest communication
Her role only brought strengths, so nothing needs to change
She should become a lost child
She has no problems
items.explain: Roles give short-term survival and some strengths but limit adults later.

items.stem: In your own words, what happens to childhood hurt that is never talked about?
items.explain: It rarely leaves on its own. It tends to come out through self-medicating with drugs or through hurting others.

items.stem: A member says he can't forgive his father yet and feels he's failing the lesson. Best response?
options: Tell him to call his father today
Skip the topic
Push him, since forgiveness is required for recovery to work at all
Say forgiveness may take years and reconciliation can also mean peace within himself
items.explain: Forgiveness takes time; reconciliation can be with family or within yourself.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's mother, still actively using, wants to reconcile. Should he reconnect now?
items.explain: No single verdict. Reconnection could heal old wounds, but her active use may threaten his recovery.
key_points: Reconnect: with clear boundaries and sober settings
Wait: until his recovery is steadier
Inner peace: reconciliation can begin within himself first

lib-25.title: Educational and Vocational Goals
summary: Many members left school because it didn't seem important, they rebelled, or use took over; there are routes back.
ABE serves adults with under 12 years of school; GED or HiSET earns an equivalency; apprenticeships pay while training.
Job fit draws on interests, work skills, job values and suitable occupations.
A cover letter is about three paragraphs; a résumé leaves out salary, age, family, legal and treatment history.
Prepare an honest, brief answer about convictions; the ADA protects people in recovery but not current use; plan for workplace triggers.

items.stem: Which program pays you while you learn a trade, usually over 1–5 years, with no tuition?
options: ABE
GED
Apprenticeship
Community college
items.explain: Apprenticeships combine paid on-the-job training with classes.

items.stem: What does the GED or HiSET test?
options: Job skills
Driving
Reading, writing, math, science and social studies
Only reading and writing, since it is a literacy test
items.explain: The HiSET tests five areas, splitting reading and writing; the GED covers the same ground in four, combining them. Passing earns a high school equivalency credential.

items.stem: A member, 34, left school in 9th grade and reads slowly. Which first step fits?
options: No schooling
Adult Basic Education, then GED or HiSET prep
An apprenticeship test tomorrow
Enroll straight into a college course to make up for lost time
items.explain: ABE serves adults with under 12 years of school and builds toward the equivalency.

items.stem: Ray takes a high-paying night job that clashes with his values (time with his kids) and interests. What does the lesson predict?
options: He'll get promoted
No effect
Poor fit raises the odds he'll be unhappy or quit
He'll be satisfied, since pay is what matters most
items.explain: Job fit comes from interests, skills, values and suitable occupations, not pay alone.

items.stem: A sports scout matches players to positions by their strengths and what they love about the game. Which lesson idea is that?
options: Apprenticeship
Workplace triggers
Writing a cover letter for each player
Matching work to interests and skills
items.explain: Fit happens where interests, skills and values meet the role.

items.stem: Which item does the book say to leave off a résumé?
options: Employment history
Education and training
Treatment history
Qualifications
items.explain: Leave out salary, age, family, legal and treatment history.

items.stem: A member's cover letter is a full page about his life story. What's the book's model?
options: About three paragraphs: why you're writing, key skills, a request for an interview
Keep it, since employers value personal stories more than skills
Attach a photo
One sentence
items.explain: A short, focused letter works best.

items.stem: An application asks about felony convictions in the last seven years. What does the lesson advise?
options: Leave it blank and explain only if the employer asks in person
Skip the job
Have an honest, brief answer ready
Lie, since it's unfair
items.explain: Being prepared with a short, honest answer is the recommended approach.

items.stem: Darius practices a 20-second answer about his record that names it, shows what's changed and moves to his skills. In an interview, what's likely?
options: He'll be asked to leave
The interviewer ignores it
He comes across as prepared and credible
The answer makes things worse, since mentioning a record always ends the interview
items.explain: A rehearsed, honest answer turns a hard question into a chance to show change.

items.stem: Under the ADA, who is protected from job discrimination?
options: People in recovery, but not someone currently using
Only veterans
Anyone who uses drugs, as long as it is off the clock
No one with a record
items.explain: The ADA protects people in recovery, not current illegal use; EAPs are confidential.

items.stem: Two weeks into a new job, Kim's coworkers invite her for drinks every Friday and she's more irritable than usual. What does the lesson suggest?
options: She should join them to build relationships, since that matters most early on
Early recovery brings work triggers and irritability, so she needs a plan
She should quit
It's not a risk
items.explain: Plan for coworker and workplace triggers before starting.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the book compare a workplace to a family?
items.explain: Bosses can feel like parents and coworkers like siblings, so old family patterns and feelings can show up at work. Knowing that helps people respond rather than react.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's state has "ban the box" rules delaying record questions. Should he disclose his record early anyway to "get it over with"?
items.explain: No single verdict. Early disclosure shows honesty, but the law allows him to be judged on skills first.
key_points: Disclose early: builds trust and avoids surprises
Wait: use the protection the law gives
Prepare: either way, have the brief answer ready

lib-26.title: Money Management
summary: Money skills like tracking, budgeting and balancing an account are rarely taught and get rusty in addiction.
Separate needs from wants when ranking priorities.
Three questions: what do you have, what do you want, how will you get it; goals are short, intermediate or long-term.
Five expense types: fixed monthly, variable monthly, fixed yearly, seasonal, emergency.
Income minus expenses shows surplus or debt; fix a shortfall by spending less, earning more, or both. Nonprofit credit counseling can help.

items.stem: Which is a need rather than a want?
options: Designer shoes
An expensive car
A gaming system
Reliable transportation to work
items.explain: Ranking pairs forces a choice between a need and a want.

items.stem: A member ranks a new phone above rent. Best facilitator move?
options: Skip ranking
Ask him to compare the two and what happens if each goes unpaid
Accept it, since priorities are personal and money is his own business
Tell him he's irresponsible
items.explain: Comparing consequences clarifies needs vs wants without lecturing.

items.stem: "Pay off my $300 fine in four months." Which timeframe?
options: No timeframe
Long-term, 5+ years
Short-term, within a year
Intermediate, 1–5 years
items.explain: Short-term goals land within a year.

items.stem: "Save a down payment for a house." Which timeframe is most likely for someone starting over?
options: Short-term
Immediate
Long-term, 5+ years
Intermediate
items.explain: Large goals like a house usually sit in the long-term range.

items.stem: Car registration paid once a year at the same amount. Which expense type?
options: Emergency
Fixed yearly
Fixed monthly
Variable monthly
items.explain: Same amount, once a year: fixed yearly.

items.stem: The electric bill, which changes each month. Which type?
options: Variable monthly
Fixed yearly
Seasonal
Fixed monthly
items.explain: It's monthly but the amount varies.

items.stem: A member says he can't plan for emergencies because they're unpredictable. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Skip that category, since emergencies by definition cannot be planned for
Use a credit card
Borrow when they happen
Estimate from what he actually spent on surprises last year, then divide by 12
items.explain: Past spending gives a realistic estimate to budget monthly.

items.stem: Lena's monthly income is $1,800 and her expenses are $2,050. What does the budget show, and what are her options?
options: A $250 shortfall, fixed by spending less, earning more, or both
Nothing; budgets are estimates
A small surplus she can save
She should borrow every month
items.explain: Income minus expenses reveals the gap and the only ways to close it.

items.stem: A club needs $1,200 for a trip in a year. The treasurer divides by twelve and asks for $100 a month. Which lesson tool is this?
options: Credit counseling
Emergency planning
Ranking needs versus wants for each member
Saving toward a goal by dividing the total by months
items.explain: Find the total, set the timeframe, divide by twelve.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the lesson encourage asking for help with money?
items.explain: Money skills are rarely taught and fade during addiction, so struggling is normal. Nonprofit credit counseling offers free or low-cost help, though some agencies aren't trustworthy.
key_points: Check that the agency is legitimate

items.stem: Toby stops opening his bills because they stress him out. What does the lesson predict?
options: The bills stop coming
The stress fades, since he no longer has to look at the numbers
No effect
Problems grow, with late fees and worse credit
items.explain: Facing the situation is the first step; avoiding it lets debt grow.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member wants to send part of every paycheck to his kids' mother, leaving almost nothing for his own needs. Should his budget allow it?
items.explain: No single verdict. Supporting his children matters deeply, but an unsustainable budget may collapse and hurt everyone.
key_points: Allow: his values and obligations come first
Adjust: set an amount he can sustain
Check: formal child support terms and his basic safety needs

lib-27.title: Insurance and Consumer Credit
summary: Insurance pays after illness, disaster or accident; shop around and know what each policy covers.
Auto insurance has six coverages; renter's covers belongings even when you don't own the home.
Three bureaus track credit; most negative items fall off after about seven years, and errors must be fixed.
Secured cards and on-time payments rebuild credit; ads guaranteeing credit or erasing bad credit are usually scams.
Compulsive spending, gambling and borrowing bring a rush and crash like drugs; Debtors Anonymous and Gamblers Anonymous help.

items.stem: Which auto coverage pays for damage to your own car from hitting something?
options: Comprehensive
Collision
Bodily injury liability
Uninsured motorist
items.explain: Collision covers your car after a crash; comprehensive covers things like theft or storms.

items.stem: Sam rents an apartment. What does renter's insurance cover?
options: Nothing
His belongings, even though he doesn't own the home
The building itself, since the landlord's policy only covers the land
Only fire
items.explain: Renter's insurance protects personal property.

items.stem: A member buys renter's insurance. What else does the book suggest he do?
options: Nothing more, since the policy covers everything automatically
Record serial numbers and take photos of what he owns
Hide valuables
Buy life insurance
items.explain: Documentation makes claims possible.

items.stem: Which policy pays only a death benefit and builds no cash value?
options: Whole life
Term life
Renter's
Disability
items.explain: Term life is death benefit only; whole life builds cash value.

items.stem: Andre had a string of late payments eight years ago and none since. What does the lesson suggest about his report?
options: They'll double
Most negative items fall off after about seven years
Those items stay on his report forever
Nothing changes
items.explain: Most negative items drop after about seven years.

items.stem: A member finds a debt on his report that isn't his. What does the lesson say?
options: Ignore it
Pay it anyway, since disputing takes too long and hurts his score
Open a new card
The bureaus must fix errors, so he should dispute it
items.explain: Bureaus are required to correct mistakes.

items.stem: How does a secured card work?
options: A deposit sets the limit and starts a credit history
It erases bad credit
It has no limit
The bank secures your debts by paying them off for you
items.explain: The deposit backs the card while you build history.

items.stem: An ad promises to "erase bad credit guaranteed" for $499. What does the lesson predict?
options: A legitimate fast fix, since the guarantee shows confidence in the service
It works for felons only
Likely a scam selling things you could get free
It's government-backed
items.explain: Guaranteed credit or credit repair for a big fee is usually a scam.

items.stem: A "miracle cure" online promises to fix any illness for one payment. How does the lesson's warning about credit apply?
options: Miracle cures are regulated
Guarantees of instant fixes for a fee are a classic scam pattern
It doesn't apply, since health and money are different areas
Only credit scams exist
items.explain: The same red flags (guarantees, upfront fees, easy fixes) mark scams across fields.

items.stem: After quitting cocaine, Rae starts gambling online and feels a rush, then guilt and depression. What does the lesson say?
options: Compulsive gambling can bring a rush and crash much like drugs
It's just entertainment
It'll fade on its own
Gambling is harmless compared with the drug she used before
items.explain: Compulsive spending, gambling and borrowing mirror the drug cycle.

items.stem: A member says he keeps maxing out cards and borrowing from everyone. Which resource fits?
options: A new credit card with a higher limit so he can consolidate
A payday loan
Ignoring it
Debtors Anonymous, plus nonprofit credit counseling
items.explain: Debtors Anonymous and Gamblers Anonymous address compulsive money problems.

items.stem: In your own words, how does a person in reentry start rebuilding credit, per the lesson?
items.explain: Open a checking or savings account, avoid bounced checks, use tools like a secured card, and pay bills on time. If a payment can't be made, call the creditor.

items.stem: Weigh it: some insurers set sobriety requirements. A member worries disclosing his history will raise rates or deny coverage. Should he disclose on an application?
items.explain: No single verdict. Honesty is usually required and protects claims, but disclosure may cost him.
key_points: Disclose: false answers can void a policy
Shop: compare carriers and their rules
Ask: get advice from a counselor or insurance agent

lib-30.title: Addiction and Loss
summary: Drugs act as a seducer, offering false good feelings, and a thief, taking friends, money, time, jobs and health.
Using erodes trust through broken promises and strange behavior, which leads to isolation.
Compulsion can outrank food, shelter and clothing; drug-linked violence often lands on family.
Recovery has real losses too: using friends, rituals and paraphernalia.
Support comes as affection, counsel and assistance; renewal builds a new identity in recovery.

items.stem: "It made me feel like a king for an hour, and I forgot how I'd feel the next morning." Which role of drugs is this?
options: The seducer
Assistance
A ritual
The thief, since he lost something important that night
items.explain: Drugs seduce with false good feelings and make people forget the aftermath.

items.stem: "Over three years it took my car, my savings and my kids' trust." Which role?
options: The thief
The seducer
A support
Compulsion only
items.explain: The thief takes friends, money, time, jobs and health, with the user's participation.

items.stem: In the Odyssey, the Sirens lure sailors with beautiful songs toward the rocks. Which lesson idea does that echo?
options: Counsel
The seducer that promises pleasure and hides the cost
Drugs as assistance, since the song comforts the sailors
Renewal
items.explain: The Sirens are a classic image of a lure that hides its price.

items.stem: After years of broken promises, Mario's family stops believing anything he says. Sober now, he says "I've changed." What is likely?
options: They stay skeptical until his behavior shows change over time
They cut him off
They ignore it
They believe him right away, since he finally sounds sincere
items.explain: Trust broken by using is rebuilt by consistent behavior, not words.

items.stem: During his addiction, Zeke spent rent money on drugs while his fridge sat empty. What does the lesson say about this?
options: He wasn't addicted
It was a choice with no pull
He simply had poor money management skills
Compulsion can outrank food, shelter and clothing
items.explain: Compulsion overrides basic needs.

items.stem: In your own words, how do different drugs link to violence, and who often gets hurt?
items.explain: Alcohol and sedatives lower control, while stimulants bring irritability, impulsiveness and paranoia. The violence often lands on family members.

items.stem: Christina misses the ritual of calling her dealer and the drive to pick up. What kind of loss is this?
options: A loss that recovery itself brings
A loss caused by her addiction
Not a real loss
A trigger only
items.explain: Recovery means losing rituals, using friends and paraphernalia, and that can hurt.

items.stem: A member keeps an old pipe "as a reminder of how bad it was." What does the lesson recommend?
options: Keep it somewhere visible so it serves as a warning every day
Give it to a friend
Throw away paraphernalia and change the rituals
Bury it in the yard
items.explain: Paraphernalia should go; keeping it holds a trigger close.

items.stem: A sponsor listens and offers advice. Which kind of support?
options: Fellowship
Counsel
Affection
Assistance
items.explain: Counsel is listening and advice; affection is warmth; assistance is practical help.

items.stem: Her brother gives her a ride to her first job interview. Which kind of support?
options: Renewal
Assistance
Affection
Counsel
items.explain: Practical help, like rides or money, is assistance.

items.stem: After losing her job, Lori thinks about skipping meetings "until things settle." What does the lesson advise?
options: Switch to a different drug
Quit permanently
Stay in self-help groups during the crisis
Take a break, since meetings add pressure during a crisis
items.explain: Crises are when support matters most.

items.stem: In your own words, how does the lesson describe the identity shift in recovery?
items.explain: People move from "it could never happen to me," to seeing themselves as an addict, to a hopeful person in recovery. Renewal adds self-awareness, focus on real needs, responsibility and helping others.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's using friends are also the people who visited him in prison. He feels grief at letting them go. How should the facilitator respond?
items.explain: No single verdict. The loss is real and deserves grief, but contact may threaten his recovery.
key_points: Validate: grieving this loss is legitimate
Protect: distance from using contacts lowers risk
Replace: build new connections before the gap widens

items.stem: A year sober, Dre starts helping newcomers find meetings and stops calling himself "just a junkie." What does the lesson's renewal model predict?
options: No change
A stronger recovery identity built on responsibility and service
He's at risk, since helping others distracts from his own recovery
He'll forget his history
items.explain: Renewal includes accepting responsibility and helping others, which builds a new self-image.

lib-31.title: Grief: Responding to Loss
summary: Grief is the response to losing something important; drugs and alcohol mute it, so losses go unmourned.
Normal grief can be mild or strong; abnormal grief lasts long, overwhelms and isolates.
Eight factors make grief heavier or lighter, including past coping, importance of the loss and how it happened.
The book's five stages (not Kübler-Ross): shock, disorganization, denial, exhaustion-and-renewal, emotional healing; they don't run in order.
Healing includes returning to routines, giving up the old role, searching for meaning and reorganizing priorities; letting go isn't forgetting.

items.stem: During active use, Jesse's grandmother died and he "barely felt it." Two months sober, he suddenly can't stop crying about her. What does the lesson say?
options: He's showing an early relapse warning sign, since crying spells often come before using
He never cared before
Grief muted by use is surfacing now that he's sober
Something new is wrong, since the loss was long ago
items.explain: Drugs flatten grief; unmourned losses often return in sobriety.

items.stem: In your own words, why can unmourned losses push people back toward using?
items.explain: Grief that was muted never got worked through. When it resurfaces in sobriety, the pain can feel overwhelming and the old way to numb it becomes tempting.

items.stem: Three years after her son's death, Ana still can't function, has severe physical symptoms and has cut off all friends. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Denial, since she has not accepted the death yet
Renewal
Signs of abnormal grief that call for professional help
Normal grief, since losing a child takes many years
items.explain: Long-lasting physical problems, years of preoccupation and isolation are signs of grief that's stuck.

items.stem: Two weeks after a breakup, Tom feels deep sadness, wants to be alone, and feels angry at times. What does the lesson say?
options: Depression
Abnormal grief
A relapse warning
Normal grief
items.explain: Normal grief moves through shock, sadness, withdrawal and protest.

items.stem: Which factor does the book say tends to make grief heavier?
options: Strong coping skills
Lots of support
A loss that was expected and peaceful after a long illness
A violent death like suicide or murder
items.explain: The circumstances of the loss shape how hard grief hits.

items.stem: Rosa lost her job and her partner in the same month, with no savings and few friends. What does the lesson predict about her grief?
options: Unaffected
Lighter, since losses that come together are processed together
Shorter
Heavier, since related problems and low support add weight
items.explain: Practical problems and support levels are among the factors that shape grief.

items.stem: The book lists five stages. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Emotional healing
Emotional shock
Bargaining
Denial
items.explain: The book's stages differ from Kübler-Ross; bargaining isn't on its list.

items.stem: A member says, "I'm back to feeling numb after I thought I was healing. Am I doing it wrong?" Best response?
options: Yes, since healing should move forward in a steady line
He's in denial
The stages don't run in order; moving in and out is normal
Yes, the return of numbness means he has slipped back to the very first stage
items.explain: People move in and out of stages; knowing that makes reactions feel normal and temporary.

items.stem: Many grief researchers now describe the Kübler-Ross stages as a loose map rather than a fixed sequence. How does the book's approach fit that view?
options: It ignores stages entirely
It uses only Kübler-Ross
It also says stages don't run in a set order
It disagrees, since it requires a strict order of stages
items.explain: Both treat stages as descriptions, not a script.

items.stem: Six months after his wife's death, Ron starts cooking and shopping again on a schedule. Which healing task?
options: Giving up the old role
Searching for meaning in the loss, since cooking for himself reflects new purpose
Reorganizing priorities
Taking back control by returning to routines
items.explain: Returning to dropped routines is the first healing task.

items.stem: Years later, Kim can talk about her brother's overdose without it running her life, though she still misses him. What does the lesson call this?
options: Denial
Letting go, which is not the same as forgetting
Stuck grief, since she still misses him years later
Forgetting, which is the goal of grief work
items.explain: Letting go means the loss no longer controls a person's life.

items.stem: A member keeps replaying the night his friend died: "If I'd called, he'd be alive." What does the lesson suggest working toward?
options: Letting go of second-guessing, including forgiving himself
Calling the family
Avoiding the memory by keeping busy, since replaying it only reopens the wound
Finding out exactly who was to blame for the death
items.explain: Second-guessing is common; letting go and forgiveness, including of oneself, are part of healing.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member in a prison unit can't attend his mother's funeral and says he'll "deal with it after release." Should the facilitator encourage him to grieve now?
items.explain: No single verdict. Delayed grief may build, but grieving openly inside can feel unsafe.
key_points: Now: offer private space and a ritual, like a letter
Later: respect his timing while staying alert to stuck grief
Both: name the loss now and plan follow-up after release

lib-33.title: Advanced Relapse Prevention
summary: The urge can return strongly even after long abstinence, set off by stress, conflict, health problems and even success.
Chain: triggers, drug thoughts, craving and obsession, relapse; stopping earlier is easier.
Five defusing steps: identify, avoid, interrupt, talk about, thought-stop; high-risk situations follow small decisions.
If a slip starts, stop it fast and get help instead of self-punishing.
The wall against relapse rises from physical well-being through emotional, relationships, spiritual growth, to knowing your weaknesses; trust must be earned.

items.stem: Five years sober, Ken gets a promotion and suddenly wants a drink to celebrate. What does the lesson say?
options: It's not a trigger
He was never fully committed, since true recovery removes the desire to drink after a few years
Strange, since cravings disappear after five years
Urges can return strongly even after long abstinence, including after success
items.explain: Success and celebrations can set off the desire to use, even years later.

items.stem: Which can set off a strong urge according to the lesson?
options: Only seeing drugs
Sleep problems, anger, or even celebrations
Mostly physical withdrawal, which can resurface for a year or so after quitting
Only negative events like loss or conflict
items.explain: The list is wide: depression, anxiety, stress, anger, conflict, health and sleep problems, and success.

items.stem: Trigger, drug thoughts, craving and obsession, then what?
options: Withdrawal
Denial
Relapse, often
Recovery
items.explain: Craving often leads to relapse unless the chain is broken earlier.

items.stem: Carla notices a drug thought and lets it run, picturing the high for twenty minutes. What does the chain predict?
options: Relief
No effect
The thought fades, since thinking it through drains its power
Dwelling on the thought builds craving and obsession
items.explain: Dwelling on drug thoughts feeds craving; stopping early is easier.

items.stem: A member's trigger is the hour after work, and he can't change his shift. Which defusing step fits?
options: Talk about it in group but keep his after-work routine the same so nothing changes
Ignore it
Interrupt it with a healthy activity, like a meeting right after work
Avoid the trigger completely by quitting the job
items.explain: Unavoidable triggers are interrupted with planned healthy activities.

items.stem: In the guided visualization, members replay a past relapse step by step to spot each small choice. What does that teach?
options: Small choices don't matter
High-risk situations usually follow a series of small decisions
Relapses happen randomly and suddenly
Relapse usually comes out of nowhere, which is why the exercise focuses on the moment of use itself
items.explain: Replaying the decisions shows where the path could have turned.

items.stem: Accident investigators reconstruct the chain of small decisions before a plane crash. How is that like the rewind exercise?
options: Neither looks at choices
Both trace a series of small choices to find where it could have been stopped
Both are mainly about assigning blame to the person who made the final mistake
It's different, since crashes are mechanical, not decisions
items.explain: Reconstruction exposes the points where a different choice would have changed the outcome.

items.stem: A member used last night and says he deserves to suffer for it. What does the lesson advise?
options: Agree that guilt will keep him from doing it again
Keep it secret
Wait a week before telling anyone, to see whether it was a one-time thing
Stop it as soon as possible and get help, possibly a higher level of care, instead of self-punishing
items.explain: Beating yourself up doesn't help; stopping fast and getting support does.

items.stem: What sits at the base of the five-level wall?
options: Relationship stability, since the people around him hold everything else up
Knowing your weaknesses
Spiritual growth, since everything rests on it
Physical well-being: food, exercise, sleep, hygiene, medical care
items.explain: The wall builds from physical well-being up.

items.stem: Which level sits at the top of the wall?
options: Relationship stability
Physical well-being, since the body comes first in everything
Knowing your weaknesses
Emotional well-being
items.explain: From the base: physical, emotional, relationships, spiritual growth, then knowing your weaknesses.

items.stem: Maslow's levels of needs also stack from basic body needs upward. How does the wall compare?
options: It reverses Maslow, putting spirit at the base
It also puts physical needs at the base, with higher levels resting on them
It mirrors Maslow exactly, with self-actualization as the final level at the top
It skips physical needs
items.explain: Both models suggest higher-level growth rests on meeting basic needs first.

items.stem: A member says he trusts no one and will "do recovery alone." What does the lesson suggest?
options: Agree, since trust is risky and he should rely on himself
Trust everyone in his recovery group equally, since they all share the same goal
Lean on others for a while, but check that trust is earned through experience and reliability
Move away
items.explain: Getting free of one dependency may mean depending on others, chosen carefully.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member's most experienced recovery mentor is an older man from his old neighborhood who still has ties to people who use. Should he trust him as a guide?
items.explain: No single verdict. Experience and understanding count for a lot, but his ties may put the member near risk.
key_points: Trust: shared experience and long sobriety are valuable
Caution: meet in recovery settings, not the old block
Check: does he meet the lesson's tests of experience and reliability

lib-15.title: Sexually Transmitted Diseases
summary: STDs are infections spread through sexual contact and body fluids; many have no symptoms yet still spread.
Most bacterial STDs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are curable with early treatment; viral ones like herpes and HPV are managed, not cured.
Substance use raises risk through lowered inhibition, sex traded for drugs, and shared equipment.
Lower risk with fewer partners, latex condoms with water-based lubricant, and regular testing even without symptoms.
Some manual details are dated; current practice includes the HPV vaccine and updated antibiotics, so medical questions go to a clinician.

items.stem: Leo's new partner looks healthy and says she feels fine. Leo decides testing is unnecessary. What does the lesson warn?
options: Little risk, since most STDs cause obvious symptoms soon after infection
Many STDs have no symptoms but can still spread
He's safe if she's had one partner
Only men carry STDs
items.explain: Symptomless infections are common, so looking healthy is no proof of being uninfected.

items.stem: "No sores, no burning, so I'm clean." Which myth does the session target?
options: That STDs come from toilet seats
That all STDs are incurable
That condoms fail so often they are not worth using with a regular partner
That no symptoms means no infection
items.explain: The session stresses that silence isn't safety; testing is the only way to know.

items.stem: Which STD does the lesson describe as treatable but not curable, because the virus stays in the body?
options: Chlamydia
Gonorrhea
Syphilis
Herpes
items.explain: Antivirals ease herpes outbreaks and lower spread but don't remove the virus.

items.stem: Tony had a painless sore that went away on its own months ago. He assumes he's healed. If it was syphilis, what does the lesson say?
options: Syphilis can keep progressing silently and still needs treatment
It's untreatable now
The infection cleared when the sore did
It was probably something minor, since syphilis sores are always painful and obvious
items.explain: Syphilis sores and rashes can vanish while the disease continues; it's curable at any stage, but damage already done stays.

items.stem: The syphilis sore that vanishes while infection continues is sometimes compared to a period of controlled use in addiction. What is the shared lesson?
options: Both show that symptoms are the most reliable sign of whether a problem is still active
Neither needs follow-up
Both prove the problem has been solved for good
A quiet stretch can be mistaken for a cure while the problem keeps progressing
items.explain: False reassurance is the common trap in both.

items.stem: In your own words, why does substance use raise STD risk?
items.explain: Intoxication lowers inhibition and narrows attention to the moment, so risks feel distant. Sex may be traded for drugs or money, and shared equipment adds exposure.

items.stem: Alcohol myopia theory says intoxication shrinks attention to immediate cues like arousal. Which everyday example fits the same idea?
options: A runner pacing a race
A sober driver planning a long trip carefully
A tipsy shopper who buys on impulse and forgets the budget
A student who stays up late but still keeps an eye on the deadline for her paper
items.explain: Narrowed attention favors the immediate over the distant, whether the risk is infection or overspending.

items.stem: Which lubricant can damage latex condoms?
options: Water-based lubricant
None
Oil-based products like lotion or petroleum jelly
Silicone lubricant that is sold for use with condoms
items.explain: Oil-based products weaken latex; water-based lubricant is recommended.

items.stem: Which condom type does the lesson warn lets viruses pass through?
options: Female condoms
Animal-skin (lambskin)
Polyurethane
Latex
items.explain: Natural membrane condoms can block pregnancy but not viruses.

items.stem: Spermicide nonoxynol-9 was once promoted for extra protection. What did later research find about HIV risk?
options: It had no effect on anything
It strongly protected against HIV and became standard
It didn't protect and could irritate tissue, raising risk
It protected against HIV only when used together with oil-based lubricant
items.explain: Trials found no HIV protection and possible harm, a striking case of a well-meant tool backfiring.

items.stem: A member says he's never had a checkup unless he was in the ER. Before release, what fits the session?
options: Give him a list of ten clinics
Skip it as private
Tell him to wait for symptoms, since testing without them wastes clinic time
Help him name one concrete health step for release week, like a clinic test
items.explain: Regular screening without symptoms is recommended; one specific plan beats a long list.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member learns he has a treatable STD and is afraid to tell past partners. Should he tell them himself or have a clinic notify them?
items.explain: No single verdict. Telling them directly shows responsibility, but clinic notification protects partners while easing fear and risk.
key_points: Clinic referral: confidential and less confrontational
Either way: partners need to be informed and tested

lib-16.title: Focus on AIDS
summary: HIV attacks the immune system's T helper cells; untreated, it can progress to AIDS, often over years without symptoms.
HIV spreads through sex, shared injection equipment and from parent to child; not through casual contact.
The window period means a recent infection may not show on a test yet, though it can still spread.
Combination antiretroviral treatment controls HIV; people who keep an undetectable viral load don't transmit it sexually.
Prevention includes condoms, never sharing needles, syringe services, PrEP, and PEP started soon after exposure.

items.stem: Which can spread HIV?
options: Hugging, kissing on the cheek and other close everyday contact
Sharing needles or injection equipment
Mosquito bites
Sharing a meal or dishes
items.explain: Shared injection gear is a main route; everyday contact isn't.

items.stem: Which everyday item does the session say not to share, out of caution?
options: Towels in general
Cups
Razors and toothbrushes
Toilet seats
items.explain: Razors and toothbrushes can carry blood, so sharing is discouraged.

items.stem: A member is afraid to share a cell with a man who has HIV. What fits the session?
options: Tell him the fear is irrational and move the discussion to another topic
Explain casual contact doesn't spread HIV and focus on real precautions like no shared razors or tattoo needles
Request a transfer, since close quarters spread HIV easily
Tell him to avoid touching anything
items.explain: Myth-busting protects both the fearful member and the person living with HIV.

items.stem: Ray tests negative one week after a risky encounter. What does the window period idea predict?
options: He can relax, since one negative test right after exposure rules infection out
It may be too early to detect, and he could still transmit; retest later
The negative result is final
The test is always wrong
items.explain: A recent infection may not show yet; follow-up testing is needed.

items.stem: Which cells does HIV mainly attack?
options: T helper cells, the white cells that coordinate immune defense
Red blood cells and platelets, the cells that carry oxygen and help clotting
Red blood cells
Skin cells
