items.explain: Losing T helper cells weakens the whole immune response.

items.stem: If T helper cells are like a band's conductor, what happens when HIV depletes them?
options: The band gets faster
Nothing much changes, since the musicians already know their parts by heart
The band gets louder, since nobody controls the volume
The players lose coordination, even though they're still there
items.explain: The analogy shows why opportunistic infections take hold.

items.stem: Dana starts HIV treatment early and takes it consistently. What does current evidence suggest about her outlook?
options: No benefit
A full cure within a year or two, as long as she never misses a dose
Short survival, since HIV remains fatal even with treatment
A life expectancy that can approach that of people without HIV
items.explain: Combination therapy has transformed survival since the mid-1990s.

items.stem: What does "Undetectable equals Untransmittable" (U=U) mean?
options: That treatment makes HIV impossible to find on any test, so people no longer need checkups
People who keep an undetectable viral load on treatment don't transmit HIV sexually
Condoms are unnecessary for STDs
That HIV disappears permanently after treatment
items.explain: U=U is a key modern finding; it applies to sexual transmission of HIV, not other STDs.

items.stem: In your own words, why does HIV treatment use several drugs at once?
items.explain: HIV mutates quickly, so one drug alone breeds resistance. Hitting several targets together makes it very hard for the virus to escape.

items.stem: A member says he had a condom break with a partner of unknown status last night. What's the urgent step?
options: Seek care right away about PEP, which works best within hours and up to about 72 hours
Wait two weeks and get an HIV test to see whether he was infected
Use bleach to clean up and just watch for symptoms over the next few weeks
Do nothing; it's too late
items.explain: Post-exposure prophylaxis must start soon after exposure to prevent infection.

items.stem: What is PrEP?
options: A one-time injection that protects against HIV and all other STDs for life
Medication taken before exposure that greatly lowers HIV risk
A one-time HIV test
A vaccine that cures HIV
items.explain: PrEP is a daily or injectable prevention medicine; it doesn't protect against other STDs.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member who shared needles for years refuses an HIV test: "I'd rather not know." Should the facilitator push?
items.explain: No single verdict. Knowing opens treatment that can save his life and protect others, but pressure can deepen avoidance.
key_points: Encourage: treatment today is effective and testing is the door to it
Explore: what he fears most about a result
Respect: the choice is his, and timing matters

items.stem: In your own words, how is avoiding an HIV test like the pattern that sustains substance use?
items.explain: Avoiding the test eases anxiety now but raises danger later. That same short-term relief and long-term cost is what keeps use going.

lib-23.title: You and Your Parents
summary: A parent is whoever raised you, and how they treated you still shapes the adult you are.
Research links parenting that is too strict, too harsh, too lenient or inconsistent to later problems, including substance use.
Pain no one noticed and fear of abandonment can turn into anger, use, and relationships that repeat old rejection.
Mothers and fathers each leave a mark; father styles include absent, distant, macho, buddy-type and unpredictable, with a healthy alternative.
Unsent letters put feelings into words; the goal is understanding and acceptance, not blame, and strong feelings may need a counselor.

items.stem: Marcus's father never spanked him but screamed, shamed and mocked him in sudden outbursts. Which style does the session describe?
options: Too strict, since he was controlled with fear
Inconsistent
Too harsh
Too lenient
items.explain: Harsh parenting isn't about rules; it's outbursts of shaming and criticism that wear down self-worth.

items.stem: Lena's mother let her do whatever she wanted and never set rules. Which style?
options: Healthy
Too lenient
Too strict
Too harsh
items.explain: Lenient parenting leaves a child without leadership or limits.

items.stem: Raised by a father who silenced every question and punished severely, Jamal enters adulthood. Which pattern does the session predict might follow?
options: Perfect discipline
No lasting effect once he leaves home and makes his own choices
Trouble speaking up, with fear or rebellion toward authority
Easy trust in authority, since he learned to respect rules
items.explain: Overly strict parenting is linked to later problems, including how a person handles authority.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session call unrecognized pain one of the worst things a child can suffer?
items.explain: A child whose hurt goes unseen learns it doesn't matter and has no one to help carry it. That pain often turns into anger, aimed outward or inward.

items.stem: Ana's father left when she was six. As an adult she keeps choosing partners who leave. What does the session suggest?
options: Buried abandonment fear can draw people into relationships that repeat the rejection
It's unrelated to childhood
She has high standards and leaves partners before they can disappoint her
Bad luck, since partners leave people all the time
items.explain: Abandonment fear can fuel use and steer people toward situations that replay it.

items.stem: In Great Expectations, Miss Havisham, jilted at the altar, raises Estella to break men's hearts. Which session idea does the novel dramatize?
options: Lenient parenting producing a confident child
The buddy-type father
A healthy bond between a mother figure and the child she raises with care
Old wounds passed on and repeated in new relationships
items.explain: The story shows how unhealed rejection gets handed down and replayed.

items.stem: "My dad tried to be my best friend: no rules, partied with me." Which style from the session?
options: Distant
Absent
Macho
Buddy-type
items.explain: The buddy-type father acts like a peer instead of a parent.

items.stem: Which describes the healthy father in the session?
options: Provides money only
Strong and silent, never showing emotion, so his children feel safe
Sees children as individuals, sets limits and talks about feelings
Lets kids decide everything
items.explain: The healthy father combines limits, attention to needs and open feelings.

items.stem: Leon was raised by an unpredictable father: warm one day, raging the next. At work, his boss's mood swings make him anxious and defensive. What does the session suggest?
options: It's just a difficult boss and has nothing to do with his past
He should quit
He's oversensitive and should learn to ignore other people's moods at work
Feelings about his father may be resurfacing with an authority figure
items.explain: Feelings about a father, even an unknown one, often resurface with partners, friends and coworkers.

items.stem: A member says writing to his mother is pointless because she died years ago. What fits the session?
options: Explain the letter is unsent; it's for him to put feelings into words, even if she has died
Ask him to write to someone else
Have him write to a living relative instead, since the letter should reach someone
Agree and skip the exercise for him
items.explain: The exercise works whether the parent is alive or not; the writer is the audience.

items.stem: In your own words, why does writing feelings down, in an unsent letter, help?
items.explain: It puts vague, tangled feelings into words, which makes them easier to understand and manage. Because no one will read it, a person can be fully honest.

items.stem: After writing about his mother's addiction, a member says, "So it's all her fault I use." Best response?
options: Tell him to focus only on the present, since the past can't be changed
Agree, since the session shows parents cause their children's addiction
Change the topic
Acknowledge the impact, and note the aim is understanding and acceptance, not blame
items.explain: The session frames this work as understanding the past, not assigning blame.

items.stem: Weigh it: in a men's unit, a member breaks down while reading his father letter aloud. Should the facilitator continue sharing letters in group?
items.explain: No single verdict. Sharing can deepen healing and connection, but the material can overwhelm members in a setting where vulnerability carries risk.
key_points: Continue: with consent and a clear option to pass
Pause: check in privately and connect him with a counselor
Adapt: share only the debrief questions, not the letters

lib-24.title: Child Development and Parenting Skills
summary: Development runs through five stages, infancy to adulthood, each with emotional, social and intellectual tasks.
Finishing a stage prepares the next; tasks left unfinished, often because of use, can still be learned as an adult.
Three foundations of parenting: express love and praise, set simple stable rules, and respect children's needs and views.
Research finds physical punishment breeds fear and behavior problems; fitting consequences and praise for good behavior work better.
Active listening, avoiding listening roadblocks, solving problems instead of blaming, and family structure support children.

items.stem: Which task does the session tie to infancy, birth to about two?
options: Building one's own identity and values
Intimacy
Bonding and learning trust when needs are met reliably
Learning to name feelings and handle fears through play with others
items.explain: Infants learn trust through reliable care.

items.stem: Ages seven to eleven: school success builds a sense of capability, failure a sense of inferiority. Which stage?
options: Preadolescence
Adolescence
Infancy
Early childhood
items.explain: Preadolescence centers on competence, which is why effort deserves praise.

items.stem: Erik Erikson described "industry versus inferiority" for the school years. Which session stage matches?
options: Preadolescence, where success builds capability and failure inferiority
Infancy, since the stage sets up all later trust
Adolescence, since teens worry most about how they compare
Adulthood
items.explain: The session's preadolescent task echoes Erikson's well-known stage.

items.stem: Rico started using at 13 and missed much of adolescence's identity work. Now 30 and sober, what does the session suggest?
options: He'll need to go back and relive adolescence before any adult growth can happen
Those tasks are lost for good, since the window has closed
It doesn't matter
He can still work on them as an adult; recovery is a chance to finish them
items.explain: Unfinished tasks cause trouble later but can be learned in adulthood.

items.stem: In your own words, how are an infant's tasks like those of an adult early in recovery?
items.explain: Both are learning to trust that needs will be met and to bond with others. Adults who never learned that may find recovery relationships are where they first practice it.

items.stem: Which is one of the session's three foundations of parenting?
options: Strict obedience, so children never question the rules
Physical discipline
Simple, stable rules without giving in to whining
Letting children set rules
items.explain: The three foundations are love and praise, clear rules, and sensitivity to children's needs.

items.stem: A father sets a bedtime but enforces it only when he's in a good mood. What does the session predict?
options: Children learn flexibility and adapt well to change
Children learn that their father's mood is the real rule, which teaches them empathy
No effect
Children feel unsure of right and wrong and learn rules don't matter
items.explain: Inconsistency confuses children and undermines rules.

items.stem: A mother spanks her son every time he misbehaves. What does the research the session cites predict?
options: Better behavior over time, since he learns quickly what not to do
No effect
Stronger bonding
More fear, anxiety and behavior problems
items.explain: Physical punishment is linked to fear, anxiety, depression and behavior problems.

items.stem: A 14-year-old breaks curfew. Which response fits the session's approach?
options: Yelling and a slap, since teens only respond to strong reactions
Grounding for six months
Letting it go this time, since teens need room to learn from mistakes on their own
A fitting consequence, like losing a weekend outing, explained calmly
items.explain: Age-fit consequences tied to the behavior work better than harsh punishment.

items.stem: A manager who mostly praises what employees do right sees better morale than one who only criticizes. Which session idea fits?
options: Praise for good behavior works better than criticism
Strict rules make better teams in any setting
Detailed criticism helps people improve faster than praise does
Inconsistency builds resilience
items.explain: Catching people doing well shapes behavior, for children and adults.

items.stem: A child says she failed a test; the parent launches into a 20-minute lecture. Which roadblock?
options: Active listening
Praise
Problem solving
Long lectures
items.explain: Lectures, blaming, shaming and "you always" statements shut down a child's willingness to talk.

items.stem: A child says, "Nobody at school likes me." Which response is active listening?
options: "Just ignore them; kids at that age are mean and it doesn't matter."
"Sounds like you feel left out at school. Is that right?"
"When I was your age it was worse."
"That's not true, you have lots of friends."
items.explain: Paraphrasing back what you heard lets the child confirm or correct it.

items.stem: A son brings home a failing grade. Which response matches the session?
options: "No phone, no friends and no TV until your grade comes up, starting now."
"You're lazy, just like your uncle."
"I don't care."
"Let's look at what's hard in this class and make a plan."
items.explain: Blaming leaves children angry and feeling like failures; solving the problem together works better.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session suggest a posted family schedule and daily talk time?
items.explain: Children learn how to organize time by seeing it modeled. A schedule for sleep, meals, homework and play, plus at least fifteen minutes of relaxed talk, gives structure and connection that also support a parent's recovery.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says, "I got whipped as a kid and turned out fine; my kids need that too." How should the facilitator respond?
items.explain: No single verdict. His experience is real to him, but research links physical punishment to harm, and arguing may close him off.
key_points: Inform: share what research finds about physical punishment
Explore: ask what he wanted his own father to do differently
Offer: practical consequences that work without hitting

lib-28.title: Sexual Abuse
summary: Sexual assault covers a family of crimes; rape is sex without consent, and consent can be withdrawn at any point.
Rape is driven by domination and control more than desire, often happens between acquaintances, and substances raise both offending and vulnerability.
Survivors often stay silent from shame, fear of retaliation or not being believed; crisis centers, therapy and support groups help.
Childhood sexual abuse is usually committed by a trusted adult, happens in secret, and must be reported to child protection.
Abuse can leave shame, rage, distrust, intimacy problems and memory gaps that resurface in sobriety; recovery plans should include specialist help.

items.stem: Midway through, Tina says she wants to stop, and her partner continues. What does the session call this?
options: A misunderstanding, since she had already agreed earlier that night
Rape; consent can be withdrawn at any point
A gray area
Rough sex
items.explain: Either partner may stop at any time; continuing without consent is rape.

items.stem: At a party, Mark's date is too drunk to stand. He thinks, "She came home with me, so she's okay with it." What does the session's definition say?
options: Someone too intoxicated can't consent; this would be assault
Going home together implies consent for the rest of the night
It's legal if both drank
It depends on her past behavior
items.explain: Consent must be real and freely given; severe intoxication rules it out.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session describe rape as violence driven by domination rather than desire?
items.explain: Rape is about overpowering and controlling another person, not about sexual need. Seeing it that way removes myths that blame the victim or excuse the offender.

items.stem: Which statement matches the session?
options: Most rapes are committed by strangers in dark places at night
Rape is rare among acquaintances
Rape is mainly caused by revealing clothing
Rape often happens between people who know each other
items.explain: Acquaintance rape is common, which challenges the stranger myth.

items.stem: According to the session, how do alcohol and drugs connect to sexual assault?
options: Only drugs matter, not alcohol
They prevent assault by relaxing people
They have no real connection, since assault is a choice made sober
They lower inhibitions, raise hostility in some, and weaken self-protection
items.explain: Substances raise risk on both sides, which ties this session to recovery.

items.stem: A member says his sister never reported her assault, and he thinks that means it "wasn't that bad." What fits the session?
options: Change the subject
Tell him to report it for her
Explain that many survivors stay silent from shame, fear or not being believed
Agree, since people report the attacks that really harm them
items.explain: Silence is common and says nothing about severity.

items.stem: Which is a reason the session gives for survivors not reporting?
options: They want publicity
They usually forget what happened within a few days of the assault
The crime isn't serious
Fear of retaliation or of not being believed
items.explain: Shame, fear of rejection, publicity and retaliation keep many quiet.

items.stem: Who usually commits childhood sexual abuse, per the session?
options: Strangers the child has never seen before
Other children only
People with no access to the child
A trusted adult the child knows
items.explain: Abusers are usually known and trusted, which is why abuse stays secret.

items.stem: A member discloses in group that his cousin is abusing a 12-year-old relative. What is the facilitator's duty?
options: Keep it confidential, since group rules protect everything said in the room
Wait for proof
Ask the group to handle it
Report it to child protection as required, and explain that limit of confidentiality
items.explain: Reporting suspected child abuse is required; confidentiality has that limit.

items.stem: Six months sober, Dani starts having vivid memories of childhood abuse she'd mostly forgotten. What does the session suggest?
options: Memories can resurface once numbing stops; she should see a trauma specialist
It means relapse is near
Ignore them
They're imagined, since real memories never go missing for years
items.explain: Most survivors remember at least part; some memories return later and deserve specialist care.

items.stem: Gabe used drugs since 13 to blot out his abuse. In early sobriety, what does the session predict?
options: Instant healing
A flood of rage, shame or fear that use had been numbing
Calm, since the abuse was long ago and he has moved past it
No change
items.explain: Stopping use removes the numbing, so old feelings can surge.

items.stem: In your own words, why should a survivor's recovery plan include specialist trauma help?
items.explain: Abuse can leave shame, rage, distrust and intimacy problems that drive use. Without addressing them, those feelings can push a person back toward using.

items.stem: A soldier home from war still scans every room for threats. How does that relate to what the session says about abused children?
options: Neither affects relationships
Both learn constant alertness for survival, which later gets in the way
It shows that only combat produces lasting hypervigilance
It's unrelated
items.explain: Abused children learn to read moods and stay on guard; the same skill can block intimacy as adults.

items.stem: Weigh it: in a men's unit, a member hints he was abused as a child but begs the facilitator not to "make it a thing." How far should the facilitator go?
items.explain: No single verdict. His privacy and pace matter, but he may need specialist help he isn't asking for yet.
key_points: Respect: let him lead and keep it private
Offer: a confidential referral to a trauma specialist
Clarify: what the facilitator must report and what stays private

lib-29.title: Compulsive Sexual Behavior
summary: Compulsive sexual behavior is defined by obsession, loss of control, continuing despite harm, and denial, not by the amount of sex.
It can work like a drug, and alcohol and stimulants often both numb its pain and fuel it, so both problems need treatment together.
Roots include chaotic or violent families, childhood sexual abuse, mixed cultural messages, stress and enabling partners.
An episode often starts with a feeling, then a passing thought, then acting out, then shame and broken promises.
Recovery means stopping unhealthy sex and building honest, committed intimacy, not giving up sex; treatment includes therapy, groups and sometimes medication.

items.stem: Which best marks compulsive sexual behavior, per the session?
options: Having sex more often than most people of the same age
Having several partners over a lifetime
Obsession, loss of control and continuing despite serious harm
Liking pornography
items.explain: It's the compulsion, not the quantity, that defines it.

items.stem: A chef who cooks for hours daily isn't a food addict; someone who can't stop binge-eating despite health damage might be. Which session idea does that parallel?
options: Cooking and sex are unrelated
Quantity is what defines a compulsion
Loss of control and harm, not amount, define a compulsion
Both are healthy
items.explain: The same test applies across behaviors: control and consequences.

items.stem: In your own words, how settled is "sex addiction" as a diagnosis?
items.explain: Experts disagree. DSM-5 doesn't list sex addiction, while ICD-11 includes compulsive sexual behavior disorder as an impulse-control problem. The behavior and its harm are real either way.

items.stem: Tyrell uses meth mainly before sex and feels sex is "boring" without it. If he quits meth but not the pattern, what does the session predict?
options: No link
The untreated compulsion can pull him back to meth
He'll lose interest in sex for good
His sexual compulsion will fade once the meth is gone
items.explain: Recovery from one doesn't fix the other; either can trigger relapse in the other.

items.stem: A member says he'll "deal with the sex stuff later" after he's off cocaine. What does the session advise?
options: Agree, since tackling two problems at once usually overwhelms people
Ignore the sexual pattern
Work on both at once, since either can pull him back
Only treat the sex
items.explain: The session insists both addictions be addressed together.

items.stem: Which is a root factor the session links to compulsive sexual behavior?
options: Childhood sexual abuse that teaches sex equals love
Having a healthy, open relationship with a partner
Strong boundaries
Regular exercise
items.explain: Abuse, chaotic families, mixed messages and stress raise the likelihood.

items.stem: A partner who joins in, ignores or quietly enables the behavior. Which factor is this?
options: Stress
Healthy intimacy
A protective factor, since the partner keeps things calm
Codependency
items.explain: Enabling partners are listed as a contributing factor.

items.stem: Lonely after a fight, Victor has a passing sexual thought. He lets it grow and acts out, then feels shame and promises "never again." What does the session predict without help?
options: He'll feel relieved
The cycle repeats, starting again from a feeling
The promise holds, since shame is a strong deterrent
The shame stops it
items.explain: Shame and broken promises are part of the cycle, not the end of it.

items.stem: The session's episode cycle (feeling, thought, acting out, shame) resembles which earlier recovery idea?
options: The CAGE questions
Maslow's needs
The trigger-thought-craving-use chain
The five levels of the wall against relapse
items.explain: Both chains start small and can be interrupted early.

items.stem: What does recovery from sexual compulsion mean, per the session?
options: Replacing sex with drugs
Only avoiding pornography
Giving up sex entirely, the same way abstinence works for drugs
Stopping unhealthy and abusive sex while building honest, committed intimacy
items.explain: Unlike substance abstinence, the goal is healthy sexuality, not none.

items.stem: Three weeks into treatment, Rae falls hard for a fellow member and they start sleeping together. What does the session warn?
options: Rushing into sex in early recovery can derail it as buried feelings surface
It will strengthen both of their recoveries
It shows healthy intimacy
It's unrelated to recovery
items.explain: Healthy intimacy rests on trust built over time; early romances often backfire.

items.stem: A member fears that telling his partner about his compulsion will end the relationship, so he stays silent. What does the session say?
options: He should tell everyone
Silence protects the relationship while he works on it alone
He should leave
Silence raises relapse risk; honest sharing, with support, helps recovery
items.explain: The session frames secrecy as a relapse risk and honest communication as protective.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member rejects the idea that he has a "sex addiction," saying he just likes sex, though his behavior has cost him two jobs. How should the facilitator proceed?
items.explain: No single verdict. The label is debated and arguing it may backfire, but the harm he describes is real.
key_points: Skip the label: focus on control and consequences
Explore: what he'd want to be different
Offer: the screening checklist and a specialist if he's willing

lib-32.title: Spirituality and Personality Change
summary: Addiction can warp a healthy personality or stop one from forming; sobriety alone brings some change, but lasting change takes work.
Surrender means dropping defenses built to protect use and the illusion of control; letting go replaces the drug "relationship" with healthier ones.
Commitment needs help and faith and means returning after setbacks.
Acceptance covers what can't change (being unable to use safely) and responsibility for past acts; restitution and service repair harm.
Meditation, linked to Step Eleven, quiets the mind; concentration and mindful styles both work, with or without belief in God.

items.stem: Jace started using at 12. Sober at 28, he says, "I don't even know who I am without it." What does the session suggest?
options: Use may have kept his adult personality from forming; recovery is a chance to build it
He's in denial about who he really is underneath
He should use again
His real personality is the one he had while using, and sobriety is just hiding it
items.explain: Early use can stop personality from developing, which recovery can address.

items.stem: On the paired list, Ana checks "blame" for her using years and "forgiveness" for now. What does comparing the two lists show?
options: Nothing useful
That her personality was healthy all along and nothing changed
That she's lying
How far she has moved since active use
items.explain: The before-and-after lists make change visible.

items.stem: In your own words, what does surrender mean in this session, and why is it the start of humility?
items.explain: It means dropping the defenses built to protect use and admitting control over it is an illusion. Giving up that false control opens a person to help and change.

items.stem: In judo, a fighter who stops resisting a throw and moves with it often avoids injury. How does that echo the session's idea of surrender?
options: It means giving up hope
It's only about sports
Stopping a losing fight can be the way out
It shows that fighting hard is always the best way to win
items.explain: The session says fighting an addiction makes it fight back; walking away is the exit.

items.stem: A member says he's quit drugs but still manipulates people to get what he wants, "like I always did." What does the session say?
options: Controlling and manipulating people, learned while using, must also be let go
That's fine, since only drug use matters for recovery
It's a fixed part of his character that recovery work can't really touch, so he should accept it
Ignore it
items.explain: Letting go includes behaviors that grew up around use.

items.stem: Ray relapses after eight months and thinks his commitment was "fake." What does the session suggest?
options: He was never committed and should stop trying
Relapse ends commitment
Commitment means returning after setbacks, with help and faith
He should start over somewhere new, without the people who saw him relapse, so he isn't judged
items.explain: Commitment isn't a single promise; it's coming back after slips.

items.stem: Which does the session say commitment requires?
options: Avoiding all risk
A perfect record from the start, since any slip shows the commitment was never real
Going it alone so the success is truly his own
Help from others and faith that the work will pay off
items.explain: Commitment draws on groups, counselors, family or a Higher Power, plus faith.

items.stem: What is the first thing the session says a person must accept?
options: That nothing can change
That relapse is certain sooner or later, so planning for it is the main task
That their family caused the addiction in the first place
That they have a substance use disorder and can't use safely
items.explain: Acceptance starts with the disorder itself and the inability to use safely.

items.stem: A member asks, "What does not accepting it actually get me?" What answer fits the session?
options: More freedom, since accepting a label would limit who he can become
Less stress
A hidden payoff, like keeping the hope of controlled use, which can hurt recovery
Nothing at all, since resistance has no benefits
items.explain: The session looks for the hidden payoff of resisting acceptance.

items.stem: A man can't repay a friend he stole from because the friend has died. What does the session suggest?
options: Forget it
Nothing can be done, so he should let the guilt go
Pay the friend's family back with interest, since money is the only real form of restitution
Service to others in recovery can stand in where direct repair is impossible
items.explain: Restitution repairs harm when possible; service fills in when it isn't.

items.stem: In the role play, a man makes amends to two sisters; one forgives, the other stays angry. What does the session want members to see?
options: He should try again until both forgive
Amends aren't worth it
The amends failed, since one sister refused to forgive him
Making amends is separate from being forgiven
items.explain: Restitution is about repairing harm, not controlling the other person's response.

items.stem: Fixing attention on one word or on the breath. Which style?
options: Concentration meditation
Mindful meditation
Walking meditation, since the attention is fixed on each step
Prayer
items.explain: Concentration focuses on one object; mindful meditation is open, nonjudging awareness.

items.stem: An atheist member asks if meditation is for him. What fits the session?
options: Yes; it quiets the mind and works with or without belief in God
No, since meditation is a form of prayer to a Higher Power
Only if he uses a religious text as the focus, since that is what meditation was built on
Only if he joins a church
items.explain: The session opens a secular door into meditation.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member says the Serenity Prayer's "accept the things I cannot change" feels like accepting injustice, such as a harsh sentence. How should the facilitator frame acceptance?
items.explain: No single verdict. Acceptance can free energy for what he controls, but it shouldn't mean silence about real injustice.
key_points: Accept: what can't change today, to focus energy
Act: courage to change what he can, like appeals or advocacy
Wisdom: telling the two apart, which is the prayer's point

lib-34.title: Medication-Assisted Treatment and Twelve Step Recovery
summary: Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) uses medicine to ease withdrawal, cut craving and prevent relapse for alcohol and opioid addiction.
Medication is one piece; it works best alongside counseling, support groups and lifestyle change.
Alcohol medicines: disulfiram (a sickening reaction to drinking), acamprosate (eases post-acute withdrawal), naltrexone (dampens craving and reward).

Opioid medicines: methadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist), naltrexone (an antagonist, also given as the monthly injection Vivitrol); strong evidence links methadone and buprenorphine to fewer overdose deaths.
Twelve Step groups vary on MAT; active participation, a supportive home group and sponsor, and calm responses to criticism help.

items.stem: Which medication makes drinking trigger a sickening reaction?
options: Buprenorphine
Methadone
Disulfiram
Acamprosate, since it changes how the brain reacts to alcohol
items.explain: Disulfiram works by deterrence: drinking on it makes a person ill.

items.stem: Which is a partial opioid agonist, with a ceiling on its effect?
options: Methadone
Disulfiram
Buprenorphine
Naltrexone
items.explain: Buprenorphine partly activates opioid receptors, which lowers misuse and overdose risk compared with full agonists.

items.stem: Which medication blocks opioid receptors and comes as a monthly injection?
options: Methadone, which is given daily at a clinic
Disulfiram
Naltrexone, as Vivitrol
Acamprosate
items.explain: Naltrexone is a non-addictive antagonist; Vivitrol is its monthly injectable form.

items.stem: A key that turns a lock fully, one that turns it partway, and one that jams the lock so no other key works. Which matches methadone, buprenorphine and naltrexone in order?
options: Naltrexone, methadone, buprenorphine
Methadone (full), buprenorphine (partial), naltrexone (blocker)
Buprenorphine, naltrexone, methadone
All three are full keys
items.explain: Agonists activate receptors, partial agonists activate them partly, antagonists block them.

items.stem: Two men leave prison with opioid use disorder. One starts buprenorphine with counseling; the other gets no medication. What does strong evidence predict?
options: Both relapse within a week
The man without medication does better
The man on buprenorphine has a lower risk of overdose death
No difference, since medication only swaps one drug for another
items.explain: Methadone and buprenorphine are linked to fewer overdose deaths, especially after release.

items.stem: A member says, "Methadone is just trading one drug for another." Best response?
options: Explain that prescribed MAT stabilizes the brain without the high-and-crash cycle, and evidence shows it saves lives
Avoid the topic
Agree, since any opioid keeps the addiction going
Tell him to quit everything cold turkey
items.explain: Prescribed, stable dosing differs from addictive use and has strong outcome research.

items.stem: In your own words, why does the session say medication alone isn't full treatment?
items.explain: Addiction affects body, mind, relationships and spirit. Medication steadies the biology, which frees attention for counseling, groups and life changes that address the rest.

items.stem: Months after stopping alcohol, Lou still has poor sleep, low energy and mood swings. What does the session call this, and which medicine targets it?
options: Post-acute withdrawal, which acamprosate can ease
Normal aging; no medicine helps
Relapse; disulfiram fixes it
A new addiction
items.explain: Acamprosate eases the lingering mood, sleep and energy problems after acute withdrawal.

items.stem: A group lets MAT patients attend but not share or take service roles. How does the session classify it?
options: Partially welcoming
Closed
Non-welcoming
Welcoming, since they are allowed to attend
items.explain: The session sorts groups as welcoming, partially welcoming or non-welcoming.

items.stem: A member on buprenorphine was told at a meeting he's "not really sober." What does the session suggest?
options: Argue with the member
Quit meetings, since they clearly don't support him
Look for an MAT-friendly group, and keep medication decisions with his doctor
Stop his medication
items.explain: Others' views are their recovery; find a supportive home group and let doctors guide medication.

items.stem: Kim attends meetings but sits in the back and leaves early. Jo arrives early, helps set up and shares. What does research the session cites predict?
options: Jo's active participation is linked to better outcomes
Neither benefits
Kim does better by staying private
Both do about equally well, since attendance is what counts
items.explain: Active participation, not mere attendance, is linked to better results.

items.stem: A new member wonders when to tell his group he's on methadone. What fits the session?
options: Lie if asked
Disclose when trust feels right, starting with a supportive sponsor
Announce it at the first meeting to get it out of the way
Never tell anyone
items.explain: Slow, chosen disclosure protects him while he builds trust.

items.stem: Weigh it: the only meeting near a member's halfway house is openly hostile to MAT. Should he keep attending?
items.explain: No single verdict. Meetings offer fellowship and structure, but repeated criticism may push him off his medication or out of recovery.
key_points: Attend: for fellowship, while keeping medication private
Seek others: online or treatment-program MAT-friendly meetings
Plan: calm responses that avoid anger and shame

lib-35.title: Chronic Pain and Opioids
summary: Chronic pain, like addiction, is a biopsychosocial process that unfolds over time; it's common and manageable, though rarely eliminated.
Untreated pain, stress and opioid tolerance can feed a pain-addiction cycle where relief turns into more pain.
Tell providers about pain and addiction history, including MAT; bring questions, notes and a support person.
Combined treatments (exercise, physical therapy, CBT, hypnosis, non-addictive medicines) beat any single one.
Opioids are sometimes appropriate, with an agreement, coordinated care on MAT, a flare plan and a plan for cravings.

items.stem: In your own words, how are chronic pain and addiction alike in this session?
items.explain: Both affect the nervous system, have genetic and environmental roots, change behavior, and unfold over time with ups and downs. Both are managed rather than cured in a single moment.

items.stem: How does the manual define chronic pain, and how does that compare with common clinical use today?
options: Pain lasting a week or more, the same as today's standard
Any pain at all
Over six months in the manual; many clinicians now use about three months
Only nerve pain
items.explain: Definitions vary; the manual uses six months, while many current guidelines use three.

items.stem: Over a year, Marco needs more pills for the same relief, and his pain seems worse between doses. What does the session describe?
options: Natural healing that makes him more sensitive to pain
Tolerance and withdrawal turning relief into more pain
Unrelated to medication
A sign he needs a stronger opioid
items.explain: Tolerance and dependence can feed a cycle where pain relief creates more pain.

items.stem: A company cuts costs each quarter with quick fixes that create bigger problems the next quarter. Which session concept has the same shape?
options: Combined treatment plans
Physical therapy
The pain-addiction cycle, where short-term relief deepens the problem
An opioid agreement
items.explain: Quick relief that worsens the underlying problem is the shared pattern.

items.stem: A member in recovery needs knee surgery and plans not to mention his history "so they'll treat my pain." What does the session advise?
options: Lie about his medications
Keep quiet, since disclosure means he'll be denied any pain medicine
Skip surgery
Share his addiction history and any MAT, since it changes how pain is treated safely
items.explain: Providers need the full picture, especially MAT, to plan safe pain care.

items.stem: Before a pain appointment, what does the session suggest bringing?
options: Written questions, notes and a family member or support person
Old pill bottles only
A request for a specific opioid
Nothing; the doctor will ask everything that matters
items.explain: Preparation helps build the plan together and remember what was said.

items.stem: Which is a non-drug pain treatment the session lists?
options: Short-acting opioids taken only at night
Alcohol in small amounts
Bed rest for months
Cognitive-behavioral therapy for pain
items.explain: CBT builds coping, relaxation, flare plans and problem solving for pain.

items.stem: Rosa uses physical therapy, a pain CBT group and an NSAID together. Tim relies on a single medication. What does the session predict?
options: Tim does better, since one strong treatment beats several weak ones
Rosa's combined approach is likely to work better
Both equal
Neither helps
items.explain: Several treatments combined tend to beat any single one.

items.stem: An orchestra sounds richer with strings, brass and percussion than with one loud instrument. How does that mirror the session's view of pain care?
options: Pain care is like music therapy only
One instrument played harder is the best approach
It's unrelated
Different treatments each cover part of the problem, together working better
items.explain: The session argues combined approaches beat any single one.

items.stem: Which is typically part of an opioid treatment agreement?
options: Drug screens, one pharmacy and refill limits
Freedom to use several doctors
No follow-up
Unlimited early refills so the patient never runs out
items.explain: Agreements set clear expectations between patient and provider.

items.stem: A member on buprenorphine has a painful injury. What does the session recommend?
options: Self-treat with street pills
Tough it out
Stop buprenorphine immediately so other opioids can work
Have the pain and addiction doctors coordinate, which may mean splitting doses
items.explain: Coordinated care keeps MAT in place while treating pain.

items.stem: Short-term opioids after surgery wake up a member's cravings. What does the session say to do?
options: Hide it
Keep quiet and finish the prescription, since stopping would look bad
Tell his provider and counselor, call his sponsor and attend meetings
Double the dose
items.explain: Being open about cravings lets the team adjust and support him.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member with severe chronic pain and a history of opioid addiction asks whether he should ever take opioids again. What should guide the decision?
items.explain: No single verdict. Opioids can be appropriate when benefits outweigh risks, but relapse risk is real and must be managed.
key_points: Consider: under an agreement, with MAT coordination and close monitoring
Avoid: if non-opioid options can control the pain
Plan: flares and cravings in writing, with supports involved

lib-36.title: Chronic Diseases
summary: Chronic diseases develop slowly, last long, have many causes, are rarely cured but can be managed; most are linked to four changeable habits.
The four risk behaviors: poor diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use and excessive alcohol.
Comorbid means two or more conditions in one person; each runs its own course and needs its own diagnosis and treatment plan.
Comorbid conditions can feed each other in a loop, and treating one with healthy habits often helps the other.
Living in balance means knowing both conditions, tracking symptoms, asking questions, eating well, moving, and using support groups, journals and apps.

items.stem: Which is a feature of chronic disease, per the session?
options: It develops slowly, lasts long and is managed rather than cured
It affects only older people
It always has one cause
It usually clears up on its own once stress goes down
items.explain: Chronic diseases are long-lasting, multi-causal and rarely curable, but manageable.

items.stem: Why does the session treat addiction like other chronic diseases such as diabetes?
options: Because both are caused by a single bad decision early in life
Both are cured by medication alone
Both are contagious
Both are long-lasting, have many causes, and are managed through ongoing care
items.explain: The chronic-disease frame fits addiction's long course and need for ongoing management.

items.stem: Which is one of the four changeable behaviors behind most chronic disease?
options: Age
Tobacco use
Air pollution
Genetic makeup
items.explain: Diet, activity, tobacco and alcohol are the four modifiable risk behaviors.

items.stem: Darnell quits cocaine, then also quits smoking, starts walking daily and eats better. What does the session predict beyond his recovery?
options: A lower risk of heart disease and other chronic illness
More cravings
Little change, since health problems are set by genes and age
Weight gain only
items.explain: Most common chronic diseases are largely preventable through these habits.

items.stem: In treatment settings, "co-occurring" usually means what?
options: Two addictions
Addiction plus a mental health disorder
A disease shared by a couple
Any two physical illnesses in one person, like diabetes and asthma
items.explain: Medicine uses "comorbid" for any two or more conditions; treatment settings often use "co-occurring" for addiction plus a mental disorder.

items.stem: Lena has diabetes and alcohol use disorder. Her blood sugar is stable this month, but cravings are strong. What does the session say?
options: Something is wrong with her diabetes care, since both conditions move together
Her diabetes caused the cravings
Both are fine
Each condition varies on its own timeline, so one can flare while the other is calm
items.explain: Comorbid disorders are independent, each with its own symptoms and course.

items.stem: A member says his addiction counselor "handles everything," including his heart condition. What does the session advise?
options: Each condition needs its own specialist care, like a primary care doctor for his heart
Ask the group
Agree, since one provider keeps care simple and avoids confusion
Skip the heart care
items.explain: Two conditions need two treatment plans and two care teams.

items.stem: Kevin neglects his heart care; he's tired, stressed, sleeps poorly and feels low. What does the session warn about his cocaine recovery?
options: It helps recovery
Fatigue, stress and low mood are classic triggers that raise relapse risk
It's unaffected, since heart care and addiction are separate problems
He'll be calmer
items.explain: Neglecting one condition can feed the other through triggers.

items.stem: Ecologists note that losing one predator can upset an entire food web. How does that resemble the session's view of comorbid conditions?
options: It means treat nothing
A change in one part of a system ripples into the others, for better or worse
It's only about animals
It shows that conditions never affect one another
items.explain: Comorbid conditions interact like parts of a system.

items.stem: In your own words, how can treating one condition help the other?
items.explain: Exercise, better eating and avoiding tobacco and alcohol lift energy, sleep, mood and thinking. Those gains lower triggers for use and support managing the chronic disease.

items.stem: Before a doctor's visit, a member wants to make the most of it. Which tool from the session fits best?
options: The Physician Question Worksheet, with questions on diagnosis, treatment and medications
A list of complaints about past doctors
Bring nothing, since the doctor will lead the visit and ask the right things
Ask a friend later
items.explain: Prepared questions help members understand and manage their conditions.

items.stem: What does the session suggest for a health journal?
options: A dedicated notebook and about fifteen minutes of writing daily
Writing only during crises
A long entry once a month so patterns stand out more clearly
Posting entries online
items.explain: Daily writing can help people understand and manage emotions about their conditions.

items.stem: Weigh it: a member with chronic pain and opioid use disorder can't afford both a specialist and his MAT program after release. Which should he prioritize?
items.explain: No single verdict. MAT protects against overdose and relapse, but untreated pain is itself a relapse risk.
key_points: MAT first: overdose risk after release is high
Pain care: unmanaged pain can drive use
Look for: integrated clinics, sliding-scale care or Medicaid coverage for both

lib-37.title: Older Adults
summary: Alcohol is the main substance problem for adults 60 and older, and prescription drug misuse is a growing risk.
For adults over 65, low-risk drinking means roughly a single daily drink and a cap of three on any occasion; medications make any drinking riskier.
Aging changes how the body handles drugs and alcohol; one doctor who sees every medication lowers risk.
Losses of a spouse, health, work, mobility and social circles can fuel problem drinking; retirement and free time can be risk factors.
Depression in later life is common and very treatable; meaning, relationships, activity and spiritual life support recovery.

items.stem: What is the low-risk drinking limit the session gives for adults over 65?
options: One drink a week
No limit if healthy
Roughly a single daily drink, with three as the most on any occasion
Up to two drinks a day and four at once, the same as for younger men
items.explain: Older adults process alcohol differently, so guidelines are lower.

items.stem: An older member meets five of the DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder. Which severity?
options: Severe
Mild
Moderate
Not a disorder
items.explain: Two or three criteria is mild, four or five moderate, six or more severe.

items.stem: At 72, Walt drinks the same two beers nightly he has for decades but now feels much more affected and has fallen twice. What does the session explain?
options: The beer got stronger
He's drinking more than he admits
Falls are unrelated
Aging changes how the body handles alcohol, so the same amount hits harder
items.explain: Aging bodies process alcohol and drugs differently, raising risk.

items.stem: Which counts as medication misuse, per the session?
options: Skipping doses or taking a medicine off schedule
Taking a medicine exactly as prescribed, even if it has side effects
Using a pill organizer
Asking a doctor about side effects
items.explain: Misuse includes taking too little, too much or not as directed.

items.stem: A member sees four doctors who don't talk to each other and takes nine medications. What does the session recommend?
options: Keep it as is, since specialists know their own areas best
Stop the medications that seem least important
Bring every bottle to one primary care doctor for review and allow the doctors to talk
Switch pharmacies
items.explain: One physician who knows every medication can catch dangerous combinations.

items.stem: An air traffic controller sees all planes in a sector at once, so none collide. How does that relate to the session's advice on medications?
options: Each pilot should fly alone
One doctor seeing every medication can spot risky combinations, like a controller seeing all planes
More controllers means safer skies
It doesn't, since medicine is too complex for one person
items.explain: A single overview prevents dangerous overlaps.

items.stem: Which is a warning sign of a substance problem in an older adult, per the session?
options: Taking walks
Starting a new hobby or volunteering more often
Memory lapses, falls, bruises and poor hygiene
Calling family often
items.explain: Many warning signs are easy to mistake for normal aging.

items.stem: Since his wife died a year ago, Ernesto drinks every evening alone and has stopped seeing friends. What does the session suggest?
options: It's unrelated
Loss of a spouse is linked to heavier drinking; grief and drinking both need attention
He's just lonely
Normal grief that will pass without any change in drinking
items.explain: Heavy drinking is more common after losing a partner.

items.stem: Rita retires suddenly with no hobbies or social plans. What does the session warn?
options: Better health
No change
Sudden free time can bring boredom, loneliness and problem drinking
Lower risk, since she no longer has work stress
items.explain: Unstructured time is itself a risk factor: about a third of older adults with alcohol problems are late-onset cases, drinking heavily only later in life.

items.stem: In your own words, what does the session say about depression in older adults?
items.explain: It's common, often missed, and very treatable. Substance use worsens memory, mood and sleep, so screening and treatment are important parts of recovery.

items.stem: An older member says feeling down is "just part of getting old." Best response?
options: Tell him to drink less and he'll be fine
Ignore it
Explain depression isn't a normal part of aging and is very treatable; suggest screening
Agree, since mood naturally declines with age
items.explain: Depression is treatable at any age; screening opens the door.

items.stem: A 68-year-old member says he has "nothing to do and no one to see." Which step fits the session?
options: Encourage him to rest, since he has earned a quiet retirement
Pick one activity from a menu, like a senior center or volunteering, and a first step like a call
Move in with family
Wait for an invitation
items.explain: Meaningful activity and social ties support recovery; small first steps overcome barriers.

items.stem: Weigh it: an older member lost his license after a DUI, which also cut him off from friends and church. Should his plan focus on transportation or on the drinking?
items.explain: No single verdict. Isolation is a relapse risk, but the drinking caused the loss and needs direct work.
key_points: Transport: senior rides and programs restore connection
Drinking: address the root so losses don't repeat
Both: a plan that rebuilds ties while treating the problem
